docs.title: 11.3. Installation and Execution
docs.text: The application is located in the [rdvmedecins2-symfony] folder, next to the [examples] folder. It is a standalone project, with its own [composer.json] and [.env] files, and its own [vendor] folder. The [README.md] file in the folder contains all of the following. The introduction to this document has already described the installation of [PHP] and [Composer]; we’ll expand on that here.

docs.title: 11.3.1. Required Software
docs.text:
Three software programs are all you need:

  • [PHP] 8.4 or later, with the extensions [pdo_mysql] and [intl] ([Symfony] 8 requires [PHP] 8.4, and the application uses features introduced in that version, such as [array_find]). Verify the installation in a terminal:
php -v
php -m

The second command lists the extensions: [pdo_mysql] and [intl] should be listed there;

  • [Composer], the library manager for [PHP] (see appendices);
  • a [MySQL] 8 server, for example, the one for [Laragon] under [Windows] (see appendices). [MariaDB] is also suitable.

The recommended editor is [Visual Studio Code], with the extensions [PHP Intelephense] and [Twig Language 2] (see appendices); however, everything can be done via the command line.

docs.title: 11.3.2. Install the libraries
docs.text:
The [vendor] folder is not provided: create it once and for all in a terminal window opened in the [rdvmedecins2-symfony] folder (you must be connected to the Internet):

composer install

[Composer] reads the file [composer.json] (discussed later), downloads [Symfony], [Doctrine], [Twig], [firebase/php-jwt], and the libraries they depend on, and generates the class loader [vendor/autoload.php], as well as the file [vendor/autoload_runtime.php] for the component [Runtime] (discussed below).

docs.title: 11.3.3. Create the database
docs.text:
The [dbrdvmedecins2] database is created by the [database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql] script. Using [Laragon], open the [HeidiSQL] tool (Database button), then run the script via the File / Run SQL menu. At the command line, in the application folder:

mysql -u root -p < database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql

The [-p] option prompts for the password for [root]; omit it if the account does not have a password (as is the case with [Laragon]). This is the same database as in other versions of the application: if it already exists, this step is optional. The script can be run at any time to revert to the original data.

docs.title: 11.3.4. Configure Database Access
docs.text: All installation configuration is contained in the file [.env] (discussed below). By default, the application connects to [MySQL] on [127.0.0.1], port 3306, using the user [root] without a password: these are the default settings for [Laragon]. If your [root] account has a password, enter it in this file, in the URL [DATABASE_URL] line, after [root:]. A system environment variable takes precedence over the file (example 25): this allows you to specify the database’s URL without writing it to a project file.

docs.title: 11.3.5. Launch the application
docs.text:
In a terminal window open to the [rdvmedecins2-symfony] folder:

php -S localhost:8081 -t public

[Sun Sep 27 18:40:12 2026] PHP 8.4.21 Development Server (http://localhost:8081) started

Next, open the URL [http://localhost:8081] in a browser, and stop the application using [Ctrl-C]. Port 8081 allows you to run a sample from the course (port 8000) at the same time. The command-line tool [symfony] (see appendices) provides a more comprehensive server that can also serve the application in HTTPS: [symfony server:start --port=8081].

docs.title: 11.3.6. Demo Accounts
docs.text:
The password for each account is its username; you must also enter the characters from the image, in uppercase or lowercase:

[admin]ADMIN (the administrator)[pelissier], [tatou], [dupont]DOCTOR (the doctors)[martin], [durand], [bistrou], [german]USER (patients)

A guide to exploring the app:

  • [admin]: Schedule, Ms. Marie PELISSIER; today: a time slot is already booked by Ms. Brigitte BISTROU. Book a slot for Mr. Jean MARTIN, then try to book a second appointment for him (declined). Doctors and Patients menus: add, edit, delete (Dr. PELISSIER, who has appointments, cannot be deleted);
  • [pelissier]: his daily schedule is displayed directly; the address [/doctors], entered manually, returns a 403 error page;
  • [martin]: My area, their appointment, the calendar where other patients appear as “Booked”; Manage my account;
  • login page: Create a patient account, then log in with the new account;
  • Buttons FR / EN: The entire interface changes languages, including dates.

docs.title: 11.3.7. Development Mode
docs.text:
The provided file [.env] configures the application for development ([APP_ENV=dev]):

  • The server console displays the log for [Symfony] (example 24): the selected route, security steps, and each SQL command sent to the database (example 28). For example, to display a calendar (abbreviated lines):
[info] Matched route "schedule".
[debug] Checking for authenticator support.
[debug] Checking support on authenticator.
[info] Authenticator successful!
[debug] Authenticator set no success response: request continues.
[info] Connecting with parameters [array]
[debug] Executing statement: SELECT d0_.id AS id_0, ..., u1_.login AS login_7, ... FROM doctors d0_ INNER JOIN users u1_ ON d0_.`user` = u1_.`id` WHERE d0_.id = ? (parameters: [array], types: [array])
[debug] Executing statement: SELECT a0_.id AS id_0, ... FROM appointments a0_ INNER JOIN clients c1_ ON a0_.client_id = c1_.id INNER JOIN slots s2_ ON a0_.slot_id = s2_.id WHERE a0_.day = ? AND s2_.doctor_id = ? (parameters: [array], types: [array])
[debug] Executing statement: SELECT s0_.id AS id_0, ... FROM slots s0_ WHERE s0_.doctor_id = ? ORDER BY s0_.start_hour ASC, s0_.start_minute ASC (parameters: [array], types: [array])
127.0.0.1:55220 [200]: GET /schedule?doctorId=1&day=2026-09-27
[info] Disconnecting

Here we can see the routing, the authenticator, and then three requests: the doctor and their account, today’s appointments and their patients, and the doctor’s available time slots. The list of doctors in the drop-down menu, however, is not read; it comes from the cache (discussed later);

  • an unexpected exception displays the [Symfony] debug page (example 03), with the exception message and the call stack. In production, the application displays its own 500 error page instead;
  • there is nothing to restart after a change: each request re-reads the [PHP] files (example 01), and, in [dev] mode, [Symfony] rebuilds its own cache (the container, routes, and compiled views) when a file has changed.

The [Xdebug] debugger also allows you to step through the application from [Visual Studio Code] ([PHP Debug] extension): This is an extension of [PHP], which must be installed separately (see xdebug.org). The debug bar in [Symfony] ([WebProfilerBundle], [composer require --dev symfony/web-profiler-bundle]) displays the query details at the bottom of each page: the route, the user, the SQL commands and their parameters, translations, execution times...

docs.title: 11.3.8. A production server
docs.text:
The [PHP] development server is not intended for production. In production, the application is served by a web server ([nginx], [Apache]), which forwards requests to [PHP-FPM], a process manager ([PHP]). The site root is the [public] folder: only its files are accessible from the browser; the [var] folder must be writable by the server. In the [.env] file, you must specify production mode, change the secret keys, and declare that the site is served from HTTPS:

APP_ENV=prod
APP_SECRET=<a long random string>
JWT_SECRET=<another long random string>
COOKIE_SECURE=1

A suitable random string can be obtained from [PHP] itself: [php -r "echo bin2hex(random_bytes(32));"]. The application is then prepared using two commands:

composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader
php bin/console cache:clear

The second command generates the production cache (the compiled container, routes, compiled views, etc.): in [prod] mode, [Symfony] no longer checks whether the files have changed, which is faster; therefore, it must be rerun after every modification. The [composer dump-env prod] command also converts the [.env] file into a [PHP] ([.env.local.php]) file, which is read more quickly.

docs.title: 11.3.9. Common Issues
docs.text:
A [PHP] application does not “start”: each request rebuilds the application (example 01). An inaccessible database therefore does not prevent the server from starting: the error appears on the first page that queries the database (the login page does not query the database; the connection process does). In [dev] mode, the error is displayed on the [Symfony] debug page; in all cases, it is logged in the log file, which the development server displays in the console. For example, with a database that does not exist:

[critical] Uncaught PHP Exception Doctrine\DBAL\Exception\ConnectionException: "An exception occurred in the driver: SQLSTATE[HY000] [1049] Unknown database 'dbunknown'" at ExceptionConverter.php line 91

The most common messages:

[Failed opening required '.../vendor/autoload_runtime.php']The command [composer install] was not executed[Your Composer dependencies require a PHP version ">= 8.4.0"]The version of [PHP] is older than 8.4[could not find driver]The extension [pdo_mysql] for [PHP] is not enabled (file [php.ini], or menu PHP / Extensions menu in [Laragon])[SQLSTATE[HY000] [2002] Connection refused][MySQL] has not started, or is not listening on [127.0.0.1:3306][SQLSTATE[HY000] [1045] Access denied for user 'root'@'localhost']The password for [MySQL] must be entered in [DATABASE_URL] (see “Configuring Database Access”)[SQLSTATE[HY000] [1049] Unknown database 'dbrdvmedecins2']The script [database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql] was not executed[JWT_SECRET must be at least 32 characters long (see .env).]The secret key for the tokens is too short in [.env][Failed to listen on localhost:8081 (reason: Address already in use)]Port 8081 is already in use (is another version of the application running?): stop it, or choose a different port

docs.title: 11.4. Application Architecture
docs.text:
• The browser sends its requests to the server ([php -S], or [nginx] + [PHP-FPM]), which forwards them to [Symfony] via the file [public/index.php]. The core of [Symfony] publishes events related to request processing (see the chapter on the lifecycle), to which listeners respond: the request language ([SetLanguage]), routing, the session, and then the security component’s firewall: The user is identified based on the JWT token from their cookie ([TokenAuthenticator]), and the [access_control] rules deny access to protected pages for visitors who are not authorized. Errors result in pages HTML ([ErrorPage]);
  • [Controller]: the web layer controllers. They all pass through a single object, [ApplicationModel] (folder [Web]), which caches the lists of doctors and clients and forwards other requests to the business layer; [Form]: forms and their constraints; [Views]: view templates;
  • [Security]: tokens, JWT, the authenticator, the CAPTCHA, the attempt limit, and the account creation pass;
  • [Web]: What controllers have in common: the cache and the facade [ApplicationModel], the parent class of controllers, flash messages, and a few utilities;
  • [Business]: business rules and transactions;
  • [Dao]: the DAO layer, one class per table;
  • [Entity]: the entities [Doctrine], which the DAO layer reads from and writes to the database; [Domain]: the calendar objects, calculated by the business layer;
  • [templates]: the [Twig] views, which generate the HTML pages; [translations]: the dictionaries; [public]: the stylesheet, the page script, and [Bootstrap];
  • the [config] folder and the [.env] file: the configuration, which brings everything together.

Two differences from the examples: the application has its own [vendor] folder (the examples shared the one in the [examples] folder), and its entry point uses the [Runtime] component from [Symfony] (discussed later). The application’s classes are organized in the [src] folder, according to the PSR-4 rule (example 01): the [App\Business\BusinessService] class is in the [src/Business/BusinessService.php] file. [Symfony] does not require any of these files: [Controller], [Entity], [EventListener], [Form] and [Twig] are the ones in use (the ones used by [MakerBundle]), while the others ([Dao], [Business], [Security]...) are part of the layered architecture in Example 28. [Bootstrap] is part of the application (folder [public/lib/bootstrap]) this time: the case study is self-contained.

docs.title: 11.5. The database
docs.text:
The [dbrdvmedecins2] database has five tables:

  • [users]: users authorized to log in;
  • [doctors] and [clients]: doctors and patients, each linked to their user account;
  • [slots]: each doctor’s available time slots;
  • [appointments]: appointments, one client per time slot on a given day.

docs.title: 11.5.1. database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql
docs.text:
-- =========================================================================
-- Database [dbrdvmedecins2] - MySQL 8
--
-- Evolution of [dbrdvmedecins]:
--   1. the [doctors] and [clients] tables get a [user] column,
--      foreign key to users(id): every doctor and every client is
--      now also a user able to log in;
--   2. a third role appears: DOCTOR (in addition to ADMIN and USER);
--   3. the script creates a [users] row for each doctor (role DOCTOR)
--      and for each client (role USER):
--        - login        = last name in lower case
--        - password     = last name in lower case, hashed with bcrypt (10 rounds)
--        - display name = first name + last name
--
--   4. uniqueness constraints, all NAMED (the application recognizes
--      the name of the violated constraint in the MySQL error message):
--        - unq_users_login                   : a login belongs to one account only;
--        - unq_doctors_first_name_last_name  : two doctors cannot have the
--                                              same first and last names;
--        - unq_clients_first_name_last_name  : same for the clients.
--      Beware: the utf8mb4_unicode_ci collation compares regardless of
--      case and accents - "Hélène DUPONT" and "helene dupont"
--      are therefore considered identical.
--
-- The [users] table must now be created BEFORE [doctors] and [clients]
-- (they reference it), and dropped AFTER them.
-- =========================================================================

-- the script is written in UTF-8
SET NAMES utf8mb4;

-- we start again from an empty database on each run of the script (handy in development)
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS dbrdvmedecins2 CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE dbrdvmedecins2;

-- drop order: from the "child" tables to the "parent" tables
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS appointments;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS slots;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS clients;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS doctors;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users;

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [users]: the users allowed to log in to the application
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE users (
  id       INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version  INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  login    VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,                 -- login identifier
  password VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,                -- HASHED password (bcrypt) - never in clear
  name     VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,                 -- name displayed once logged in
  role     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,                 -- 'ADMIN', 'DOCTOR' or 'USER'
  -- a login can belong to one account only
  CONSTRAINT unq_users_login UNIQUE (login)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [doctors]: the doctors of the practice
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE doctors (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,   -- primary key (technical identifier)
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,            -- row version number (optimistic lock)
  title      VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,              -- Melle, Mme, Mr
  last_name  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  first_name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  `user`     INT NOT NULL,                      -- foreign key -> users(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_doctors_user FOREIGN KEY (`user`) REFERENCES users(id),
  -- one account per doctor, and one doctor per account
  CONSTRAINT unq_doctors_user UNIQUE (`user`),
  -- two doctors cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_doctors_first_name_last_name UNIQUE (first_name, last_name)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [clients]: the doctors' patients
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE clients (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  title      VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,
  last_name  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  first_name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  `user`     INT NOT NULL,                      -- foreign key -> users(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_clients_user FOREIGN KEY (`user`) REFERENCES users(id),
  -- one account per client, and one client per account
  CONSTRAINT unq_clients_user UNIQUE (`user`),
  -- two clients cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_clients_first_name_last_name UNIQUE (first_name, last_name)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [slots]: the time slots of each doctor
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE slots (
  id           INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version      INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  doctor_id    INT NOT NULL,                     -- foreign key -> doctors(id)
  start_hour   INT NOT NULL,                     -- start hour of the slot
  start_minute INT NOT NULL,                     -- start minute of the slot
  end_hour     INT NOT NULL,                     -- end hour of the slot
  end_minute   INT NOT NULL,                     -- end minute of the slot
  CONSTRAINT fk_slots_doctor FOREIGN KEY (doctor_id) REFERENCES doctors(id)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [appointments]: the appointments booked by the clients
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE appointments (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  day        DATE NOT NULL,                      -- day of the appointment
  slot_id    INT NOT NULL,                       -- foreign key -> slots(id)
  client_id  INT NOT NULL,                       -- foreign key -> clients(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_appointments_slot   FOREIGN KEY (slot_id)   REFERENCES slots(id),
  CONSTRAINT fk_appointments_client FOREIGN KEY (client_id) REFERENCES clients(id),
  -- the same slot, on the same day, can be booked only once
  CONSTRAINT unq1_appointments UNIQUE (day, slot_id)
);

-- =========================================================================
-- Demo data
-- =========================================================================

-- the users: passwords hashed with bcrypt (10 salt rounds)
--   admin/admin (ADMIN)
--   one DOCTOR account per doctor, one USER account per client
--   (the user/user demo account is gone: a USER account is
--   now ALWAYS a client's account, who can book and manage the account)
--   (login = password = last name in lower case)
INSERT INTO users (login, password, name, role) VALUES
  ('admin',     '$2b$10$YSNBJXXHX9mp13nPZb6YGu8M1jR6uvPwO1s2X73z0QAqBR7TOQjoq', 'Administrator',    'ADMIN'),
  -- doctors
  ('pelissier', '$2b$10$DnSDOK5ONrdMxTTr1NKCHOphR3WSp5QAyG9S9ueruw9HwlxI.16ba', 'Marie PELISSIER',  'DOCTOR'),
  ('tatou',     '$2b$10$PeovBO.gmJUKP4PglI/fwu4xtWOYSxoM5VTWjTj7uQ4wcd9P9.htS', 'Paul TATOU',       'DOCTOR'),
  ('dupont',    '$2b$10$az7wvPKC1h0EiAxXwu/PU.vYjzmB04rd5B7QnK0mvxp4niYIHVoc.', 'Sophie DUPONT',    'DOCTOR'),
  -- clients
  ('martin',    '$2b$10$GT6S5pp.WdGapFw/UmocXesbC6LEjJfZzgatCUyG9Sf4o1iBNlqZW', 'Jean MARTIN',      'USER'),
  ('durand',    '$2b$10$l2gl/zCder8E7Nh4VxGRX.0.SsO3FDiXt6YwqYq3v9nFzgC/jQCy6', 'Alice DURAND',     'USER'),
  ('bistrou',   '$2b$10$naeRp2YUU6c.QDl5itJMAum3Y5aHdUV6jwIcsbp0D.64jPG4F6E9m', 'Brigitte BISTROU', 'USER'),
  ('german',    '$2b$10$tTWxh3ROWF7NjhZOMnWDMOsZcnSWUiwwfy5C3G0.xhccTXALKyLeW', 'Luc GERMAN',       'USER');

-- the doctors: the [user] column is looked up from the login,
-- rather than assuming the values of the primary keys of [users]
INSERT INTO doctors (title, last_name, first_name, `user`) VALUES
  ('Mme',  'PELISSIER', 'Marie',  (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'pelissier')),
  ('Mr',   'TATOU',     'Paul',   (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'tatou')),
  ('Melle','DUPONT',    'Sophie', (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'dupont'));

INSERT INTO clients (title, last_name, first_name, `user`) VALUES
  ('Mr',   'MARTIN',  'Jean',     (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'martin')),
  ('Mme',  'DURAND',  'Alice',    (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'durand')),
  ('Melle','BISTROU', 'Brigitte', (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'bistrou')),
  ('Mr',   'GERMAN',  'Luc',      (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'german'));

-- slots of doctor PELISSIER (doctor_id = 1): from 8:00 to 12:00 in 20-minute steps
INSERT INTO slots (doctor_id, start_hour, start_minute, end_hour, end_minute) VALUES
  (1, 8, 0, 8, 20), (1, 8, 20, 8, 40), (1, 8, 40, 9, 0),
  (1, 9, 0, 9, 20), (1, 9, 20, 9, 40), (1, 9, 40, 10, 0),
  (1, 10, 0, 10, 20), (1, 10, 20, 10, 40), (1, 10, 40, 11, 0),
  (1, 11, 0, 11, 20), (1, 11, 20, 11, 40), (1, 11, 40, 12, 0);

-- slots of doctor TATOU (doctor_id = 2): from 14:00 to 18:00 in 20-minute steps
INSERT INTO slots (doctor_id, start_hour, start_minute, end_hour, end_minute) VALUES
  (2, 14, 0, 14, 20), (2, 14, 20, 14, 40), (2, 14, 40, 15, 0),
  (2, 15, 0, 15, 20), (2, 15, 20, 15, 40), (2, 15, 40, 16, 0),
  (2, 16, 0, 16, 20), (2, 16, 20, 16, 40), (2, 16, 40, 17, 0),
  (2, 17, 0, 17, 20), (2, 17, 20, 17, 40), (2, 17, 40, 18, 0);

-- an appointment already booked, to see an occupied slot right away in the schedule
INSERT INTO appointments (day, slot_id, client_id) VALUES
  (CURDATE(), 2, 3);
  • line 33: the database is created if it does not exist, with the character set [utf8mb4] and the collation [utf8mb4_unicode_ci], which compares strings without regard to uppercase letters or accents (example 28);
  • lines 37–41: the tables are dropped and then recreated; the script restores the database to its initial state. The order matters: a table cannot be dropped as long as another table references it via a foreign key;
  • Lines 46–55: Users: a username and a password hashed with [bcrypt] (example 25), the display name after logging in, and the role ([ADMIN], [DOCTOR], or [USER]). The constraint [unq_users_login] ensures that a username belongs to only one account;
  • Lines 60–72: Each table has a primary key [id], generated by the database, and a column [version], which is the optimistic lock (Example 28). The column [user] is a foreign key referencing [users(id)]: the database rejects any value that is not the ID of an existing user. Since [user] is a word in the SQL language, it is surrounded by grave accents. Three constraints: [fk_doctors_user] (the foreign key), [unq_doctors_user] (one account per doctor, and one doctor per account), and [unq_doctors_first_name_last_name] (no homonyms). All constraints are named: the application recognizes a violated constraint by its name;
  • lines 77–89: the [clients] table has exactly the same columns;
  • lines 94–103: a time slot belongs to a doctor; its start and end times are stored in hours and minutes;
  • lines 108–118: an appointment consists of a day (type [DATE], without a time), a time slot, and a client. The constraint [unq1_appointments] prevents the same time slot from being booked twice on the same day: the database enforces this rule, even if two users attempt to book it at the same time;
  • lines 130–140: demo users, whose password is their login. The hashes begin with [$2b$10$]: the algorithm ([bcrypt], variant [2b]) and the cost (10). Next come the salt and the hash. These hashes were calculated by the [Flask] version of the application; [PHP] writes its own with the prefix [$2y$], but verifies both equally well;
  • lines 144–147: the [user] column for each doctor is retrieved via a subquery based on the login, rather than by assuming the values of the primary keys;
  • lines 170–171: an appointment already scheduled for today ([CURDATE()]) in Dr. PELISSIER’s second time slot for Ms. BISTROU: the calendar thus immediately shows a booked time slot.

Unlike in the case of [Symfony], the database is not created by [Doctrine] from the entities, nor through migrations (example 28): it is shared with the other versions of the application, and the script SQL is common to all of them. The command [php bin/console doctrine:schema:validate] verifies that the entity descriptions are consistent and that they correspond to the database tables.

docs.title: 11.6.1. composer.json
docs.text:
{
    "name": "rdvmedecins/rdvmedecins2-symfony",
    "description": "RdvMedecins: booking medical appointments, HTML pages built by the server (Symfony + Twig + Doctrine)",
    "type": "project",
    "license": "MIT",
    "require": {
        "php": ">=8.4",
        "ext-intl": "*",
        "ext-pdo_mysql": "*",
        "doctrine/doctrine-bundle": "^3.3",
        "doctrine/orm": "^3.7",
        "firebase/php-jwt": "^7.2",
        "symfony/asset": "^8.1",
        "symfony/console": "^8.1",
        "symfony/dotenv": "^8.1",
        "symfony/form": "^8.1",
        "symfony/framework-bundle": "^8.1",
        "symfony/lock": "^8.1",
        "symfony/rate-limiter": "^8.1",
        "symfony/runtime": "^8.1",
        "symfony/security-bundle": "^8.1",
        "symfony/translation": "^8.1",
        "symfony/twig-bundle": "^8.1",
        "symfony/validator": "^8.1",
        "symfony/yaml": "^8.1",
        "twig/twig": "^3.30"
    },
    "autoload": {
        "psr-4": {
            "App\\": "src/"
        }
    },
    "config": {
        "allow-plugins": {
            "symfony/runtime": true
        },
        "optimize-autoloader": true,
        "sort-packages": true
    },
    "minimum-stability": "stable",
    "prefer-stable": true
}
  • Lines 6–27: the libraries required by the application and the constraints they must meet. [^8.1] reads “version 8.1 or a newer version of the same major version 8”: [Composer] accepts versions that fix bugs or add features, but not those that could break the application (version 9). The lines [php], [ext-intl], and [ext-pdo_mysql] do not refer to libraries, but to environment requirements: [Composer] will refuse installation if the version of [PHP] or its extensions are incompatible, rather than allowing the application to fail later. [Symfony] is not a single library: each of its components (routing, forms, security, etc.) is a library, and the application requests only those it needs; [Composer] additionally installs the libraries on which they depend;
  • Lines 28–32: The application’s PSR-4 rule: classes in the [App] namespace are located in the [src] folder (Example 01: In the examples, the file [public/index.php] itself declared this rule to the class loader via [addPsr4]);
  • Lines 34–36: The component [Runtime] is a plugin (plugin) for [Composer]; it runs during installation to write the file [vendor/autoload_runtime.php]. [Composer] requests permission to execute a plugin’s code; this permission is granted here.

[composer install] installs the versions that meet these constraints and records the exact versions installed in a file named [composer.lock]. Subsequent installations (on another machine, for example) use this file: they install exactly the same versions. [composer update], on the other hand, searches for the most recent versions permitted by [composer.json] and updates [composer.lock]. The command [composer show] lists what is installed in the [vendor] folder. In a typical project, this file is supplemented by [Symfony Flex] for each [composer require] (example 01).

docs.title: 11.6.2. .env
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# .env: the settings specific to THIS installation, read at the start of each
# request by the Dotenv component (see public/index.php). They become
# environment variables, which the configuration (config folder) reads through
# %env(NAME)%. A real system environment variable takes precedence over this file.
# =========================================================================

# dev: development; prod: production (see README.md)
APP_ENV=dev
# Symfony's secret key (anti-CSRF tokens, signatures...). In production:
# another value, long and random
APP_SECRET=34b2364cc4c93df6e4ee35251a048088

# ---- the MySQL database [dbrdvmedecins2] (script: database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql):
# the DBMS, the user and their password (those of Laragon: root, without
# password), the server, its port, the database, then the server version (for MariaDB:
# serverVersion=10.11.2-MariaDB, for example) and the character set
DATABASE_URL="mysql://root:@127.0.0.1:3306/dbrdvmedecins2?serverVersion=8.0.32&charset=utf8mb4"

# ---- authentication (see src/Security/AuthService.php)
# secret key of the JWT tokens: at least 32 characters (HMAC-SHA256)
JWT_SECRET=ef1cfc9709f10b5b5d183b4deb6d5dbbe69518629c3b12a8
# validity duration of a token, in minutes (120 min = 2 h)
JWT_DURATION_MINUTES=120
# 1 in production (site served over HTTPS): cookies never travel unencrypted
COOKIE_SECURE=0

# ---- protection against robots (see src/Security/AttemptLimiter.php)
# login failures allowed for the same login from the same IP address, then
# block for this duration (in minutes); an IP address is also blocked if it
# accumulates LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES_IP failures, all logins together (a robot trying
# thousands of different logins)
LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES=5
LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES_IP=25
LOGIN_BLOCK_MINUTES=15
# client accounts created at most per hour and per IP address. In a classroom, all
# the computers often go out through the same address: increase if needed
REGISTRATION_MAX_PER_HOUR=10

The file containing settings specific to this installation (example 25): these vary from one machine to another (the database, its credentials) or are confidential (the keys). In a real project, production secrets are not included here: they are provided by actual environment variables, by a [.env.local] file that is never published, or by the [Symfony] secrets vault (example 25).

  • line 9: the application mode: [dev] (development: debug mode, debug page, cache rebuilt with every change) or [prod];
  • line 12: the secret key for [Symfony], which is used in particular for anti-CSRF tokens (example 21);
  • line 18: the database connection (example 28);
  • lines 20–38: application-specific settings: the JWT tokens (example 25) and bot protection (example 27).

docs.title: 11.6.3. config/bundles.php and config/packages/framework.yaml
docs.text:
<?php
// config/bundles.php: the bundles of the application (see example 01): the core of
// Symfony, the Twig views, security, and Doctrine (database access)
return [
    Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\FrameworkBundle::class => ['all' => true],
    Symfony\Bundle\TwigBundle\TwigBundle::class => ['all' => true],
    Symfony\Bundle\SecurityBundle\SecurityBundle::class => ['all' => true],
    Doctrine\Bundle\DoctrineBundle\DoctrineBundle::class => ['all' => true],
];

The application’s four bundles: the core [Symfony], [Twig] (Example 13), security (Example 25), and [Doctrine] (Example 28).

# =========================================================================
# config/packages/framework.yaml: the configuration of the FrameworkBundle
# =========================================================================
framework:
    secret: '%env(APP_SECRET)%'

    # ---- the languages (see example 22): English by default, French; the
    # translation service and its dictionaries (translations folder)
    default_locale: en
    enabled_locales: ['en', 'fr']
    translator:
        default_path: '%kernel.project_dir%/translations'
        fallbacks: ['en']

    # ---- form validation: its messages are KEYS of our
    # dictionaries (ERRORS.FIRSTNAME_REQUIRED...), translated in the domain
    # [messages], the same as that of the views (by default: the [validators] domain)
    validation:
        translation_domain: messages

    # ---- the SESSION (flash messages, anti-CSRF tokens): files of the folder
    # var/sessions. The session cookie is never readable by the JavaScript of
    # the page (httponly), nor sent with a POST request coming from another site
    # (samesite lax), nor, in production, sent unencrypted (secure)
    session:
        handler_id: null
        save_path: '%kernel.project_dir%/var/sessions/%kernel.environment%'
        name: rdvmedecins_session
        cookie_httponly: true
        cookie_samesite: lax
        cookie_secure: '%env(bool:COOKIE_SECURE)%'
    csrf_protection: true

    # ---- the locks (see example 20), for the attempt limiters
    lock: 'flock://%kernel.project_dir%/var/lock'

    # ---- the attempt LIMITERS (see example 27 and src/Security/AttemptLimiter.php).
    # fixed_window: at most [limit] attempts per period [interval], counted
    # from the first attempt
    rate_limiter:
        # the login failures of a login, from an IP address
        login:
            policy: fixed_window
            limit: '%env(int:LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES)%'
            interval: '%env(LOGIN_BLOCK_MINUTES)% minutes'
        # the login failures of an IP address, all logins together
        login_ip:
            policy: fixed_window
            limit: '%env(int:LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES_IP)%'
            interval: '%env(LOGIN_BLOCK_MINUTES)% minutes'
        # the accounts created from an IP address, per hour
        registration:
            policy: fixed_window
            limit: '%env(int:REGISTRATION_MAX_PER_HOUR)%'
            interval: '1 hour'
  • lines 9–13: languages and the translator (Example 22);
  • lines 18–19: the validation component translates its messages into the [validators] domain (example 09); Our constraints use keys from our dictionaries ([ERRORS.FIRSTNAME_REQUIRED]...) as message keys, which are in the [messages] domain: we specify this to the validation component. Thus, a single dictionary per language is sufficient for the entire application;
  • Lines 25–32: the session (example 20): files in the [var/sessions] folder. The application stores very little there: flash messages and anti-CSRF tokens. The session cookie is named [rdvmedecins_session]; it is never readable by the [JavaScript] on the page, nor is it sent with a POST request from another site, nor, in production, sent in plain text (the prefix [bool:] converts the variable to a Boolean, example 25);
  • line 35: the locks (example 20), used by the attempt limiters and the CAPTCHA service;
  • lines 40–55: the three anti-bot limiters (example 27), whose settings come from the file [.env]. A value may combine text and a variable: ['%env(LOGIN_BLOCK_MINUTES)% minutes'].

The application cache (the [cache.app] service, Example 20) does not need to be configured: it is stored in files within the [var/cache/dev/pools] (or [prod]) folder. The application stores lists of doctors and clients, CAPTCHAs, attempt counters, and passes there—all of which must be shared across all requests. With multiple servers, you would choose a shared cache, such as [Redis] ([framework.cache.app: cache.adapter.redis]).

docs.title: 11.6.4. config/packages/security.yaml
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# config/packages/security.yaml: security (see examples 25 and 26)
# =========================================================================
security:
    # the hashing of the accounts' passwords: bcrypt, 10 rounds, like the
    # hashes of the SQL script. PHP also verifies the $2b$ (Python) and $2a$
    # (Java) hashes of the other versions of the application, which share the same database
    password_hashers:
        App\Entity\User:
            algorithm: bcrypt
            cost: 10

    # the user provider: irrelevant here, the logged-in user is
    # described by their token (see src/Security/TokenAuthenticator.php); Symfony
    # nevertheless requires one: an empty list
    providers:
        none:
            memory: ~

    firewalls:
        # ONE firewall for the whole application, STATELESS: the user is not
        # stored in the session, they are found again on each request from the
        # JWT token of their cookie
        main:
            stateless: true
            provider: none
            custom_authenticators:
                - App\Security\TokenAuthenticator

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # THE ACCESS RULE: the rules are examined in order, the first one whose
    # pattern (path) matches the path of the URL applies:
    #   - a few PUBLIC URLs (PUBLIC_ACCESS): the home page, the login, the
    #     choice of the language, the creation of an account;
    #   - URLs reserved to certain roles (a list of roles: ONE of them is enough);
    #   - all the OTHERS require an authenticated user (last rule).
    # It is the rule "everything is forbidden except what is allowed": a URL added
    # later, and that one would have forgotten to protect, is protected by default.
    # A refused anonymous visitor is sent to the login page (the entry
    # point of the firewall); an authenticated user without the requested role
    # receives a 403 error page.
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    access_control:
        - { path: ^/$, roles: PUBLIC_ACCESS }
        - { path: ^/(login|logout)$, roles: PUBLIC_ACCESS }
        - { path: ^/language/, roles: PUBLIC_ACCESS }
        - { path: ^/register, roles: PUBLIC_ACCESS }
        # a patient cancels THEIR appointment from "My area", not from the schedule
        - { path: ^/schedule/cancel$, roles: [ROLE_ADMIN, ROLE_DOCTOR] }
        - { path: ^/(doctors|clients), roles: ROLE_ADMIN }
        - { path: ^/my-, roles: ROLE_USER }
        - { path: ^/, roles: IS_AUTHENTICATED }

Security configuration (examples 25 and 26):

  • Lines 8–11: Password hashing: [bcrypt], 10 rounds, like the hashes in the script SQL. To verify a password, [PHP] reads the algorithm and cost from the hash itself: the hashes in the database, written by [Python] ([$2b$]) or by [Java] ([$2a$]), are verified just as much as those of [PHP] ([$2y$]);
  • lines 16–18: the user provider. The application authenticator does not need one: the logged-in user is identified by their token, without reading the database (example 25). But the security component requires one: a provider [memory], with no users;
  • lines 24–28: a single, stateless firewall for the entire application, with our authenticator. No pattern ([pattern]): it covers all URL. The files in the [public] folder ([Bootstrap], the stylesheet, the script) do not pass through [Symfony]: the web server serves them directly;
  • Lines 43–52: the application’s access rule. The [access_control] rules are evaluated in order, and the first one whose pattern matches the path of URL is applied. [PUBLIC_ACCESS] grants access to URL to everyone, including anonymous visitors: the home page, login, language selection, and account creation. Next come the URL rules reserved for certain roles: a list of roles (line 49) means that any one of them is sufficient. The last rule, [^/], applies to all remaining URL rules and requires an authenticated user. This is the “everything is prohibited except what is permitted” rule: a URL added later—even if you forgot to protect it—is automatically protected. The opposite error—a public URL that was accidentally left unprotected—is immediately apparent; the error of a forgotten protected page is much less so.

Roles are verified here, in a single file, using URL patterns, rather than [#[IsGranted]] attributes on actions (example 26): both are possible and can be combined.

docs.title: 11.6.5. config/packages/doctrine.yaml, twig.yaml, config/routes.yaml
docs.text:
# config/packages/doctrine.yaml: Doctrine, database access (see example 28)
doctrine:
    # the connection: the DATABASE_URL of the .env file. In debug mode, each SQL
    # statement is written to the log, which the development server displays
    dbal:
        url: '%env(resolve:DATABASE_URL)%'
    # the ENTITIES: the classes of the src/Entity folder, described by PHP attributes
    orm:
        mappings:
            App:
                type: attribute
                dir: '%kernel.project_dir%/src/Entity'
                prefix: 'App\Entity'

The configuration for [Doctrine] is the one shown in Example 28.

# config/packages/twig.yaml: the Twig views (templates folder)
twig:
    default_path: '%kernel.project_dir%/templates'
    # the forms are drawn with the Bootstrap 5 classes (see example 18)
    form_themes: ['bootstrap_5_layout.html.twig']

The form fields are drawn using the classes from [Bootstrap] 5 (Example 18).

# config/routes.yaml: the routes are described by the #[Route] attributes of the
# controllers of the src/Controller folder (see example 01)
controllers:
    resource: routing.controllers

The routes are described by the [#[Route]] attributes of the controllers (Example 01). The [php bin/console debug:router] command lists them all (see below, the web layer).

docs.title: 11.7.1. public/index.php and bin/console
docs.text:
<?php
// public/index.php: the entry point of ALL the HTTP requests. The folder
// [public] is the root of the site: only its files are accessible from the
// browser (Bootstrap, style sheet, script), never the code of the application.
//
// The file vendor/autoload_runtime.php is written by Symfony's Runtime component
// (the symfony/runtime library): it loads the classes, reads the file
// .env, enables the debug mode, then calls the function below, which returns the
// kernel of the application; it finally makes it handle the current request, sends the
// response, and ends the request (see the index.php file of the examples)

use App\Kernel;

require_once dirname(__DIR__).'/vendor/autoload_runtime.php';

return function (array $context) {
    return new Kernel($context['APP_ENV'], (bool) $context['APP_DEBUG']);
};

The entry point for the examples (Example 01) loaded the classes, read the file [.env], enabled debug mode, created the core, had it process the request, sent the response, and terminated the request. All of this is handled here by the [Runtime] component of [Symfony] (line 14): this is the form of the [public/index.php] file in a standard [Symfony] application.

  • Line 14: The file [vendor/autoload_runtime.php], written by [Composer] (see [composer.json]), loads the class loader, then executes the script that included it, in this case, [public/index.php], to obtain its return value: an included [PHP] file can return a value ([return]), just like a function;
  • Lines 16–18: This value is an anonymous function that receives the application context (the environment variables, read from [.env] by the [Runtime] component) and returns the core. The [Runtime] component handles the rest: the [Request], [handle], [send], and [terminate] objects.

The advantage of this approach is that the same [index.php] works with servers other than [PHP-FPM]. With the worker mode of [FrankenPHP] (see the section on scopes), for example, a different “runtime” keeps the kernel in memory and has it process requests sequentially, without this file changing. The file [bin/console] has the same structure: its function handles the execution of commands, built around the kernel.

docs.title: 11.7.2. src/Kernel.php and config/services.yaml
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Kernel.php: the kernel of the application (see example 01)

namespace App;

use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Kernel\MicroKernelTrait;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Kernel as BaseKernel;

class Kernel extends BaseKernel
{
    use MicroKernelTrait;

    public function boot(): void
    {
        parent::boot();
        // the time zone: that of the medical practice. It sets today's date (no
        // appointment in the past, see src/Business/Dates.php)
        date_default_timezone_set('Europe/Paris');
    }
}

The core of the examples (Example 01), with one additional method:

  • lines 13–19: [boot] is called when the kernel starts up, for each request. It sets the time zone for [PHP]. By default, [PHP] operates in the time zone specified in its configuration ([date.timezone], in the file [php.ini]), which is often Coordinated Universal Time (UTC); however, the current date is used for a business rule: no appointments in the past. In Paris, between midnight and 2:00 a.m. in the summer, the day UTC is still the previous day: the firm’s time zone takes precedence.
# =========================================================================
# config/services.yaml: the SERVICES of the application (see example 06). All the
# classes of the src/ folder are declared to the container, which creates them on demand and
# gives each one the objects it needs (dependency injection): a
# controller receives the ApplicationModel, which receives the business layer, which receives the
# DAOs, which receive Doctrine's entity manager...
# Only one object of each class during a request.
# =========================================================================
services:
    _defaults:
        autowire: true
        autoconfigure: true

    App\:
        resource: '../src/'
        # DATA objects, created by the code (or by Doctrine), never by the
        # container: they are not services
        exclude:
            - '../src/Entity/'
            - '../src/Domain/'
            - '../src/Views/'
            - '../src/Kernel.php'
  • Lines 10–15: All classes in the [src] folder are services created by the container, which provides each one with the objects it requests in its constructor (example 06). The services are shared: a single [ApplicationModel], a single [BusinessService]... for the entire request (see the chapter on scopes);
  • lines 16–22: except for data classes: entities created by [Doctrine] or by the business layer, calculated calendar objects, and view models created by actions. These are excluded: they are not services. (Other data classes, such as [PersonData] or [Message], are declared, but since no one requests them from the container, the container discards them on its own.)

There is nothing else to declare: the listeners ([#[AsEventListener]]), the controllers ([#[Route]]), the extensions [Twig], the form types, and the authenticator are recognized by the container based on their attributes or their parent class ([autoconfigure]), and configured accordingly. The command [php bin/console debug:container App] lists the application’s services.

docs.title: 11.8. The entities
docs.text: The [Doctrine] entities (Example 28): one class per table, in the [src/Entity] folder.

docs.title: 11.8.1. src/Entity/Role.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Entity/Role.php: the three roles of a user (column users.role):
//   - ADMIN : the administrator - appointments + management of doctors and clients;
//   - DOCTOR: a doctor - books and cancels appointments;
//   - USER  : a client (patient) - books for themselves, manages their account.
// A "backed" enumeration (backed enum): each case has a value, the string
// stored as is in the database; Role::from('ADMIN') goes the other way.

namespace App\Entity;

enum Role: string
{
    case ADMIN = 'ADMIN';
    case DOCTOR = 'DOCTOR';
    case USER = 'USER';

    // the role in Symfony's sense (see config/packages/security.yaml): ROLE_ADMIN...
    public function symfonyRole(): string
    {
        return 'ROLE_'.$this->value;
    }
}

The three roles, listed as follows ([enum], [PHP] 8.1): a type whose only possible values are its cases: [Role::ADMIN], [Role::DOCTOR], and [Role::USER]. A variable of type [Role] cannot contain ['ADMINN']: the typo is detected. [enum Role: string] declares a backed enumeration: each case has a value, in this case the base-sorted string. [Role::ADMIN->value] is equal to ['ADMIN']; [Role::from('ADMIN')] returns the corresponding case (and throws an exception for an unknown value); [Role::tryFrom(...)] returns [null] in this case. An enumeration can have methods: [symfonyRole()] (lines 18–21) returns the role as defined by [Symfony], [ROLE_ADMIN], [ROLE_DOCTOR], or [ROLE_USER] (example 25)—the one verified by the rules [access_control]. [$this] designates the case here.

docs.title: 11.8.2. src/Entity/User.php
docs.text:
<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/Entity/User.php: a user allowed to log in (table [users]).
// Each doctor and each client has THEIR account (column [user] of the tables
// [doctors] and [clients], see Person.php).
//
// SQL uniqueness constraint: unq_users_login (a login belongs to only one
// account). It is created by the script database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql; the business
// layer recognizes it by its NAME (see src/Business/BusinessService.php).
//
// PasswordAuthenticatedUserInterface: a user who has a (hashed) password;
// it is what Symfony's hashing service expects (see AuthService).
// =========================================================================

namespace App\Entity;

use Doctrine\DBAL\Types\Types;
use Doctrine\ORM\Mapping as ORM;
use Symfony\Component\Security\Core\User\PasswordAuthenticatedUserInterface;

#[ORM\Entity]
#[ORM\Table(name: 'users')]
class User implements PasswordAuthenticatedUserInterface
{
    #[ORM\Id]
    #[ORM\GeneratedValue]
    #[ORM\Column]
    private ?int $id = null;

    // the version number of the row: the optimistic lock (see example 28)
    #[ORM\Version]
    #[ORM\Column(type: Types::INTEGER)]
    private int $version = 0;

    public function __construct(
        #[ORM\Column(length: 30)]
        private string $login,
        // the HASHED password (bcrypt), never the password itself
        #[ORM\Column(length: 100)]
        private string $password,
        // the name displayed once logged in: "Marie PELISSIER"
        #[ORM\Column(length: 40)]
        private string $name,
        // enumType: the column (a text) becomes a Role, and vice versa
        #[ORM\Column(length: 10, enumType: Role::class)]
        private Role $role,
    ) {
    }

    public function getId(): ?int
    {
        return $this->id;
    }

    public function getVersion(): int
    {
        return $this->version;
    }

    public function getLogin(): string
    {
        return $this->login;
    }

    public function getPassword(): string
    {
        return $this->password;
    }

    public function getName(): string
    {
        return $this->name;
    }

    public function getRole(): Role
    {
        return $this->role;
    }

    public function setLogin(string $login): void
    {
        $this->login = $login;
    }

    public function setPassword(string $hash): void
    {
        $this->password = $hash;
    }

    public function setName(string $name): void
    {
        $this->name = $name;
    }
}
  • lines 21–23: the entity in table [users]. It implements the [PasswordAuthenticatedUserInterface] interface of the security component (Example 25): this is what the password hashing service expects;
  • lines 25–33: the primary key and version, the optimistic lock (Example 28);
  • lines 35–48: the other columns are declared in the constructor using constructor promotion (Example 03): the attributes [#[ORM\Column]] can be applied to both a promoted parameter and a property. [length] specifies the length of the [VARCHAR] columns. Line 45: The option [enumType] converts the column [role] (text) to [Role] during read operations, and vice versa during write operations: [$user->getRole()] returns a [Role], never a string;
  • Lines 50–93: the getters and three setter methods. The primary key and the version do not have setter methods: [Doctrine] keeps them up to date.

docs.title: 11.8.3. src/Entity/Person.php
docs.text:
<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/Entity/Person.php: what the doctors (table [doctors]) and the clients
// (table [clients]) have in common: a title, a last name, a first name - and the
// associated user account (column [user]).
//
// The two tables have exactly the same columns: they are described ONCE,
// in this ABSTRACT class (a "Person" is never created), from which
// Doctor and Client inherit; each one only specifies the name of its table.
// #[ORM\MappedSuperclass]: a parent class whose columns are those of the
// entities that inherit from it, but which has no table of its own.
//
// Beware: [Client] here means a PATIENT of the medical practice, not an HTTP
// client! It is the vocabulary of the original business domain, kept as is.
// =========================================================================

namespace App\Entity;

use Doctrine\DBAL\Types\Types;
use Doctrine\ORM\Mapping as ORM;

#[ORM\MappedSuperclass]
abstract class Person
{
    #[ORM\Id]
    #[ORM\GeneratedValue]
    #[ORM\Column]
    protected ?int $id = null;

    // optimistic lock (see example 28)
    #[ORM\Version]
    #[ORM\Column(type: Types::INTEGER)]
    protected int $version = 0;

    public function __construct(
        // Mr, Mme, Melle
        #[ORM\Column(length: 5)]
        protected string $title,
        #[ORM\Column(name: 'last_name', length: 20)]
        protected string $lastName,
        #[ORM\Column(name: 'first_name', length: 20)]
        protected string $firstName,
        // -------------------------------------------------------------------
        // The RELATION to the user account: a person has ONE account,
        // designated by the foreign key [user]. #[ORM\OneToOne]: one account per
        // person, one person per account; #[ORM\JoinColumn]: the column of the
        // foreign key (surrounded by backticks: `user` is a word of the SQL
        // language of MySQL). $doctor->getAccount() returns a User object, read from the database on
        // first access - or right away by the query, if it asks for it (see src/Dao)
        // -------------------------------------------------------------------
        #[ORM\OneToOne]
        #[ORM\JoinColumn(name: '`user`', nullable: false)]
        protected User $account,
    ) {
    }

    public function getId(): ?int
    {
        return $this->id;
    }

    public function getVersion(): int
    {
        return $this->version;
    }

    public function getTitle(): string
    {
        return $this->title;
    }

    public function getLastName(): string
    {
        return $this->lastName;
    }

    public function getFirstName(): string
    {
        return $this->firstName;
    }

    public function getAccount(): User
    {
        return $this->account;
    }

    public function edit(string $title, string $lastName, string $firstName): void
    {
        $this->title = $title;
        $this->lastName = $lastName;
        $this->firstName = $firstName;
    }

    // "Mme Alice DURAND"
    public function label(): string
    {
        return "{$this->title} {$this->firstName} {$this->lastName}";
    }
}

The tables [doctors] and [clients] have the same columns. Their shared description is written once, in an abstract class ([abstract class]): a class for which no objects are ever created, serving only as a base class for inheritance. The classes [Doctor] and [Client] inherit from it.

  • Line 22: The attribute [#[ORM\MappedSuperclass]] makes the class a superclass: its columns are those of each of the entities that inherit from it, but it does not have its own table. ([Doctrine] also supports true entity hierarchies, organized in a single table or in one table per class: this is not the case here, where the two tables are independent.) The properties are [protected]: visible to child classes;
  • Lines 51–53: The relationship to the account. [#[ORM\OneToOne]]: A person has an account, and an account belongs to at most one person. [#[ORM\JoinColumn]] refers to the foreign key column, [user], and ensures that it is not empty ([nullable: false]). The column name is enclosed in grave accents: [user] is a word in the language SQL of [MySQL], and [Doctrine] will enclose it in this way in the SQL commands it writes (see the console output above). The property [account] is a [User] object, not a number: that is the purpose of a ORM. When [Doctrine] reads a person, it also reads their account if the request calls for it (lazy loading; see the DAO layer); otherwise, it places a lazy [User] object (lazy) in the property, which will only be read from the database upon the first access to one of its properties—except for its ID, which it already knows;
  • lines 87–92: modification of the three identity columns;
  • lines 95–98: the name of a person, “Ms. Alice DURAND,” used by all pages. In a string enclosed in quotation marks, [{$this->title}] inserts the value of a property.

<?php
// src/Entity/Doctor.php: a doctor (table [doctors]).
// SQL uniqueness constraint: unq_doctors_first_name_last_name (two doctors cannot
// have the same first and last names).

namespace App\Entity;

use Doctrine\ORM\Mapping as ORM;

#[ORM\Entity]
#[ORM\Table(name: 'doctors')]
class Doctor extends Person
{
}

<?php
// src/Entity/Client.php: a client, that is to say a PATIENT (table [clients]).
// SQL uniqueness constraint: unq_clients_first_name_last_name.

namespace App\Entity;

use Doctrine\ORM\Mapping as ORM;

#[ORM\Entity]
#[ORM\Table(name: 'clients')]

docs.title: 11.8.5. src/Entity/Slot.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Entity/Slot.php: a time slot of a doctor (table [slots]):
// 8:00 - 8:20, etc. The slots are created by the SQL script: the application
// only reads them.

namespace App\Entity;

use Doctrine\DBAL\Types\Types;
use Doctrine\ORM\Mapping as ORM;

#[ORM\Entity]
#[ORM\Table(name: 'slots')]
class Slot
{
    #[ORM\Id]
    #[ORM\GeneratedValue]
    #[ORM\Column]
    private ?int $id = null;

    #[ORM\Version]
    #[ORM\Column(type: Types::INTEGER)]
    private int $version = 0;

    // several slots for the same doctor: #[ORM\ManyToOne], through the foreign
    // key [doctor_id]
    #[ORM\ManyToOne]
    #[ORM\JoinColumn(name: 'doctor_id', nullable: false)]
    private Doctor $doctor;

    #[ORM\Column(name: 'start_hour')]
    private int $startHour;

    #[ORM\Column(name: 'start_minute')]
    private int $startMinute;

    #[ORM\Column(name: 'end_hour')]
    private int $endHour;

    #[ORM\Column(name: 'end_minute')]
    private int $endMinute;

    public function getId(): ?int
    {
        return $this->id;
    }

    public function getDoctor(): Doctor
    {
        return $this->doctor;
    }

    // "8:00 - 8:20"; sprintf('%02d'): "8:05" rather than "8:5"
    public function time(): string
    {
        return sprintf('%d:%02d - %d:%02d', $this->startHour, $this->startMinute, $this->endHour, $this->endMinute);
    }
}
  • lines 26–28: the relationship to the doctor for the time slot. [#[ORM\ManyToOne]]: multiple time slots for the same doctor, via the foreign key [doctor_id];
  • lines 30–40: the start and end hours and minutes. The time slots are created by the script SQL: the class has no constructor, and [Doctrine] populates its properties itself;
  • lines 53–56: the time range, “8:00 – 8:20.” The [%02d] format of [sprintf] writes a two-digit integer, padded with zeros: [8:05] rather than [8:5].

docs.title: 11.8.6. src/Entity/Appointment.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Entity/Appointment.php: an appointment (table [appointments]): a client, on a slot,
// on a given day.
// SQL uniqueness constraint: unq1_appointments (day, slot_id) - a slot is booked
// only once per day. Created by the SQL script, recognized by its name in the
// business layer.

namespace App\Entity;

use DateTimeImmutable;
use Doctrine\DBAL\Types\Types;
use Doctrine\ORM\Mapping as ORM;

#[ORM\Entity]
#[ORM\Table(name: 'appointments')]
class Appointment
{
    #[ORM\Id]
    #[ORM\GeneratedValue]
    #[ORM\Column]
    private ?int $id = null;

    #[ORM\Version]
    #[ORM\Column(type: Types::INTEGER)]
    private int $version = 0;

    public function __construct(
        // the date_immutable type: the column [day] (SQL type DATE) becomes a date
        // DateTimeImmutable, at midnight; it is written to the database in the yyyy-mm-dd format
        #[ORM\Column(type: Types::DATE_IMMUTABLE)]
        private DateTimeImmutable $day,
        #[ORM\ManyToOne]
        #[ORM\JoinColumn(name: 'slot_id', nullable: false)]
        private Slot $slot,
        #[ORM\ManyToOne]
        #[ORM\JoinColumn(name: 'client_id', nullable: false)]
        private Client $client,
    ) {
    }

    public function getId(): ?int
    {
        return $this->id;
    }

    public function getDay(): DateTimeImmutable
    {
        return $this->day;
    }

    public function getSlot(): Slot
    {
        return $this->slot;
    }

    public function getClient(): Client
    {
        return $this->client;
    }
}
  • lines 30–31: the column [day] (type SQL [DATE]) is converted to [DateTimeImmutable] at midnight (type [Doctrine] [date_immutable]). Immutable: its methods never modify the object; they return a new one ([$day->modify('+1 day')] returns the next day, [$day] remains unchanged). The entire application works with immutable dates: a date shared among multiple objects cannot be modified by one of them without the others’ knowledge;
  • lines 32–37: two relationships, one to the time slot and one to the appointment’s client.

docs.title: 11.9.1. src/Domain/DoctorDaySlot.php and DoctorDaySchedule.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Domain/DoctorDaySlot.php: a time slot, and the appointment possibly
// booked on that slot on a given day (null if the slot is free).
// A computed "business" object, which matches no table.
//
// readonly: the properties are set once and for all by the constructor -
// exactly what is needed for a computed object, which nobody modifies afterwards.

namespace App\Domain;

use App\Entity\Slot;
use App\Entity\Appointment;

readonly class DoctorDaySlot
{
    public function __construct(
        public Slot $slot,
        public ?Appointment $appointment,
    ) {
    }
}

<?php
// src/Domain/DoctorDaySchedule.php: the complete schedule of a doctor for a given
// day, the list of their slots, each one free or taken. Computed by
// BusinessService::getDoctorDaySchedule, turned into an HTML table by
// ScheduleController.

namespace App\Domain;

use App\Entity\Doctor;
use DateTimeImmutable;

readonly class DoctorDaySchedule
{
    /** @param list<DoctorDaySlot> $doctorDaySlots */
    public function __construct(
        public Doctor $doctor,
        public DateTimeImmutable $day,
        public array $doctorDaySlots,
    ) {
    }
}

Two calculated objects that do not correspond to any table: a time slot and its potential appointment on a given day; a doctor’s calendar for a single day, listing their available time slots. These are [readonly] classes (example 03), whose properties are declared in the constructor. The comment [/** @param list<DoctorDaySlot> ... */] specifies the contents of the array: [PHP] cannot determine the type of an array’s contents, but editors ([PHP Intelephense]) and analysis tools read these comments, known as [PHPDoc].

docs.title: 11.10. The DAO layer
docs.text: The DAO layer (Example 28) groups together the queries: one class per table, with no business logic. Its methods do not start a transaction; the business layer calls them within its own transactions. They are written in DQL (Example 28), or using the query builder in [Doctrine], which generates a DQL query through method calls; the values are query parameters: SQL injection is not possible.

docs.title: 11.10.1. src/Dao/PersonDao.php
docs.text:
<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/Dao/PersonDao.php: the DAO layer common to the doctors and the clients.
//
// The DAOs of the doctors and of the clients would be identical: this ABSTRACT class
// writes them only once. $this->entityClass is the class of the entity concerned
// (Doctor::class or Client::class): the DQL queries are about ITS table.
//
// The queries are written in DQL, Doctrine's query language (see
// example 28), which Doctrine translates into SQL. The values (first name, last name...) are
// PARAMETERS of the query (:firstName): no string concatenation, therefore no
// SQL injection. These methods open no transaction: it is the business
// layer that calls them, inside its own.
// =========================================================================

namespace App\Dao;

use App\Entity\Person;
use Doctrine\ORM\EntityManagerInterface;
use Doctrine\ORM\QueryBuilder;

abstract class PersonDao
{
    /** @param class-string<Person> $entityClass */
    public function __construct(protected EntityManagerInterface $em, protected string $entityClass)
    {
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // a query on the table of the class, user account included. Doctrine's
    // QUERY BUILDER (createQueryBuilder) builds the DQL query
    // through method calls:
    //   SELECT p, a FROM App\Entity\Doctor p JOIN p.account a
    // JOIN p.account a: the SQL join with the [users] table; SELECT p, a: the
    // accounts are loaded BY THE SAME query. Without it, each access to
    // $person->getAccount() would trigger its own query
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    protected function query(): QueryBuilder
    {
        return $this->em->createQueryBuilder()
            ->select('p', 'a')
            ->from($this->entityClass, 'p')
            ->join('p.account', 'a');
    }

    // list sorted by last name then first name
    /** @return list<Person> */
    public function list(): array
    {
        return $this->query()->orderBy('p.lastName')->addOrderBy('p.firstName')->getQuery()->getResult();
    }

    // a person and their account; null if they do not exist
    public function read(int $id): ?Person
    {
        return $this->query()->where('p.id = :id')->setParameter('id', $id)
            ->getQuery()->getOneOrNullResult();
    }

    // the person whose user account is [$userId]
    public function readByUser(int $userId): ?Person
    {
        return $this->query()->where('a.id = :userId')->setParameter('userId', $userId)
            ->getQuery()->getOneOrNullResult();
    }

    // the person who has these first and last names, if there is one. The comparison is
    // made by MySQL, therefore with the collation of the database (utf8mb4_unicode_ci: regardless
    // of case and accents) - exactly the same rule as
    // that of the SQL uniqueness constraint
    public function namesake(string $firstName, string $lastName): ?Person
    {
        return $this->query()->where('p.firstName = :firstName')->andWhere('p.lastName = :lastName')
            ->setParameter('firstName', $firstName)->setParameter('lastName', $lastName)
            ->setMaxResults(1)->getQuery()->getOneOrNullResult();
    }

    // the person will be inserted by the next flush (that of the transaction of
    // the business layer); the database will generate their id, which Doctrine will store in the object
    public function add(Person $person): void
    {
        $this->em->persist($person);
    }

    // the person will be deleted by the next flush
    public function remove(Person $person): void
    {
        $this->em->remove($person);
    }
}

The DAO layer common to both doctors and clients, implemented once in an abstract class.

  • Line 25: The constructor receives the entity manager (Example 28) and the relevant class, [Doctor::class] or [Client::class] (a string representing the full class name). The comment [@param class-string<Person>] clarifies this for developers. The service container does not know which string to provide: it is the child classes that call this constructor;
  • lines 38–44: a query that also loads the accounts of the read users. [createQueryBuilder] creates a query builder; [select('p', 'a')], [from($this->entityClass, 'p')], and [join('p.account', 'a')] write the query DQL [SELECT p, a FROM App\Entity\Doctor p JOIN p.account a]. The join ([JOIN]) follows the relationship [account] of the entity: [Doctrine] derives the condition SQL ([ON d0_.user = u1_.id]). The [SELECT] for both aliases requires eager loading of the accounts: a single query retrieves the people and their accounts. Without it, the list of doctors displayed by the administrator would trigger one query per doctor upon the first access to [$doctor->getAccount()->getLogin()]: this is the so-called “N + 1 queries” problem. Another reason: the lists of doctors and clients are stored in the cache ([ApplicationModel], discussed later); the objects added to the cache must be complete;
  • lines 48–51: the list, sorted by last name then first name ([orderBy], then [addOrderBy]: a second criterion; a second [orderBy] would replace the first). [getQuery()] returns the query DQL; [getResult()] executes it and returns the array of entities;
  • lines 54–58: [where] adds a condition with a named parameter ([:id]), whose value is provided by [setParameter]. [getOneOrNullResult] returns the single entity found, or [null];
  • lines 61–65: the person whose account is [$userId], condition based on the linked account ID;
  • lines 71–76: the person with the same first and last names. [andWhere] adds a second condition (a second [where] would replace the first). The comparison is performed by [MySQL], using the database’s collation: case-insensitive and ignoring accents, exactly like the uniqueness constraint (Example 28);
  • lines 80–89: the insertion and deletion, which will be sent to the database by [flush] as part of the business layer transaction (Example 28).

There is no update method: the business layer modifies the read entity, and [Doctrine] will send [UPDATE] to [flush] (change tracking, Example 28), using an optimistic lock.

docs.title: 11.10.2. src/Dao/DoctorDao.php and ClientDao.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Dao/DoctorDao.php: the DAO of the doctors - everything is inherited from PersonDao.

namespace App\Dao;

use App\Entity\Doctor;
use Doctrine\ORM\EntityManagerInterface;

class DoctorDao extends PersonDao
{
    public function __construct(EntityManagerInterface $em)
    {
        parent::__construct($em, Doctor::class);
    }
}

Everything is inherited: the constructor receives the container’s entity manager and passes it to [PersonDao] along with the entity class ([parent::__construct] calls the parent class’s constructor).

<?php
// src/Dao/ClientDao.php: the DAO of the clients - that of the persons, plus a
// locking method.

namespace App\Dao;

use App\Entity\Client;
use Doctrine\DBAL\LockMode;
use Doctrine\ORM\EntityManagerInterface;

class ClientDao extends PersonDao
{
    public function __construct(EntityManagerInterface $em)
    {
        parent::__construct($em, Client::class);
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // puts a LOCK on a client's row until the end of the current transaction
    // (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), and returns its id (null if the client does not
    // exist). A second transaction asking for the same lock WAITS until the
    // first one is finished. LockMode::PESSIMISTIC_WRITE: Doctrine's "pessimistic"
    // lock, which requires an open transaction.
    // Used for booking (see BusinessService::addAppointment): two
    // simultaneous bookings for the same patient are thus processed one
    // AFTER the other, and the second one sees the appointment created by the first one.
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    public function lock(int $id): ?int
    {
        $row = $this->em->createQuery('SELECT c.id FROM App\Entity\Client c WHERE c.id = :id')
            ->setParameter('id', $id)
            ->setLockMode(LockMode::PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
            ->getOneOrNullResult();
        return $row['id'] ?? null;
    }
}
  • Lines 28–35: a pessimistic lock, the other type of lock. [setLockMode(LockMode::PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)] adds [FOR UPDATE] to the query: [SELECT c0_.id AS id_0 FROM clients c0_ WHERE c0_.id = ? FOR UPDATE]. The row being read is locked until the end of the current transaction: another transaction requesting the same lock waits for the first one to finish. [Doctrine] denies this lock outside of a transaction. The query reads only the ID ([SELECT c.id]): its result is not an entity, but an associative array ([['id' => 3]]), or [null]. We will see, in the business layer, what this lock is used for.

docs.title: 11.10.3. src/Dao/SlotDao.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Dao/SlotDao.php: DAO layer of the time slots.

namespace App\Dao;

use App\Entity\Slot;
use Doctrine\ORM\EntityManagerInterface;

class SlotDao
{
    public function __construct(private EntityManagerInterface $em)
    {
    }

    // a slot and its doctor
    public function read(int $id): ?Slot
    {
        return $this->em->createQuery(
            'SELECT s, d FROM App\Entity\Slot s JOIN s.doctor d WHERE s.id = :id')
            ->setParameter('id', $id)->getOneOrNullResult();
    }

    // the slots of a doctor, in chronological order. s.doctor = :doctorId:
    // an association compared to an id, that of the foreign key
    /** @return list<Slot> */
    public function listByDoctor(int $doctorId): array
    {
        return $this->em->createQuery(
            'SELECT s FROM App\Entity\Slot s WHERE s.doctor = :doctorId ORDER BY s.startHour, s.startMinute')
            ->setParameter('doctorId', $doctorId)->getResult();
    }

    // deletes all the slots of a doctor (deletion of a doctor): a
    // DQL DELETE query, executed right away:
    //   DELETE FROM slots WHERE doctor_id = ?
    public function deleteByDoctor(int $doctorId): void
    {
        $this->em->createQuery('DELETE FROM App\Entity\Slot s WHERE s.doctor = :doctorId')
            ->setParameter('doctorId', $doctorId)->execute();
    }
}

An appointment slot and its doctor (preloaded); a doctor’s appointment slots, in chronological order: [s.doctor = :doctorId] compares a relationship to an ID—that of the foreign key; and a [DELETE] written as DQL, executed immediately ([execute()]), without reading the rows first.

docs.title: 11.10.4. src/Dao/AppointmentDao.php
docs.text:
<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/Dao/AppointmentDao.php: DAO layer of the appointments.
//
// The [appointments] table does not reference the doctor directly: we go through the slot
// (JOIN a.slot s ... WHERE s.doctor = ...).
// The dates are passed with their type (Types::DATE_IMMUTABLE): Doctrine
// writes them in the format of the database, yyyy-mm-dd.
// =========================================================================

namespace App\Dao;

use App\Entity\Appointment;
use DateTimeImmutable;
use Doctrine\DBAL\Types\Types;
use Doctrine\ORM\EntityManagerInterface;

class AppointmentDao
{
    public function __construct(private EntityManagerInterface $em)
    {
    }

    // an appointment, its client and its slot
    public function read(int $id): ?Appointment
    {
        return $this->em->createQuery(
            'SELECT a, c, s FROM App\Entity\Appointment a JOIN a.client c JOIN a.slot s WHERE a.id = :id')
            ->setParameter('id', $id)->getOneOrNullResult();
    }

    // the appointments of a doctor on a given day, with their client
    /** @return list<Appointment> */
    public function doctorDayAppointments(int $doctorId, DateTimeImmutable $day): array
    {
        return $this->em->createQuery(
            'SELECT a, c FROM App\Entity\Appointment a JOIN a.client c JOIN a.slot s
             WHERE a.day = :day AND s.doctor = :doctorId')
            ->setParameter('day', $day, Types::DATE_IMMUTABLE)
            ->setParameter('doctorId', $doctorId)
            ->getResult();
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // the appointments of a client from the day [$since] (included), in chronological
    // order, with the slot AND the doctor of that slot (two joins:
    // JOIN a.slot s JOIN s.doctor d, and SELECT a, s, d)
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    /** @return list<Appointment> */
    public function clientUpcomingAppointments(int $clientId, DateTimeImmutable $since): array
    {
        return $this->em->createQuery(
            'SELECT a, s, d FROM App\Entity\Appointment a JOIN a.slot s JOIN s.doctor d
             WHERE a.client = :clientId AND a.day >= :since
             ORDER BY a.day, s.startHour, s.startMinute')
            ->setParameter('clientId', $clientId)
            ->setParameter('since', $since, Types::DATE_IMMUTABLE)
            ->getResult();
    }

    // number of appointments of a client from the day [$since] (included);
    // getSingleScalarResult: the only value of the only row of the result
    public function countClientUpcoming(int $clientId, DateTimeImmutable $since): int
    {
        return (int) $this->em->createQuery(
            'SELECT COUNT(a.id) FROM App\Entity\Appointment a WHERE a.client = :clientId AND a.day >= :since')
            ->setParameter('clientId', $clientId)
            ->setParameter('since', $since, Types::DATE_IMMUTABLE)
            ->getSingleScalarResult();
    }

    // number of appointments (past or future) of a doctor
    public function countByDoctor(int $doctorId): int
    {
        return (int) $this->em->createQuery(
            'SELECT COUNT(a.id) FROM App\Entity\Appointment a JOIN a.slot s WHERE s.doctor = :doctorId')
            ->setParameter('doctorId', $doctorId)
            ->getSingleScalarResult();
    }

    // the appointment will be inserted by the next flush
    public function add(Appointment $appointment): void
    {
        $this->em->persist($appointment);
    }

    public function remove(Appointment $appointment): void
    {
        $this->em->remove($appointment);
    }

    // deletes ALL the appointments (past and future) of a client, right away
    public function deleteByClient(int $clientId): void
    {
        $this->em->createQuery('DELETE FROM App\Entity\Appointment a WHERE a.client = :clientId')
            ->setParameter('clientId', $clientId)->execute();
    }
}

The table [appointments] does not directly reference the doctor: it goes through the time slot.

  • Lines 34–42: a doctor’s appointments on a given day, and their clients. Two joins: one ([a.client c]) to load the clients ([SELECT a, c]), the other ([a.slot s]) for the filter on the doctor. The third parameter of [setParameter] specifies the value type [Doctrine]: a [DateTimeImmutable] is then written in the column format [DATE], [yyyy-mm-dd];
  • lines 50–59: a patient’s upcoming appointments, with their time slot and the doctor assigned to that slot: [JOIN s.doctor d] follows a relationship from the relation. Sorting is also performed based on the time slot, a column from another table: this is made possible by the join;
