  • lines 63–79: counts. [COUNT(a.id)] counts the appointments; [getSingleScalarResult] returns the single value from the single row in the result (a string, converted to an integer by [(int)]);
  • lines 93–97: Deleting all appointments for a client, using DQL.

docs.title: 11.10.5. src/Dao/UserDao.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Dao/UserDao.php: DAO layer of the user accounts. Creating (or deleting)
// a doctor or a client also creates (or deletes) their account - see src/Business.
// A modified account is modified through its methods (setLogin...): Doctrine will send
// the UPDATE at the next flush (change tracking, see example 28).

namespace App\Dao;

use App\Entity\User;
use Doctrine\ORM\EntityManagerInterface;

class UserDao
{
    public function __construct(private EntityManagerInterface $em)
    {
    }

    // null if no user has this login; findOneBy: the repository of the entity
    // looks for the row whose columns have these values
    public function readByLogin(string $login): ?User
    {
        return $this->em->getRepository(User::class)->findOneBy(['login' => $login]);
    }

    public function add(User $user): void
    {
        $this->em->persist($user);
    }

    public function remove(User $user): void
    {
        $this->em->remove($user);
    }
}

Accounts: retrieval by login, with entity storage (example 28): [findOneBy(criteria)] returns the single entity that matches the criteria, or [null]; addition and deletion.

docs.title: 11.11. The Business Layer
docs.text: The business layer brings together business rules and transactions (Example 28). It is described by an interface, implemented by two classes: [BusinessService], the business layer itself, and [ApplicationModel], the web layer cache (discussed later).

docs.title: 11.11.1. src/Business/Dates.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Business/Dates.php: today's date. It is used by BUSINESS RULES (no
// booking in the past, only one UPCOMING appointment per patient): it therefore
// lives in the business layer. The web layer reuses it.

namespace App\Business;

use DateTimeImmutable;

class Dates
{
    // today at midnight, in the application's time zone (see src/Kernel.php)
    public static function today(): DateTimeImmutable
    {
        return new DateTimeImmutable('today');
    }
}

The current date at midnight (['today']), in the application’s time zone (see [src/Kernel.php]). It is used for business rules (no past reservations, only one upcoming appointment): it resides in the business layer. A static method ([static]) is called without creating an object: [Dates::today()].

docs.title: 11.11.2. src/Business/BusinessException.php
docs.text:
<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/Business/BusinessException.php: the exception thrown by the business layer when a
// BUSINESS RULE is violated (login already taken, doctor who still has
// appointments, slot already booked...). It does not carry a text, but a
// translation KEY (e.g. "ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN"): it is the web layer that will
// translate it into French or English when displaying the page (see translations).
//
// A BusinessException is not an anomaly: it is a normal answer ("this login
// is already taken"), displayed to the user. Any other exception is a real
// anomaly, which ends up on the 500 error page.
// =========================================================================

namespace App\Business;

use RuntimeException;
use Throwable;

class BusinessException extends RuntimeException
{
    public function __construct(
        // translation key of the message
        public readonly string $key,
        // possible parameters of the message ({minutes}...)
        public readonly array $params = [],
        ?Throwable $previous = null,
    ) {
        parent::__construct($key, 0, $previous);
    }
}

The exception thrown when a business rule is violated. It does not carry text, but rather a translation key ([ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN]) and its parameters: the web layer will translate it into the page’s language (Example 22). The business layer knows nothing about the interface languages. [RuntimeException] is a subclass of [PHP]. The constructor properties [public readonly] are declared and initialized by the constructor promotion (Example 03); [parent::__construct($key, 0, $previous)] calls the constructor of [RuntimeException], passing the message, the code, and the previous exception (the one that caused this one—a database error, for example: it appears in the log along with the new one).

docs.title: 11.11.3. src/Business/PersonData.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Business/PersonData.php: the data entered in a "doctor" or "client" form,
// as the web layer passes them to the business layer.

namespace App\Business;

readonly class PersonData
{
    public function __construct(
        public string $title,        // Mr, Mme, Melle
        public string $lastName,
        public string $firstName,
        // creation: optional (null), defaults to the last name in lower case
        // modification: optional, the login is unchanged if it is absent
        public ?string $login = null,
        // creation: optional, defaults to the login
        // modification: optional, the password is unchanged if it is absent
        public ?string $password = null,
        // modification: the version of the record when the form was
        // displayed (optimistic lock)
        public ?int $version = null,
    ) {
    }
}

Data from a “person” form, as transmitted by the web layer to the business layer: a class named [readonly]. The login, password, and version are optional ([?string], [?int], default value [null]); the comments explain what their absence means.

docs.title: 11.11.4. src/Business/Business.php
docs.text:
<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/Business/Business.php: the CONTRACT of the business layer: reads, schedule,
// appointments, management of doctors and clients.
//
// An INTERFACE describes the methods a class must have, without saying how
// they are written. BusinessService (the business layer) and ApplicationModel (the cache
// of the web layer) both implement it; PHP checks, when loading
// the class, that no method is missing.
//
// ?Type: a result that may be absent (null: a doctor who does not exist...).
// list<Doctor> (in a /** */ comment): an array of doctors, indexed 0, 1, 2...
// =========================================================================

namespace App\Business;

use App\Domain\DoctorDaySchedule;
use App\Entity\Client;
use App\Entity\Slot;
use App\Entity\Doctor;
use App\Entity\Appointment;
use DateTimeImmutable;

interface Business
{
    // ------------------------------------------------ reads
    /** @return list<Client> */
    public function getAllClients(): array;

    /** @return list<Doctor> */
    public function getAllDoctors(): array;

    /** @return list<Slot> */
    public function getAllSlots(int $doctorId): array;

    /** @return list<Appointment> */
    public function getDoctorDayAppointments(int $doctorId, DateTimeImmutable $day): array;

    public function getClientById(int $id): ?Client;

    public function getDoctorById(int $id): ?Doctor;

    public function getAppointmentById(int $id): ?Appointment;

    public function getSlotById(int $id): ?Slot;

    public function getDoctorDaySchedule(int $doctorId, DateTimeImmutable $day): ?DoctorDaySchedule;

    // the client (patient) whose user account is [$userId]
    public function getClientByUserId(int $userId): ?Client;

    // the appointments of a client, today's or future ones, with slot and doctor
    /** @return list<Appointment> */
    public function getClientUpcomingAppointments(int $clientId): array;

    // ------------------------------------------------ appointments (ADMIN, DOCTOR, USER)
    // throws a BusinessException if:
    //  - the day is past ("ERRORS.PAST_DATE");
    //  - the patient already has an upcoming appointment ("ERRORS.PATIENT_HAS_UPCOMING_APPOINTMENT");
    //  - the slot is already taken on that day ("ERRORS.SLOT_ALREADY_BOOKED").
    public function addAppointment(DateTimeImmutable $day, Slot $slot, Client $client): Appointment;

    public function deleteAppointment(Appointment $appointment): void;

    // ------------------------------------------------ doctors (ADMIN)
    // creates the doctor AND their user account (role DOCTOR)
    public function addDoctor(PersonData $data): Doctor;

    // modifies the doctor AND their user account
    public function editDoctor(int $id, PersonData $data): Doctor;

    // deletes the doctor, their slots AND their account - refused if they have appointments
    public function deleteDoctor(int $id): void;

    // ------------------------------------------------ clients
    // (the ADMIN; addClient is also used for the registration of a patient,
    // editClient and deleteClient by the patient for their own account)
    // creates the client AND their user account (role USER)
    public function addClient(PersonData $data): Client;

    public function editClient(int $id, PersonData $data): Client;

    // deletes the client, their account AND all their appointments (past and future)
    public function deleteClient(int $id): void;
}

The business layer contract: an interface (example 06), the list of methods, without their code. Read operations return entities or arrays of entities (the comment [@return list<Client>] specifies their content); [?Client]: a client, or [null] if it does not exist. The comments specify the rules for each write operation and the keys of the [BusinessException] entities it may raise.

docs.title: 11.11.5. src/Business/Descriptor.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Business/Descriptor.php: everything that distinguishes a doctor from a client for the
// business rules (see BusinessService). Doctors and clients follow the
// same rules: the common code is written ONCE, and parameterized by a descriptor.

namespace App\Business;

use App\Dao\PersonDao;
use App\Entity\Role;
use Closure;

readonly class Descriptor
{
    public function __construct(
        public PersonDao $dao,
        public Role $role,              // DOCTOR or USER
        // the class of the entity, to create a person: Doctor::class or Client::class
        public string $entityClass,
        public string $notFoundKey,     // message if the person does not exist
        public string $alreadyExistsKey, // message if the same first and last names already exist
        // optional (null): if present, the deletion is REFUSED as long as the
        // person has appointments (countAppointments(id) > 0), with the message hasAppointmentsKey
        public ?Closure $countAppointments,
        public ?string $hasAppointmentsKey,
        // optional: what must be deleted BEFORE the person (the rows that
        // reference them through a foreign key); receives their id
        public ?Closure $beforeDelete,
    ) {
    }
}

Doctors and clients follow the same management rules, with a few minor differences: the DAO, the account role, the class of the entity to be created, the error messages, and the deletion rule. This descriptor consolidates these details; the common code reads them. Two properties are functions ([?Closure]: a function, or [null]): the appointment count, which prevents deletion (doctors only), and the deletion of references to the person.

docs.title: 11.11.6. src/Business/BusinessService.php
docs.text:
<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/Business/BusinessService.php: the implementation of the business layer.
//
// The management of doctors and clients obeys three business rules:
//
//   1. a person (doctor or client) and their user account ALWAYS go
//      together: they are created, modified and deleted together, in the same
//      TRANSACTION - either everything succeeds, or nothing is written;
//   2. the login is unique in the whole application, and two doctors (or two
//      clients) cannot have the same first and last names;
//   3. deletion:
//      - a DOCTOR who has appointments cannot be deleted (their patients
//        would lose their appointment without being notified): they must first
//        be cancelled. Their time slots disappear with them;
//      - a CLIENT, on the other hand, disappears with ALL their appointments (past and future) -
//        whether the deletion comes from the ADMIN or from the patient themselves.
//
// And two rules for booking, whatever the role of the person who
// books (ADMIN, DOCTOR or the patient themselves):
//   4. no appointment in the past;
//   5. a patient has only ONE upcoming appointment at a time.
//
// Doctors and clients follow exactly the same rules: the common code is
// written ONCE (private methods xxxPerson), and parameterized by a descriptor
// that says which type of person we are dealing with.
//
// The TRANSACTIONS are opened by the transaction method (at the end of the file),
// which also translates into BusinessException the errors reported by the database.
// =========================================================================

namespace App\Business;

use App\Dao\ClientDao;
use App\Dao\SlotDao;
use App\Dao\DoctorDao;
use App\Dao\AppointmentDao;
use App\Dao\UserDao;
use App\Domain\DoctorDaySchedule;
use App\Domain\DoctorDaySlot;
use App\Entity\Client;
use App\Entity\Slot;
use App\Entity\Doctor;
use App\Entity\Person;
use App\Entity\Role;
use App\Entity\Appointment;
use App\Entity\User;
use Closure;
use DateTimeImmutable;
use Doctrine\DBAL\Exception\UniqueConstraintViolationException;
use Doctrine\ORM\EntityManagerInterface;
use Doctrine\ORM\OptimisticLockException;
use Symfony\Component\PasswordHasher\Hasher\PasswordHasherFactoryInterface;
use Symfony\Component\PasswordHasher\PasswordHasherInterface;

class BusinessService implements Business
{
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // Database errors -> BusinessException
    //
    // When a UNIQUE constraint refuses a write, Doctrine throws a
    // UniqueConstraintViolationException, whose message is that of MySQL. It
    // quotes the NAME of the constraint:
    //   Duplicate entry 'Marie-PELISSIER' for key 'doctors.unq_doctors_first_name_last_name'
    // (MySQL 8 prefixes the name with that of the table, MariaDB does not). That is why
    // the SQL script NAMES all its constraints.
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    private const CONSTRAINT_MESSAGES = [
        'unq_users_login' => 'ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN',
        'unq_doctors_first_name_last_name' => 'ERRORS.DOCTOR_ALREADY_EXISTS',
        'unq_clients_first_name_last_name' => 'ERRORS.PATIENT_ALREADY_EXISTS',
        'unq1_appointments' => 'ERRORS.SLOT_ALREADY_BOOKED',
    ];

    private const CONSTRAINT = "/for key '(?:[^'.]*\\.)?([^']+)'/";

    private Descriptor $doctor;

    private Descriptor $client;

    // the hashing of passwords (bcrypt, see config/packages/security.yaml)
    private PasswordHasherInterface $hasher;

    // all the dependencies are provided by Symfony's service container
    // (dependency injection, see example 06)
    public function __construct(
        private EntityManagerInterface $em,
        private DoctorDao $doctors,
        private ClientDao $clients,
        private SlotDao $slots,
        private AppointmentDao $appointments,
        private UserDao $users,
        PasswordHasherFactoryInterface $hashers,
    ) {
        $this->hasher = $hashers->getPasswordHasher(User::class);

        $this->doctor = new Descriptor(
            dao: $doctors,
            role: Role::DOCTOR,
            entityClass: Doctor::class,
            notFoundKey: 'ERRORS.DOCTOR_NOT_FOUND',
            alreadyExistsKey: 'ERRORS.DOCTOR_ALREADY_EXISTS',
            // $appointments->countByDoctor(...): the method itself, as a Closure
            // (so-called "first-class callable" syntax)
            countAppointments: $appointments->countByDoctor(...),
            hasAppointmentsKey: 'ERRORS.DOCTOR_HAS_APPOINTMENTS',
            // a doctor without appointments may still have time slots:
            // they make no sense without them, they are deleted with them (otherwise the
            // foreign key slots.doctor_id would forbid the deletion)
            beforeDelete: $slots->deleteByDoctor(...));

        $this->client = new Descriptor(
            dao: $clients,
            role: Role::USER,
            entityClass: Client::class,
            notFoundKey: 'ERRORS.PATIENT_NOT_FOUND',
            alreadyExistsKey: 'ERRORS.PATIENT_ALREADY_EXISTS',
            // no countAppointments: the deletion of a client is never refused;
            // their appointments (past and future) are deleted with them (otherwise
            // the foreign key appointments.client_id would forbid the deletion)
            countAppointments: null,
            hasAppointmentsKey: null,
            beforeDelete: $appointments->deleteByClient(...));
    }

    // =======================================================================
    // reads
    // =======================================================================

    public function getAllClients(): array
    {
        return $this->clients->list();
    }

    public function getAllDoctors(): array
    {
        return $this->doctors->list();
    }

    public function getAllSlots(int $doctorId): array
    {
        return $this->slots->listByDoctor($doctorId);
    }

    public function getDoctorDayAppointments(int $doctorId, DateTimeImmutable $day): array
    {
        return $this->appointments->doctorDayAppointments($doctorId, $day);
    }

    public function getClientById(int $id): ?Client
    {
        return $this->clients->read($id);
    }

    public function getDoctorById(int $id): ?Doctor
    {
        return $this->doctors->read($id);
    }

    public function getAppointmentById(int $id): ?Appointment
    {
        return $this->appointments->read($id);
    }

    public function getSlotById(int $id): ?Slot
    {
        return $this->slots->read($id);
    }

    public function getClientByUserId(int $userId): ?Client
    {
        return $this->clients->readByUser($userId);
    }

    public function getClientUpcomingAppointments(int $clientId): array
    {
        return $this->appointments->clientUpcomingAppointments($clientId, Dates::today());
    }

    // the schedule of a doctor on a given day: their slots, and for each one the
    // appointment booked on that day (null if it is free)
    public function getDoctorDaySchedule(int $doctorId, DateTimeImmutable $day): ?DoctorDaySchedule
    {
        $doctor = $this->getDoctorById($doctorId);
        if ($doctor === null) {
            return null;
        }
        // slot number -> appointment booked on that slot
        $bookings = [];
        foreach ($this->getDoctorDayAppointments($doctorId, $day) as $appointment) {
            $bookings[$appointment->getSlot()->getId()] = $appointment;
        }
        // array_map: applies the function to each slot, and returns the array of the results
        $doctorDaySlots = array_map(
            fn (Slot $slot) => new DoctorDaySlot($slot, $bookings[$slot->getId()] ?? null),
            $this->getAllSlots($doctorId));
        return new DoctorDaySchedule($doctor, $day, $doctorDaySlots);
    }

    // =======================================================================
    // appointments
    // =======================================================================

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // booking, in a transaction:
    //   1. no appointment in the past;
    //   2. we LOCK the patient's row (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE): if the same
    //      patient books two slots at the same moment (two tabs, double
    //      click...), the second transaction waits for the end of the first one - and then sees
    //      the appointment it has just created;
    //   3. only one upcoming appointment per patient;
    //   4. finally the insertion. If the slot has just been taken by ANOTHER patient,
    //      it is the SQL constraint unq1_appointments (day, slot_id) that refuses
    //      the insertion - translated into BusinessException by transaction().
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    public function addAppointment(DateTimeImmutable $day, Slot $slot, Client $client): Appointment
    {
        return $this->transaction(function () use ($day, $slot, $client) {
            $today = Dates::today();
            if ($day < $today) {
                throw new BusinessException('ERRORS.PAST_DATE');
            }
            $patientId = $this->clients->lock($client->getId())
                ?? throw new BusinessException('ERRORS.PATIENT_NOT_FOUND');
            if ($this->appointments->countClientUpcoming($patientId, $today) > 0) {
                throw new BusinessException('ERRORS.PATIENT_HAS_UPCOMING_APPOINTMENT');
            }
            $appointment = new Appointment($day, $slot, $client);
            $this->appointments->add($appointment);
            return $appointment;
        });
    }

    public function deleteAppointment(Appointment $appointment): void
    {
        $this->transaction(fn () => $this->appointments->remove($appointment));
    }

    // =======================================================================
    // doctors and clients - the public methods delegate to the common private
    // methods, with the right descriptor
    // =======================================================================

    public function addDoctor(PersonData $data): Doctor
    {
        return $this->addPerson($this->doctor, $data);
    }

    public function editDoctor(int $id, PersonData $data): Doctor
    {
        return $this->editPerson($this->doctor, $id, $data);
    }

    public function deleteDoctor(int $id): void
    {
        $this->deletePerson($this->doctor, $id);
    }

    public function addClient(PersonData $data): Client
    {
        return $this->addPerson($this->client, $data);
    }

    public function editClient(int $id, PersonData $data): Client
    {
        return $this->editPerson($this->client, $id, $data);
    }

    // the client, their account AND all their appointments (ADMIN, or the patient themselves
    // from "Manage my account": same method, same rule)
    public function deleteClient(int $id): void
    {
        $this->deletePerson($this->client, $id);
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // creation: the user account AND the person (who references it), in ONE
    // transaction. Doctrine first inserts the account, then the person, whose foreign
    // key [user] receives the id the database has just generated for the account.
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    private function addPerson(Descriptor $d, PersonData $data): Person
    {
        $lastName = mb_strtoupper(trim($data->lastName));
        $firstName = trim($data->firstName);
        // the rules of the dbrdvmedecins2 database: login = last name in lower case,
        // password = login - unless the ADMIN (or the patient) entered other ones
        $login = mb_strtolower($data->login ?: $lastName);
        $password = $data->password ?: $login;

        return $this->transaction(function () use ($d, $data, $lastName, $firstName, $login, $password) {
            $this->checkPersonUnique($d, $firstName, $lastName, null);
            $this->checkLoginFree($login);
            // hash: the bcrypt hash of the password
            $user = new User($login, $this->hasher->hash($password), "$firstName $lastName", $d->role);
            $this->users->add($user);
            // new ($d->entityClass)(...): an instance of the class whose name is in the
            // property [entityClass] of the descriptor (Doctor or Client)
            $person = new ($d->entityClass)($data->title, $lastName, $firstName, $user);
            $d->dao->add($person);
            return $person;
        });
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // modification: the person AND their account (the displayed name "firstName LASTNAME" must
    // follow; the login and the password only change if they have been entered).
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    private function editPerson(Descriptor $d, int $id, PersonData $data): Person
    {
        return $this->transaction(function () use ($d, $id, $data) {
            $person = $d->dao->read($id) ?? throw new BusinessException($d->notFoundKey);

            // optimistic lock: if the version in the database is no longer that of the
            // form, someone has modified this record in the meantime - we refuse
            // rather than silently overwrite their changes
            if ($data->version !== null && $data->version !== $person->getVersion()) {
                throw new BusinessException('ERRORS.CONCURRENT_UPDATE');
            }

            $lastName = mb_strtoupper(trim($data->lastName));
            $firstName = trim($data->firstName);
            $this->checkPersonUnique($d, $firstName, $lastName, $id);
            $person->edit($data->title, $lastName, $firstName);

            // their account: the displayed name, and, if they have been entered, the login and the
            // password
            $account = $person->getAccount();
            $account->setName("$firstName $lastName");
            $login = $data->login ? mb_strtolower($data->login) : null;
            if ($login !== null && $login !== $account->getLogin()) {
                $this->checkLoginFree($login);
                $account->setLogin($login);
            }
            if ($data->password) {
                $account->setPassword($this->hasher->hash($data->password));
            }
            // nothing else to do: at the end of the transaction, Doctrine sends the
            // UPDATEs of the modified rows, with their optimistic lock
            //   UPDATE ... SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?
            // If the record has been modified AFTER the read above, no row
            // is modified, and Doctrine throws an OptimisticLockException
            return $person;
        });
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // deletion, in ONE transaction, in the order imposed by the foreign
    // keys:
    //   1. possible refusal if appointments remain (doctor);
    //   2. what references the person (slots of a doctor, appointments of a
    //      client), right away;
    //   3. the person (they reference their account), then their account: Doctrine
    //      deletes them in that order at the end of the transaction.
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    private function deletePerson(Descriptor $d, int $id): void
    {
        $this->transaction(function () use ($d, $id) {
            $person = $d->dao->read($id) ?? throw new BusinessException($d->notFoundKey);
            if ($d->countAppointments !== null && ($d->countAppointments)($id) > 0) {
                throw new BusinessException($d->hasAppointmentsKey);
            }
            if ($d->beforeDelete !== null) {
                ($d->beforeDelete)($id);
            }
            $d->dao->remove($person);
            $this->users->remove($person->getAccount());
        });
    }

    // refuses first and last names already used by ANOTHER person of the same type
    // ($currentId: the person being modified, who of course has the right
    // to keep their own first and last names; null for a creation)
    private function checkPersonUnique(Descriptor $d, string $firstName, string $lastName, ?int $currentId): void
    {
        $namesake = $d->dao->namesake($firstName, $lastName);
        if ($namesake !== null && $namesake->getId() !== $currentId) {
            throw new BusinessException($d->alreadyExistsKey);
        }
    }

    private function checkLoginFree(string $login): void
    {
        if ($this->users->readByLogin($login) !== null) {
            throw new BusinessException('ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN');
        }
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // executes [$work] in a transaction (wrapInTransaction, see example 28):
    // if the function ends normally, Doctrine sends the pending writes
    // to the database (flush), then commits the transaction (COMMIT); if an
    // exception comes out of it (BusinessException included), ROLLBACK: nothing is written.
    //
    // The "login free" and "unique first + last names" checks are made BEFORE
    // the write, to give a clear message. But two ADMINs could
    // save the same login (or the same doctor) at the same moment: in this
    // rare case, it is an SQL uniqueness constraint that refuses the second write.
    // Likewise, two simultaneous modifications of the same record are decided by the
    // optimistic lock. We therefore catch these errors AROUND the transaction,
    // to translate them into BusinessException. Any other error is a real
    // anomaly: we let it go up.
    // After an exception, Doctrine CLOSES the entity manager: the current request
    // must no longer write anything (the controllers redirect, or
    // redisplay a form).
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    private function transaction(Closure $work): mixed
    {
        try {
            return $this->em->wrapInTransaction($work);
        } catch (UniqueConstraintViolationException $e) {
            if (preg_match(self::CONSTRAINT, $e->getMessage(), $m)
                && isset(self::CONSTRAINT_MESSAGES[$m[1]])) {
                throw new BusinessException(self::CONSTRAINT_MESSAGES[$m[1]], previous: $e);
            }
            throw $e;
        } catch (OptimisticLockException $e) {
            throw new BusinessException('ERRORS.CONCURRENT_UPDATE', previous: $e);
        }
    }
}

The most important file in the application. We’ll go through it by topic.

docs.title: 11.11.6.1. Dependencies and descriptors
docs.text: Lines 86–124: The constructor receives from the container the entity manager (for transactions), the five DAO instances, and the hash service factory ([PasswordHasherFactoryInterface]), which is asked to provide the one for accounts: [getPasswordHasher(User::class)] provides the service that applies the algorithm chosen for class [User] in [security.yaml] ([bcrypt], 10 iterations). Next come the two descriptors. Named arguments ([dao: $doctors], example 01) make the call readable. [$appointments->countByDoctor(...)] (with three dots in parentheses) has no significance: it is the syntax of [PHP] 8.1 that creates, from a method, a [Closure]—a function that will be called later ([($d->countAppointments)($id)], line 359). A doctor is removed along with their time slots ([deleteByDoctor]), but not if they have appointments; a client is removed along with all their appointments ([deleteByClient]).

docs.title: 11.11.6.2. Read operations and the calendar
docs.text: The read operations (lines 130–178) delegate to the DAO layer. A doctor’s schedule (lines 182–198) is calculated: the doctor, their time slots, and the appointments for that day. Appointments are stored in an array indexed by slot number: [$bookings[$slot->getId()] ?? null] returns the appointment for a slot, or [null] if the slot is free. [array_map] converts each time slot to [DoctorDaySlot].

docs.title: 11.11.6.3. Scheduling an Appointment
docs.text:
Lines 216–232: four steps, in a single transaction.

  • No past appointments: The [DateTimeImmutable] entries match the usual operators ([<], [>=]...);
  • the patient’s record is locked ([lock], [SELECT ... FOR UPDATE]). Why? The rule “only one upcoming appointment per patient” is verified by a count (third step), then the insertion takes place (fourth step). If the same patient books two time slots at the same time (two tabs, a double-click), both transactions could count zero appointments and then each insert its own: the rule would be violated. With the lock, the second transaction waits for the first one to finish, then counts... one appointment. [?? throw new BusinessException(...)]: if the client no longer exists, [lock] returns [null], and the operator [??] evaluates its second operand, which raises the exception (since [PHP] 8, [throw] is an expression);
  • counting upcoming appointments;
  • insertion, at the end of the transaction. If the time slot has just been taken by another patient, the database constraint [unq1_appointments] rejects the insertion: the method [transaction] translates this error into [BusinessException].

docs.title: 11.11.6.4. Managing Doctors and Patients
docs.text:
The public methods (lines 244–274) call the shared private methods, using the correct descriptor.

  • Lines 281–302: creation. The last name is capitalized ([mb_strtoupper]: the version of [strtoupper] that supports accented letters), and the first name and last name are stripped of unnecessary spaces ([trim]). By default, the login is the last name in lowercase, and the password is the login (as per the rules for demo accounts): [$a ?: $b] is equivalent to [$a] if it is “true” (neither [null] nor an empty string), and [$b] otherwise. In the transaction: the validations (first and last names can be any value, login can be any value), then the account, whose password is hashed ([hash]), then the person, who references the account. [new ($d->entityClass)(...)] creates an object of the class whose name is in the [entityClass] property of the descriptor (parentheses are required around an expression). [Doctrine] will insert the account before the person: it knows the relationships between the entities and deduces the order of the [INSERT] objects. [use (...)]: An ordinary anonymous function ([function () use ($d, ...)]) cannot see the variables of the method that contains it; [use] passes them to it (an arrow function, [fn () =>], sees them on its own, but can only contain an expression);
  • Lines 308–344: the update, with two optimistic locks. The first is a comparison (lines 316–318): the form’s version (hidden field, Example 28) must match that of the record in the database; otherwise, someone modified the record between the time the form was displayed and the time it was submitted. The second is that of [Doctrine]: the [UPDATE] records sent at the end of the transaction carry the condition [WHERE version = ?], which detects a change that occurred between reading and writing ([OptimisticLockException]). The account follows: its displayed name (“firstName LASTNAME”) is always updated; its login and password are updated only if they were entered; its own optimistic lock also protects the row in the [users] table. There is nothing to “save”: the entity being read is tracked by the entity manager, which will write its changes. At the end of the transaction, [Doctrine] stores the new versions of the entities: the caller receives the updated person;
  • lines 355–368: deletion, in the order dictated by the foreign keys: first, the records referencing the person (time slots or appointments), immediately followed by [DELETE] from DAO; then the person, then their account, which [Doctrine] deletes in that order at the end of the transaction. The reverse order would be rejected by the database: a row that is still referenced by a foreign key cannot be deleted;
  • lines 373–387: the person being modified is allowed to retain their own first and last names; [$currentId] is equivalent to [null] for a creation.

docs.title: 11.11.6.5. Database Transactions and Errors
docs.text:
Lines 406–419: All postings use this method. [wrapInTransaction] executes the function within a transaction (Example 28): [flush], then [COMMIT] if it completes normally, and [ROLLBACK] if an exception occurs—including a [BusinessException]: a rule violation in the middle of an operation leaves no trace. The “login available” and “first and last names available” checks are performed before writing, to provide a clear message. However, two administrators could attempt to register the same login at the same time: each finds it available, and the second [INSERT] is rejected by the constraint [unq_users_login]. [Doctrine] then raises a [UniqueConstraintViolationException] (example 28), whose message is that of [MySQL]; it contains the name of the violated constraint:

SQLSTATE[23000]: Integrity constraint violation: 1062 Duplicate entry 'dupont' for key 'users.unq_users_login'

The regular expression on line 75 extracts this name ([MySQL] 8 prefixes it with the table name, [users.unq_users_login], but not [MariaDB]: the part [(?:[^'.]*\.)?] accepts both forms), and the table in lines 68–73 provides the message key. Another constraint violation is a true anomaly: it is retried ([throw $e]) and will result in a 500 error page. Finally, the conflict detected by the optimistic lock on [Doctrine] ([OptimisticLockException]) becomes the same [BusinessException] as the one detected by the version comparison.

Recall a consequence of [wrapInTransaction] (Example 28): after an exception, the entity manager is closed and can no longer write during the current request. The controllers take this into account: after a [BusinessException], they redirect or re-display a form without writing anything else.

docs.title: 11.12. Authentication
docs.text: The [src/Security] folder includes examples 25 through 27, featuring database users and a few additional security measures. Let’s review the principle (Example 25): the [main] firewall for [config/packages/security.yaml] is stateless ([stateless]); for each request, an authenticator of our own design reads the token JWT from the cookie [rdvmedecins_jwt] and identifies the user; the rules [access_control] then determine access to the pages.

docs.title: 11.12.1. src/Security/ConnectedUser.php
docs.text:
<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/Security/ConnectedUser.php: the logged-in user, as described by
// their JWT token (see example 25). UserInterface: the interface Symfony expects from
// authenticated users ($this->getUser() in a controller, #[CurrentUser],
// app.user and is_granted() in a view...).
//
// The claims of our tokens (see AuthService::tokenCookie):
//   sub   : the id of the user account (JWT convention: "subject"), as text
//   login : the login
//   name  : the displayed name ("Marie PELISSIER"), for the navigation bar
//   role  : ADMIN, DOCTOR or USER
//   iat, exp : creation and expiry dates of the token
//
// This object does NOT come from the database: it is rebuilt, on each request, from
// the token, whose signature guarantees the content.
// =========================================================================

namespace App\Security;

use App\Entity\Role;
use Symfony\Component\Security\Core\User\UserInterface;

readonly class ConnectedUser implements UserInterface
{
    public function __construct(
        public int $userId,
        public string $login,
        public string $name,
        public Role $role,
    ) {
    }

    // the user described by the claims of an already verified token; null if a claim
    // is missing or does not have the expected form. Role::tryFrom: null for an unknown role
    public static function of(array $claims): ?self
    {
        $role = Role::tryFrom((string) ($claims['role'] ?? ''));
        if (! isset($claims['sub'], $claims['login'], $claims['name']) || $role === null
            || ! ctype_digit((string) $claims['sub'])) {
            return null;
        }
        return new self((int) $claims['sub'], (string) $claims['login'], (string) $claims['name'], $role);
    }

    public function isAdmin(): bool
    {
        return $this->role === Role::ADMIN;
    }

    public function isPatient(): bool
    {
        return $this->role === Role::USER;
    }

    // ---- the UserInterface interface: the identifier of the user (their login),
    // and their roles in Symfony's sense (ROLE_ADMIN, ROLE_DOCTOR or ROLE_USER, see
    // the Role enumeration), checked by the access_control rules of
    // config/packages/security.yaml
    public function getUserIdentifier(): string
    {
        return $this->login;
    }

    public function getRoles(): array
    {
        return [$this->role->symfonyRole()];
    }
}

The logged-in user, as described by their token: their account ID, username, name, and role. Like [User] in Example 25, it implements the [UserInterface] interface, which [Symfony] expects from authenticated users. This object does not come from the database: it is reconstructed with each request, based on the token, whose signature guarantees its content. The application therefore does not read the account from the database with each request. The class is [readonly] (Example 08): its public properties cannot be modified after construction.

  • Lines 36–44: the user is described by the claims (claims) of a token that has already been verified, or [null] if one of the claims is missing or does not have the expected format. A properly signed token should never be malformed; however, the secret key could be shared with another application, which might generate different tokens: it costs nothing to be cautious. [Role::tryFrom] returns the role, or [null] for an unknown value; [ctype_digit] verifies that a string consists only of digits;
  • lines 46–54: two questions that views and controllers often ask;
  • Lines 60–68: the [UserInterface] interface. The user’s identifier is their login; their roles, as defined by [Symfony], are limited to a single role, [ROLE_ADMIN], [ROLE_DOCTOR] or [ROLE_USER], calculated by the enumeration [Role]. These are the ones checked by the rules [access_control], the attribute [#[IsGranted]], and the function [is_granted] of the views. (The [eraseCredentials] method, which cleared the plaintext password after login, has been removed from the interface with [Symfony] 8.)

docs.title: 11.12.2. src/Security/AuthService.php
docs.text:
<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/Security/AuthService.php: the authentication logic:
//   - validate()       : checks a login / password pair;
//   - tokenCookie()    : builds the JWT token of a validated user, and the
//                        cookie that carries it;
//   - currentUser()    : the user described by a token.
//
// Where does the JWT token travel? In a COOKIE (see example 25): a browser
// that displays ordinary HTML pages thus presents it on its own, on each
// request. The options of this cookie matter for security:
//   - HttpOnly: the JavaScript of the page cannot read the cookie (an injected
//     script could therefore not steal the token);
//   - SameSite=Lax: the browser does NOT send the cookie with a POST coming from another
//     site (first protection against the so-called CSRF attack; the second one is
//     the anti-CSRF token of the forms);
//   - Secure: in production (HTTPS), the cookie never travels unencrypted;
//   - lifetime: the cookie disappears at the same time as the token expires.
// =========================================================================

namespace App\Security;

use App\Dao\UserDao;
use App\Entity\User;
use Firebase\JWT\JWT;
use Firebase\JWT\Key;
use RuntimeException;
use Symfony\Component\DependencyInjection\Attribute\Autowire;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Cookie;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\PasswordHasher\Hasher\PasswordHasherFactoryInterface;
use Throwable;

class AuthService
{
    // the name of the cookie that carries the token
    public const COOKIE = 'rdvmedecins_jwt';

    // the settings of the .env file: #[Autowire(env: ...)] (see example 25)
    public function __construct(
        private UserDao $users,
        private PasswordHasherFactoryInterface $hashers,
        #[Autowire(env: 'JWT_SECRET')] private string $secret,
        #[Autowire(env: 'int:JWT_DURATION_MINUTES')] private int $duration,
        #[Autowire(env: 'bool:COOKIE_SECURE')] private bool $cookieSecure,
    ) {
        // HMAC-SHA256 requires a key of at least 256 bits: we say it clearly,
        // rather than letting the library fail further on
        if (strlen($this->secret) < 32) {
            throw new RuntimeException('JWT_SECRET must be at least 32 characters long (see .env).');
        }
    }

    // null if the login does not exist or if the password is wrong. verify hashes the
    // entered password with the "salt" contained in the stored hash, then
    // compares the two results
    public function validate(string $login, string $password): ?User
    {
        $user = $this->users->readByLogin($login);
        if ($user === null
            || ! $this->hashers->getPasswordHasher(User::class)->verify($user->getPassword(), $password)) {
            return null;
        }
        return $user;
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // the JWT token of [$user], in the cookie that carries it. The token is SIGNED
    // (HMAC-SHA256) with the secret key: the browser can read it (it is not
    // encrypted), but not modify it - any modification would make the signature
    // invalid.
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    public function tokenCookie(User $user): Cookie
    {
        $now = time();
        $claims = [
            'sub' => (string) $user->getId(),
            'login' => $user->getLogin(),
            'name' => $user->getName(),
            'role' => $user->getRole()->value,
            'iat' => $now,
            'exp' => $now + $this->duration * 60,
        ];
        $token = JWT::encode($claims, $this->secret, 'HS256');
        return Cookie::create(self::COOKIE, $token)
            ->withExpires($now + $this->duration * 60)
            ->withSecure($this->cookieSecure)
            ->withHttpOnly(true)
            ->withSameSite(Cookie::SAMESITE_LAX);
    }

    // clears the token cookie: the response carries a cookie of the same name, empty, already expired
    public static function clearCookie(Response $response): Response
    {
        $response->headers->clearCookie(self::COOKIE);
        return $response;
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // the user described by a token; null if the token is expired, forged or
    // malformed. JWT::decode checks the signature AND the expiry date (claim exp).
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    public function currentUser(string $token): ?ConnectedUser
    {
        try {
            // decode returns an object; (array) converts it into an associative array
            $claims = (array) JWT::decode($token, new Key($this->secret, 'HS256'));
        } catch (Throwable) {
            return null;
        }
        return ConnectedUser::of($claims);
    }
}
  • line 37: the name of the token cookie, a class constant, read by [AuthService::COOKIE];
  • lines 40–52: the service receives the DAO layer for accounts; the hash service factory (the one corresponding to the [User] class, bcrypt, is declared in [security.yaml]), and three settings from the [.env] file, via the [#[Autowire(env: ...)]] attribute (Example 25). The prefixes [int:] and [bool:] convert the text of the environment variable. If a key is too short, this is reported as soon as the service is started, with a clear message (see “Common Problems”);
  • Lines 57–65: Verification of a username and password (Example 25), with the account retrieved from the database by the DAO layer. Note that this service uses the DAO layer directly, without going through the business layer: password verification is not a business rule;
  • Lines 73–90: the user’s token and the cookie that carries it. The statements are the same as in Example 25, with the account ID ([sub], a string, as required by the standard) and the username. [Cookie::create] creates a cookie, which the [with...] methods supplement (each returns a new cookie: the object is immutable): its expiration date (that of the token), [Secure] (in production, on HTTPS), [HttpOnly], and [SameSite=Lax] (see the comment on lines 9–18);
  • lines 93–97: Deleting the cookie. [clearCookie(name)] adds a cookie with the same name to the response—empty and already expired—so the browser deletes it. The method is static: it requires no configuration, and the classes that call it do not need to receive the service;
  • lines 103–112: token verification (example 25).

docs.title: 11.12.3. src/Security/TokenAuthenticator.php
docs.text:
<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/Security/TokenAuthenticator.php: the AUTHENTICATOR of the firewall (see
// config/packages/security.yaml and example 25): on each request, it establishes who
// the user is, from the JWT token of the cookie [rdvmedecins_jwt].
//
// It refuses nothing itself: a missing or invalid token leaves the visitor
// ANONYMOUS. It is the access_control rules that then refuse access to the protected
// pages; a refused anonymous visitor is then handed over to the ENTRY POINT (the
// start method), which sends them back to the login page.
// =========================================================================

namespace App\Security;

use App\Web\Flash;
use Symfony\Component\EventDispatcher\Attribute\AsEventListener;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\RedirectResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Event\ResponseEvent;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\KernelEvents;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Generator\UrlGeneratorInterface;
use Symfony\Component\Security\Core\Authentication\Token\TokenInterface;
use Symfony\Component\Security\Core\Exception\AuthenticationException;
use Symfony\Component\Security\Core\Exception\CustomUserMessageAuthenticationException;
use Symfony\Component\Security\Http\Authenticator\AbstractAuthenticator;
use Symfony\Component\Security\Http\Authenticator\Passport\Badge\UserBadge;
use Symfony\Component\Security\Http\Authenticator\Passport\Passport;
use Symfony\Component\Security\Http\Authenticator\Passport\SelfValidatingPassport;
use Symfony\Component\Security\Http\EntryPoint\AuthenticationEntryPointInterface;

class TokenAuthenticator extends AbstractAuthenticator implements AuthenticationEntryPointInterface
{
    // the request attribute that signals an invalid token, to be cleared
    private const INVALID_TOKEN = '_invalid_token';

    public function __construct(
        private AuthService $auth,
        private Flash $flash,
        private UrlGeneratorInterface $urls,
    ) {
    }

    // the authenticator only acts if the request carries the token cookie
    public function supports(Request $request): ?bool
    {
        return $request->cookies->getString(AuthService::COOKIE) !== '';
    }

    // the token, checked by AuthService, describes the user: the passport
    // validates itself, and the badge returns this user directly (without
    // looking for them in the database, see example 25)
    public function authenticate(Request $request): Passport
    {
        $user = $this->auth->currentUser($request->cookies->getString(AuthService::COOKIE))
            ?? throw new CustomUserMessageAuthenticationException('invalid token');
        return new SelfValidatingPassport(new UserBadge($user->login, fn () => $user));
    }

    public function onAuthenticationSuccess(Request $request, TokenInterface $token, string $firewallName): ?Response
    {
        return null;
    }

    // an invalid token (expired, forged): the visitor stays anonymous (null), and the
    // cookie will be cleared from the response, whatever it is (see clearInvalidToken)
    public function onAuthenticationFailure(Request $request, AuthenticationException $exception): ?Response
    {
        $request->attributes->set(self::INVALID_TOKEN, true);
        return null;
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // the ENTRY POINT: an anonymous visitor asks for a protected page. Off to
    // the login page. If they had a token cookie, it means their token is no
    // longer valid (expired, forged): their session has expired, we tell them so
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    public function start(Request $request, ?AuthenticationException $authException = null): Response
    {
        if ($request->cookies->has(AuthService::COOKIE)) {
            $this->flash->error('ERRORS.SESSION_EXPIRED');
        }
        return new RedirectResponse($this->urls->generate('login'));
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    // a kernel.response listener (see example 24), written in the same class:
    // it clears the cookie of an invalid token, on all the responses
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    #[AsEventListener(event: KernelEvents::RESPONSE)]
    public function clearInvalidToken(ResponseEvent $event): void
    {
        if ($event->getRequest()->attributes->get(self::INVALID_TOKEN)) {
            AuthService::clearCookie($event->getResponse());
        }
    }
}

The authenticator from Example 25, declared in [security.yaml] ([custom_authenticators]). It also serves as the firewall’s entry point: it implements the [AuthenticationEntryPointInterface] interface, and [Symfony] selects it automatically, since it is the firewall’s only authenticator.

  • lines 45–48: [supports] determines whether the authenticator should intervene: only if the request contains the token cookie. Without a cookie, the visitor is anonymous, and no further action is taken;
  • lines 53–58: [authenticate] verifies the token. An invalid token triggers a [AuthenticationException] (its subclass, [CustomUserMessageAuthenticationException], carries a free message). Otherwise, a self-validating passport ([SelfValidatingPassport]: there is no password to verify; the token’s signature serves as the password), whose user is constructed from the token without looking it up in the database;
  • lines 60–63: after a successful authentication, [null]: the request continues on to the requested action;
  • lines 67–71: after a failure (expired or forged token), [null] as well: the visitor remains anonymous. The rules [access_control] will redirect the visitor to the login page if they request a protected page, but they can view public pages (including the login page itself!). The only indication is in a request attribute stating that the cookie should be deleted;
  • lines 78–84: the entry point, called by the firewall when an anonymous visitor requests a protected page: a redirect to the login page. If the request contained a token cookie, it means that token is no longer valid: the message “Your session has expired: please log in again.” is displayed (a pop-up message, discussed later);
  • Lines 90–96: A listener for event [kernel.response] (Example 24), defined within the same class: the [#[AsEventListener]] attribute is applied to a method, and the authenticator—a service like any other—also becomes a listener. It deletes the cookie for an invalid token, regardless of the response: the login page, a public page, or a redirect from the entry point. An invalid cookie serves no purpose and would corrupt the message of the next request.

docs.title: 11.12.4. src/Security/InvalidSession.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Security/InvalidSession.php: the token is valid, but the account it
// designates no longer exists: it has been deleted since the login (by the patient
// themselves in another tab, or by the ADMIN). We treat this case as an
// expired session: the ErrorPage listener clears the cookie and sends back to the login
// page.

namespace App\Security;

use RuntimeException;

class InvalidSession extends RuntimeException
{
}

A scenario not covered in Example 25: the token is valid, but the account it refers to no longer exists. A patient has deleted their account in one tab, but the token is still present in another tab; or the administrator has deleted the account of a logged-in patient. The token’s signature provides no indication of the account’s existence; it is only when the application searches for the patient associated with the account ([Utils::connectedPatient], discussed later) that it discovers the account no longer exists. It then throws this exception, which the listener [ErrorPage] (discussed later) treats as an expired session. The class is empty: only its type matters, which the listener recognizes ([instanceof]).

docs.title: 11.12.5. src/Security/CaptchaService.php, Captcha.php, and CaptchaDrawing.php
docs.text:
[CaptchaDrawing.php] and [Captcha.php] are from Example 27. The service is almost the same:

<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/Security/CaptchaService.php: a CAPTCHA ("test to tell a human from a
// robot") built by the server itself, without any external service (see example 27).
//
// How it works:
//   1. generate() draws a random text, makes an image of it, and stores the right
//      answer IN THE CACHE of the server, under a random identifier;
//   2. the page displays the image and puts the identifier in a hidden field of the
//      form (the answer itself never leaves the server);
//   3. verify(id, typed) compares the input with the expected answer, then FORGETS
//      this captcha: each image is used only once, a robot cannot replay
//      an answer already found.
//
// Why the cache? A PHP application keeps NOTHING in memory from one request to
// the next: each request starts from scratch. What must last beyond a request
// therefore goes into the cache (here files, in var/cache), shared by all the
// requests, and even by several servers with a cache like Redis.
// =========================================================================

namespace App\Security;

use Psr\Cache\CacheItemPoolInterface;
use Symfony\Component\Lock\LockFactory;

class CaptchaService
{
    // validity duration of an image, in seconds: 10 minutes to fill in the form
    private const LIFETIME = 600;

    public function __construct(private CacheItemPoolInterface $cache, private LockFactory $locks)
    {
    }

    public function generate(): Captcha
    {
        $text = CaptchaDrawing::randomText(5);        // 5 characters
        $id = bin2hex(random_bytes(12));              // an identifier impossible to guess
        // the cache will forget the answer by itself after 10 minutes
        $item = $this->cache->getItem("captcha.$id");
        $this->cache->save($item->set($text)->expiresAfter(self::LIFETIME));
        return new Captcha($id, CaptchaDrawing::svg($text));
    }

    // true if [$typed] is the right answer to the captcha [$id] (regardless of
    // case). The captcha is consumed in all cases.
    public function verify(?string $id, ?string $typed): bool
    {
        // the identifier comes from the browser: hexadecimal digits, or nothing
        if ($id === null || ! ctype_xdigit($id) || $typed === null) {
            return false;
        }
        // if two requests present the same captcha at the same moment, only one
        // gets the lock (acquire(false): without waiting) - the other one fails
        $lock = $this->locks->createLock("captcha.$id");
        if (! $lock->acquire(false)) {
            return false;
        }
        try {
            $item = $this->cache->getItem("captcha.$id");
            $this->cache->deleteItem("captcha.$id");
        } finally {
            $lock->release();
        }
        return $item->isHit() && strcasecmp($item->get(), trim($typed)) === 0;
    }
}
  • lines 35–43: a 5-character string generated at random, a random identifier ([random_bytes], a cryptographic generator, whose bytes are written in hexadecimal as [bin2hex]), and the correct answer stored in the cache (example 20) for 10 minutes ([expiresAfter], in seconds);
  • lines 47–66: a difference from Example 27. The answer is read, then removed from the cache. Between the reading and the removal, a second request presenting the same CAPTCHA could also read it: two attempts for a single solved image. A lock (Example 20), specific to this CAPTCHA, therefore protects both the reading and the removal. [acquire(false)] acquires it immediately: it returns [false] if another request already holds it, and that request, which loses the race, fails. The block [finally] releases the lock in all cases. The comparison ignores uppercase letters ([strcasecmp] returns 0 for two strings that are case-insensitive matches) and spaces around the input ([trim]).

docs.title: 11.12.6. src/Security/AttemptLimiter.php
docs.text:
<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/Security/AttemptLimiter.php: second rampart against robots (the first one
// is the captcha): we COUNT the attempts, and beyond a threshold we BLOCK
// for a while (see example 27).
//
//   - login: after LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES failures (wrong captcha or wrong
//     password) for the same login from the same IP address, this pair is
//     blocked until the end of a window of LOGIN_BLOCK_MINUTES minutes, counted
//     from the first failure. The same IP address is also blocked if it accumulates
//     LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES_IP failures, all logins together (a robot trying
//     thousands of different logins);
//   - account creation: at most REGISTRATION_MAX_PER_HOUR accounts created per
//     hour from the same IP address.
//
// Beware in a classroom: all the computers often go out to the Internet through the
// SAME IP address. That is why the login block first applies to the
// pair (IP, login) - a student who mistypes their password does not block their
// neighbours - and why the thresholds can be adjusted (.env file).
//
// The counters are those of the three limiters of the RateLimiter component, declared
// in config/packages/framework.yaml, and stored in the cache.
// =========================================================================

namespace App\Security;

use Symfony\Component\RateLimiter\LimiterInterface;
use Symfony\Component\RateLimiter\RateLimiterFactoryInterface;

class AttemptLimiter
{
    // the factories of the limiters [login], [login_ip] and [registration]: the name
    // of the parameter designates the limiter (see example 27)
    public function __construct(
        private RateLimiterFactoryInterface $loginLimiter,
        private RateLimiterFactoryInterface $loginIpLimiter,
        private RateLimiterFactoryInterface $registrationLimiter,
    ) {
    }

    // ---------------------------------------------------------------- login

    // number of remaining block minutes (0 = the attempt is allowed)
    public function loginBlockMinutes(string $ip, string $login): int
    {
        return max(self::remainingMinutes($this->ipLoginLimiter($ip, $login)),
            self::remainingMinutes($this->loginIpLimiter->create($ip)));
    }

    // consume(): one more failure; the first one opens a window of
    // LOGIN_BLOCK_MINUTES minutes, at the end of which the counter starts again from zero
    public function loginFailure(string $ip, string $login): void
    {
        $this->ipLoginLimiter($ip, $login)->consume();
        $this->loginIpLimiter->create($ip)->consume();
    }

    // a successful login resets the counter of THIS login
    public function loginSuccess(string $ip, string $login): void
    {
        $this->ipLoginLimiter($ip, $login)->reset();
    }

    // ---------------------------------------------------------------- registration

    public function registrationBlockMinutes(string $ip): int
    {
        return self::remainingMinutes($this->registrationLimiter->create($ip));
    }

    public function registrationSuccess(string $ip): void
    {
        $this->registrationLimiter->create($ip)->consume();
    }

    // ---------------------------------------------------------------- common mechanics

    // the limiter of the pair (IP, login): create(key) returns a limiter that has its
    // own counter, under this key
    private function ipLoginLimiter(string $ip, string $login): LimiterInterface
    {
        return $this->loginLimiter->create("$ip|".mb_strtolower(trim($login)));
    }

    // consume(0) queries the limiter without consuming anything: no "token" left?
    // getRetryAfter: the date of the end of the current window; the seconds that
    // remain until then are rounded UP to the minute: 30 s -> "1 minute"
    private static function remainingMinutes(LimiterInterface $limiter): int
    {
        $state = $limiter->consume(0);
        if ($state->getRemainingTokens() > 0) {
            return 0;
        }
        return max(1, (int) ceil(($state->getRetryAfter()->getTimestamp() - time()) / 60));
    }
}

The second line of defense against bots, after the CAPTCHA: we count the attempts, and once a threshold is exceeded, we block access. Example 27 presented the [RateLimiter] component of [Symfony]. The three limiters are declared in [config/packages/framework.yaml] (policy [fixed_window]: a fixed-duration window, opened by the first token consumed); the service receives their factories, identified by the parameter names (lines 34–38): [$loginLimiter] for the limiter [login], [$loginIpLimiter] for [login_ip], [$registrationLimiter] for [registration]. A factory uses its method [create(key)] to create a limiter that has its own counter under this key. Two rules:

  • the connection (lines 44–62): each failure (incorrect CAPTCHA or password) is counted twice: for the pair (address IP, login), and for the address IP alone. The pair is blocked after 5 failed attempts (setting [LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES]), and the address IP after 25 (setting [LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES_IP]), across all logins: It’s the bot trying thousands of different logins. Why not block the address IP first? In a classroom (or at a company), all machines often access the Internet through the same address, IP: a student who enters the wrong password shouldn’t block their neighbors. [consume()] consumes a token (counts as a failed attempt); the first attempt opens a 15-minute window (setting [LOGIN_BLOCK_MINUTES]), at the end of which the counter resets to zero. A successful connection resets the counter for that user ([reset]);
  • account creation (lines 66–74): no more than 10 accounts per hour per address IP (setting [REGISTRATION_MAX_PER_HOUR]);
  • lines 80–83: the key for a torque limiter. The login is in lowercase: [Admin] and [admin] are considered the same (as with the database; see its collation);
  • Lines 88–95: [consume(0)] queries the limiter without consuming any tokens (example 27): there are tokens remaining, so the attempt is allowed; otherwise, [getRetryAfter] returns the end date of the current window, and the number of seconds remaining until then is rounded up to the next minute ([ceil]): there are 30 seconds left, so “1 minute” is displayed. The message displayed depends on this: “Too many failed attempts. Try again in 15 minutes.”

The limiters’ counters are stored in the cache: they are shared by all requests and survive a server restart. The command [php bin/console cache:pool:clear cache.rate_limiter] resets them all to zero (useful during development, when you’ve gotten yourself stuck); [php bin/console cache:clear], which clears the entire [var/cache] directory, does the same.

docs.title: 11.12.7. src/Security/RegistrationPass.php and RegistrationPassRequired.php
docs.text:
<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/Security/RegistrationPass.php: the "pass" of the account creation.
//
// To open the page "Create a patient account", one must first have copied the
// captcha of the login page (see RegistrationController, POST
// /register/access). The server then issues a pass:
//   - a random identifier, stored in an HttpOnly cookie;
//   - valid for 15 minutes (the time to fill in the form, even when trying
//     several times after input errors);
//   - consumed as soon as an account is created: ONE solved captcha = ONE account at most.
//     A robot cannot create accounts in series.
//
// Without a valid pass, GET and POST /register send back to the login
// page (see the #[RegistrationPassRequired] attribute and the listener
// CheckRegistrationPass): typing the URL /register directly does not allow
// getting around the captcha.
//
// Like the captchas, the passes live in the cache.
// =========================================================================

namespace App\Security;

use Psr\Cache\CacheItemPoolInterface;
use Symfony\Component\DependencyInjection\Attribute\Autowire;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Cookie;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;

class RegistrationPass
{
    public const COOKIE = 'rdvmedecins_registration';

    // the cookie is sent by the browser only to the /register... addresses
    private const PATH = '/register';

    // lifetime of a pass, in minutes
    private const LIFETIME = 15;

    public function __construct(
        private CacheItemPoolInterface $cache,
        #[Autowire(env: 'bool:COOKIE_SECURE')] private bool $cookieSecure,
    ) {
    }

    // issues a new pass; returns the cookie that carries it
    public function issue(): Cookie
    {
        $id = bin2hex(random_bytes(12));
        $item = $this->cache->getItem("pass.$id");
        $this->cache->save($item->set(true)->expiresAfter(self::LIFETIME * 60));
        return Cookie::create(self::COOKIE, $id)
            ->withExpires(time() + self::LIFETIME * 60)
            ->withPath(self::PATH)
            ->withSecure($this->cookieSecure)
            ->withHttpOnly(true)
            ->withSameSite(Cookie::SAMESITE_LAX);
    }

    // true if [$id] is an existing, non-expired pass; hasItem: does the
    // cache have this item?
    public function isValid(?string $id): bool
    {
        return $id !== null && ctype_xdigit($id) && $this->cache->hasItem("pass.$id");
    }

    // the pass has been used: we forget it...
    public function consume(?string $id): void
    {
        if ($id !== null && ctype_xdigit($id)) {
            $this->cache->deleteItem("pass.$id");
        }
    }

    // ... and its cookie is cleared by a cookie of the same name and the same path, already expired
    public static function clearCookie(Response $response): Response
    {
        $response->headers->clearCookie(self::COOKIE, self::PATH);
        return $response;
    }
}

Creating a patient account is protected by the CAPTCHA on the login page. But the account creation form is on a different page ([/register]): how can the system know, when the form is requested, that the CAPTCHA was solved just before? Through a token: when the CAPTCHA is solved, the server generates a random identifier, stores it in the cache for 15 minutes, and sends it to the browser in a cookie. The form is only displayed—and the account is only created—with a valid token; the token is consumed when the account is created. A solved CAPTCHA thus allows you to create an account, and typing the address [/register] directly leads nowhere.

  • Lines 46–57: The cookie has the path [/register] ([withPath]): the browser sends it only to addresses that begin with this path. It contains only a random identifier—impossible to guess—and only the server’s cache knows whether it is valid: the cookie does not need to be signed;
  • lines 61–64: [hasItem] indicates whether the cache contains an (unexpired) entry under this key;
  • lines 75–79: To delete a cookie, you must specify the same name and the same path: to the browser, two cookies with the same name but different paths are two distinct cookies.
<?php
// src/Security/RegistrationPassRequired.php: a PHP ATTRIBUTE of our own (see
// example 24), placed on the actions that require an account creation pass
// (see RegistrationPass and the listener CheckRegistrationPass).

namespace App\Security;

use Attribute;

#[Attribute(Attribute::TARGET_METHOD)]
class RegistrationPassRequired
{
}

An attribute [PHP] of our own invention, like the [#[Timed]] in Example 24, is applied to actions that require a pass. It is read by the listener [CheckRegistrationPass].

docs.title: 11.13. The listeners: src/EventListener
docs.text: Three kernel event listeners (Example 24), stored in the [src/EventListener] folder, as is customary. The [#[AsEventListener]] attribute, set on the class, specifies the event and priority; the method called is then [__invoke].

docs.title: 11.13.1. src/EventListener/SetLanguage.php
docs.text:
<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/EventListener/SetLanguage.php: the language of the request (see example 22):
// that of the cookie [rdvmedecins_language] if it is a supported language, English otherwise.
//
// Priority 40: the listener runs BEFORE Symfony's routing (priority 32). It
// thus runs for ALL the requests, even those that lead to no
// route (404, 405 page...): their error page is in the right language. For the
// same reason, it also sets the language of the translator itself, which would otherwise be done by
// a Symfony listener (priority 15) that a routing error would prevent
// from running.
// =========================================================================

namespace App\EventListener;

use Symfony\Component\EventDispatcher\Attribute\AsEventListener;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Event\RequestEvent;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\KernelEvents;
use Symfony\Contracts\Translation\LocaleAwareInterface;

#[AsEventListener(event: KernelEvents::REQUEST, priority: 40)]
class SetLanguage
{
    // the cookie that remembers the chosen language (see LanguageController)
    public const COOKIE = 'rdvmedecins_language';

    // the supported languages (translations folder); the first one is the default language
    public const LANGUAGES = ['en', 'fr'];

    // LocaleAwareInterface: a service that has a language, here the translator
    public function __construct(private LocaleAwareInterface $translator)
    {
    }

    public function __invoke(RequestEvent $event): void
    {
        $request = $event->getRequest();
        $language = $request->cookies->get(self::COOKIE);
        $language = in_array($language, self::LANGUAGES, true) ? $language : self::LANGUAGES[0];
        $request->setLocale($language);
        $this->translator->setLocale($language);
    }
}

The request language (Example 22): the language of the cookie, if it is a supported language; otherwise, the default language (English). A difference from Example 22: priority 40 (line 21), which is higher than the routing priority (32). The listener in Example 22 (priority 20) ran after the routing; for a URL that does not match any route, the routing throws an exception before the listener, and the 404 page would have been in English even for a French-speaking user. For the same reason, the listener itself sets the translator’s language (line 41), which is typically done by a listener for [Symfony] ([LocaleAwareListener]), which is also placed after the routing. [LocaleAwareInterface] is the interface for services that have a language; the translator is one of them, and it is this translator that [Symfony] injects here.

docs.title: 11.13.2. src/EventListener/CheckRegistrationPass.php
docs.text:
<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/EventListener/CheckRegistrationPass.php: the actions marked with
// the #[RegistrationPassRequired] attribute (GET and POST /register) require a
// valid pass (see src/Security/RegistrationPass.php); otherwise, back to
// the login page, with a message. Typing the URL
// /register directly therefore does not allow getting around the captcha.
//
// A kernel.controller listener (see example 24): the action is chosen, but
// not called yet. To refuse, it REPLACES it (setController) with a
// function that returns a redirection.
// =========================================================================

namespace App\EventListener;

use App\Security\RegistrationPass;
use App\Security\RegistrationPassRequired;
use App\Web\Flash;
use Symfony\Component\EventDispatcher\Attribute\AsEventListener;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\RedirectResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Event\ControllerEvent;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\KernelEvents;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Generator\UrlGeneratorInterface;

#[AsEventListener(event: KernelEvents::CONTROLLER)]
class CheckRegistrationPass
{
    public function __construct(
        private RegistrationPass $passes,
        private Flash $flash,
        private UrlGeneratorInterface $urls,
    ) {
    }

    public function __invoke(ControllerEvent $event): void
    {
        if ($event->getAttributes(RegistrationPassRequired::class) === []) {
            return;
        }
        if (! $this->passes->isValid($event->getRequest()->cookies->get(RegistrationPass::COOKIE))) {
            $this->flash->error('ERRORS.CAPTCHA_BEFORE_ACCOUNT');
            $url = $this->urls->generate('login');
            $event->setController(fn () => new RedirectResponse($url));
        }
    }
}

A listener for [kernel.controller] (example 24): the action is selected but not yet called.

  • lines 37–39: [getAttributes(class)] returns the attributes of this class carried by the action: an empty list; the action does not require a token; the listener does nothing;
  • lines 40–44: no valid token: a message is displayed, and the action is replaced ([setController]) by a function that redirects to the login page. The kernel calls this function instead of the action. URL is calculated outside the arrow function, which therefore requires only one variable.

The listener receives its services through its constructor: a listener is a service, created by the container, just like controllers.

docs.title: 11.13.3. src/EventListener/ErrorPage.php
docs.text:
<?php
// =========================================================================
// src/EventListener/ErrorPage.php: how errors become HTML pages
// (see example 24). Three cases:
//   1. an InvalidSession (account deleted since the login) -> back to the
//      login page, as for an expired session;
//   2. an HTTP error: invalid request (400), insufficient role (403), unknown
//      page (404), unsupported method (405), missing or wrong anti-CSRF
//      token (419)... -> the error page, with the original code;
//   3. any other exception (a real anomaly): Symfony has already written it to
//      the log, with its call stack; in production (APP_ENV=prod),
//      the user sees the 500 error page - never the call stack; in
//      development, Symfony's debug page.
//
// Priority -10: after Symfony's listener that writes the exception to the log
// (0) and after that of security (1), which turns an access refusal into a
// redirection to the login page (anonymous visitor) or into a 403 error
// (authenticated user); before the one that builds Symfony's error page
// (-128).
// =========================================================================

namespace App\EventListener;

use App\Security\AuthService;
use App\Security\InvalidSession;
use App\Web\Flash;
