docs.title: 11.21.2. public/js/app.js
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// public/js/app.js - the ONLY JavaScript of the application.
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The whole application works without JavaScript. This script adds a
// convenience: before sending a form that carries the attribute
// data-confirmation="...", a modal dialog asks "Are you sure?"
// (the dialog itself is in the page: templates/fragments/confirmation.html.twig).
// If JavaScript is disabled, the form is simply sent without
// confirmation - nothing breaks ("progressive enhancement" principle).
//
// Why not window.confirm()? Its box cannot be styled, and its
// buttons stay in the language of the browser, not in that of the page.
// =========================================================================

(() => {
  const modal = document.getElementById('confirmation-modal');
  if (!modal) {
    return;
  }
  const message = document.getElementById('confirmation-modal-message');
  const noButton = modal.querySelector('.modal-footer [data-action="no"]');

  let pendingForm = null; // the form to send if the user confirms
  let previousFocus = null; // the element to give the focus back to on closing

  function open(form) {
    pendingForm = form;
    previousFocus = document.activeElement;
    // textContent (and not innerHTML): the message is displayed as TEXT,
    // never interpreted as HTML
    message.textContent = form.dataset.confirmation;
    modal.classList.remove('d-none');
    // the focus goes on "No": an absent-minded press on Enter deletes nothing
    noButton.focus();
  }

  function close() {
    modal.classList.add('d-none');
    pendingForm = null;
    if (previousFocus) {
      previousFocus.focus();
    }
  }

  // 1. we intercept the sending of the forms to confirm
  document.querySelectorAll('form[data-confirmation]').forEach((form) => {
    form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
      event.preventDefault();
      open(form);
    });
  });

  // 2. the buttons of the dialog (Yes / No / close cross)
  modal.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
    const action = event.target.closest('[data-action]')?.dataset.action;
    if (action === 'yes') {
      const form = pendingForm;
      close();
      // form.submit() sends the form WITHOUT triggering the
      // 'submit' event again: no new confirmation request
      form.submit();
    } else if (action === 'no') {
      close();
    } else if (event.target.classList.contains('modal')) {
      close(); // click on the grey background, outside the dialog
    }
  });

  // 3. keyboard: Escape closes the dialog; Tab stays INSIDE the dialog
  //    (otherwise the focus would go to the greyed-out page, behind)
  modal.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
    if (event.key === 'Escape') {
      close();
    } else if (event.key === 'Tab') {
      const buttons = [...modal.querySelectorAll('button')];
      const first = buttons[0];
      const last = buttons[buttons.length - 1];
      if (event.shiftKey && document.activeElement === first) {
        event.preventDefault();
        last.focus();
      } else if (!event.shiftKey && document.activeElement === last) {
        event.preventDefault();
        first.focus();
      }
    }
  });
})();

The only [JavaScript] in the application—the one from Example 21—with a few additions. The entire application works without [JavaScript]: this script adds convenience by providing a confirmation before submitting a form that carries the [data-confirmation] attribute. If [JavaScript] is disabled, the form submits without confirmation: nothing breaks (principle of progressive enhancement).

  • Lines 15–19: The script is a function called as soon as it is defined ([(() => { ... })()]); its variables are not visible to the rest of the page. Without a confirmation window on the page, it does nothing;
  • Lines 26–35: Opening the window: the form to be submitted if the user confirms is stored, and the form’s message is displayed in the window. [textContent], not [innerHTML]: the message is displayed as text and is never interpreted as HTML. Focus moves to the “No” button: accidentally pressing Enter does not delete anything;
  • lines 37–43: closing the window; focus returns to the element that had it previously;
  • lines 46–51: the submission of each form to be confirmed is intercepted ([preventDefault] prevents it), and the window opens;
  • lines 54–67: the window’s buttons. A single handler for the entire window: [closest('[data-action]')] finds the clicked button or the element containing it. “Yes” submits the form via [form.submit()], which does not trigger the [submit] event: no new confirmation request is issued. Clicking on the grayed-out background outside the window closes it;
  • lines 71–86: the keyboard. Esc closes the window; the Tab key moves focus from one button to another without leaving the window (otherwise, it would move to the grayed-out page behind it): this is what users who navigate with the keyboard and screen readers expect.

docs.title: 12. Conclusion
docs.text:
This document described the development of a MVC web application using the [Symfony] framework: an application whose HTML pages are generated by the server, using [Twig] views, without a browser-side [JavaScript] framework. He followed the [Laravel] course step by step, which itself builds upon the courses [Flask], [Spring MVC], [ASP.NET Core MVC], and [NestJS]: actions and routing to views, forms, internationalization, security, and data access, followed by a comprehensive case study.

The same 28 examples and the same application were thus written using six frameworks: in [TypeScript], in [C#], in [Java], in [Python], and twice in [PHP]. The concepts are the same; only the names and mechanisms differ. The correspondences between [Laravel] and [Symfony], the two major frameworks of the [PHP] world:

[Laravel][Symfony][bootstrap/app.php], service providers,([src/Kernel.php]), bundles, compiled container ([config/services.yaml], [#[Autowire]])[composer.json], folder [vendor], [php artisan][composer.json], folder [vendor], [php bin/console]file [.env], folder [config] (files [PHP]), functions [env] and [config]file [.env], folder [config/packages] (files YAML), [%env(...)%], container settings[routes/web.php], named routes, route groupscontroller attributes [#[Route]], on the action and on the class[view], [redirect], [route][render], [redirectToRoute], [generateUrl] ([AbstractController]); [path] in viewsobject [Request], constraints ([whereNumber]), model linkobject [Request], [requirements] ([{id<\d+>}]), argument resolvers, [#[MapQueryString]], [#[MapRequestPayload]][Validator], form requests ([FormRequest]), rules, [$errors], [old()]Validator component (attribute constraints), Form component (types, [handleRequest], [isValid])views [Blade], [{{ }}], [@foreach], [@if]views [Twig], [{{ }}], [{% for %}], [{% if %}][@extends] and sections, [@include], components ([<x-...>])[{% extends %}] and blocks, [{% include %}], macrosview composer ([View::composer])global variables of [Twig], extensions [Twig] (functions, filters)session flash data ([session()->flash], [with])flash messages ([addFlash], [app.flashes]), session in files(global, group, route), [terminate] methodkernel event listeners ([kernel.request], [kernel.controller], [kernel.response], [kernel.terminate]...)[withExceptions], [render], [abort]Listeners: [kernel.exception], [HttpException], [createNotFoundException]guards ([Auth::viaRequest]), middleware [auth], [Gate], facade [Hash]firewall, authenticators, [access_control], [#[IsGranted]], voters, hashing ([security.yaml])[PreventRequestForgery] middleware, [@csrf] directive (419 response)Form component token, [csrf_token()] and [isCsrfTokenValid] (403 response, or 419 in our application)[RateLimiter] (facade)Component [RateLimiter] (limiters declared in [framework.yaml])folder [lang], function [__()], [App::setLocale]folder [translations] (YAML, ICU), filter [trans], [TranslatorInterface], query language[Carbon] ([isoFormat]), [Number]Extension [intl]: [IntlDateFormatter], [NumberFormatter]Cache ([Cache], [Cache::lock])Cache component (PSR-6 and contracts), Lock component[Eloquent]: Active Record models, relationships ([belongsTo], [with])[Doctrine]: Data Mapper entities, entity manager, DQL and QueryBuilder, relationships ([ManyToOne], [OneToOne])[DB::transaction(...)][wrapInTransaction(...)], [flush][WHERE version = ?] and [version + 1], written to layer DAO[#[ORM\Version]], managed by [Doctrine] ([OptimisticLockException])[php artisan serve][php -S localhost:8000 -t public], or [symfony server:start]

Regarding [Laravel], the key points to note are:

  • [Symfony] is a set of independent components, assembled into bundles. Each component is self-contained, and [Laravel] uses several of them ([HttpFoundation], [HttpKernel], [Routing], [Console]...) : Readers of the previous lesson will recognize the same objects here: [Request] and [Response]. An application named [Symfony] installs only the components it needs: the examples started with just [framework-bundle], and then added, one by one, [Twig], validation, forms, security, and [Doctrine];
  • Everything goes through the service container and dependency injection: no facades or global functions, but services passed to the constructor and declared by type (autowiring). A class’s dependencies are always visible in its constructor. The container is compiled into code [PHP] and cached: this offsets the cost of rebuilding the application with each request (Example 01);
  • The processing of a request consists of a sequence of kernel events to which listeners respond: this is where language, security, application controls (the pass), and error pages are handled. The mechanism is more explicit than the middleware in [Laravel]: each listener chooses its event and priority, and the command [debug:event-dispatcher] displays the order of all listeners;
  • the configuration is explicit, in YAML (or [PHP]) files that describe each bundle: the firewall, access rules, limiters, and session, [Doctrine]. The commands [debug:router], [debug:container], and [debug:config] display what [Symfony] has interpreted;
  • The [PHP] attributes describe the code: routes ([#[Route]]), constraints ([#[Assert\NotBlank]]), entities ([#[ORM\Column]]), listeners ([#[AsEventListener]]), permissions ([#[IsGranted]]), and injection ([#[Autowire]]). We’ve even written some ([#[Timed]], [#[RegistrationPassRequired]]);
  • forms are objects, described by classes such as: fields, constraints, value conversion, input redispatch, error messages, and anti-CSRF tokens. This is more code than the form requests in [Laravel] for a small form, and much less for a large one: a theme ([Bootstrap] 5) styles all fields the same way;
  • security is a fully-fledged component: a firewall, authenticators that verify the user, access rules, a role hierarchy, and voters. We adapted it to our needs (a JWT token in a cookie) using an authenticator consisting of a few dozen lines, without losing any of the other features: [access_control], [#[IsGranted]], [is_granted] in the views;
  • [Doctrine] follows the Data Mapper pattern: the entities are ordinary [PHP] objects that are unaware of the database; it is the entity manager that reads them, tracks their changes, and writes them all together, in a single transaction, at the time of the [flush]. More abstract than [Eloquent]’s Active Record, it clearly separates objects from their records and supports mechanisms such as optimistic locking. The SQL order log allows you, as with [Eloquent], to verify what is sent to the database;
  • the [Twig] views have their own language, which is more limited than the [PHP] used in the [Blade] views: a view can only display the data provided to it. This is both a constraint and a guarantee: the logic remains within the classes. They are compiled into [PHP], cached, and automatically escape the content they display.

The case study shows that a classic HTML application, without the essential [JavaScript], remains a simple and robust solution: each page is a URL, the browser’s “Back” button works, and the server controls everything. The limited use of [JavaScript] (confirmation windows) enhances the user experience without being necessary for operation. [Symfony] can also support more interactive applications without leaving [Twig] ([Symfony UX]: [Turbo], [Stimulus], Live Components) or with a browser-side [JavaScript] framework, to which it provides a API JSON ([API Platform]): this will be covered in other documents.

For further information, please refer to the [Symfony] documentation (symfony.com/doc), particularly the pages dedicated to the service container, kernel events, forms, security, and [Doctrine], as well as the documentation for [Twig] (twig.symfony.com), the documentation for [Doctrine] (doctrine-project.org), the documentation for [PHP] (php.net/manual/en), and compare this application with its counterparts [Laravel], [Flask], [Spring MVC], [ASP.NET Core MVC], and [NestJS].

docs.title: 6. Data Scopes
docs.text:
A web application serves many users at once, and each user makes numerous requests. Data can therefore be shared at several levels, known as its scope:

  • application scope: the data is shared by all users throughout the application’s lifetime (the list of doctors, for example);
  • request scope: the data exists only for the duration of processing a request (a view’s model, the logged-in user as identified for that request);
  • session scope: the data is specific to a user and must persist from one request to the next (the selected language, a shopping cart);
  • client scope: data stored in the browser itself, in a cookie.

In [PHP], these scopes behave in a particular way because the application is rebuilt with every request (Example 01): nothing survives in memory from one request to the next. Any data that needs to last longer than a single request is therefore stored outside of [PHP]: in the cache, a database, files, or on the client’s side. This is the so-called “shared-nothing” architecture: each request is processed in isolation by a process that shares nothing with those processing other requests. This approach has significant advantages: an error affects only a single request, no data leaks from one user to another, and multiple identical servers can be run behind a load balancer, provided they share the same cache and database.

In [Symfony], each scope has its own container:

ScopeContainerLifetimeapplicationthe cache (service [cache.app], example 20), or the databasethe selected duration, or unlimitedQuerythe container’s services (one object per class, during the request), the request attributes (example 12)processing a requestsessionthe session ([$request->getSession()], Example 20), maintained by the server and retrieved via a cookieuntil the browser is closed by default, and at most for the duration of the [PHP] session (24 minutes of inactivity by default)clienta cookie ([Cookie::create], example 22), in plain textThe cookie's expiration time

The [Symfony] session is a server-side session, like those for [Java] ([JSESSIONID]) or the standard [PHP], from which it actually borrows the mechanism and the cookie ([PHPSESSID]): its data is stored on the server (one file per session, with the configuration used in our examples), and the browser holds only the identifier—a random number that is impossible to guess. This differs from [Flask], whose entire session is stored in a signed cookie on the client’s side.
