docs.title: 9.1.1. The database
docs.text:
The [dbpersons] database is created by the SQL script. Using [Laragon], you can run it, for example, in the [HeidiSQL] tool (File menu / Run a SQL file), or from the command line, from the example folder:

mysql -u root < database/dbpersons.sql

The [database/dbpersons.sql] file:

-- database of example 28: a single table, [persons]
-- the script is written in UTF-8
SET NAMES utf8mb4;
DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS dbpersons;
CREATE DATABASE dbpersons CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE dbpersons;

CREATE TABLE persons (
  id INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
  -- the version of the row, increased at each modification (see DAO layer)
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  first_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  last_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  age INT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (id),
  -- two persons cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_persons_first_name_last_name UNIQUE (first_name, last_name)
) ENGINE = InnoDB;

INSERT INTO persons (first_name, last_name, age) VALUES
  ('Marie', 'Pélissier', 42),
  ('Jacques', 'Bromard', 35),
  ('Philippe', 'Jandot', 58);
  • Line 3: The script is written in [UTF-8]; this is specified to the server so that the accents in the data ([Pélissier]) remain intact;
  • Line 5: The character set [utf8mb4] accepts all characters (accents, emojis, etc.). The [utf8mb4_unicode_ci] collation compares strings without regard to uppercase letters or accents: for [MySQL], [pelissier], and [Pélissier] are equal;
  • line 11: a version number, incremented each time the line is modified (see “optimistic lock,” below);
  • line 17: a named uniqueness constraint: the database does not allow two people with the same first and last names.

[Doctrine] can also create the tables itself, based on entities (command [bin/console doctrine:schema:create]), or through migrations: [PHP] classes that describe, step by step, the creation and modification of each table (library [DoctrineMigrationsBundle], command [bin/console doctrine:migrations:migrate]). We maintain a script, SQL, which is common to all versions of the case study and shows exactly what the database contains.

docs.title: 9.1.2. Configuration
docs.text:
DoctrineBundle is added to the list of bundles:

<?php
// config/bundles.php: the bundles of the application; the DoctrineBundle integrates
// Doctrine (DBAL and ORM), the database access library
return [
    Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\FrameworkBundle::class => ['all' => true],
    Symfony\Bundle\TwigBundle\TwigBundle::class => ['all' => true],
    Doctrine\Bundle\DoctrineBundle\DoctrineBundle::class => ['all' => true],
];

The connection to the database is described in the file [.env] by a URL:

# .env: the configuration of example 28 (see example 01)
APP_ENV=dev
APP_SECRET=fe7d5dd3bafdb5b7ffcab097dd4e1c0c
# the database connection: the MySQL DBMS, on this machine (127.0.0.1), port 3306,
# the dbpersons database, the root user without password (Laragon's settings)
DATABASE_URL="mysql://root:@127.0.0.1:3306/dbpersons?serverVersion=8.0.32&charset=utf8mb4"

The URL [DATABASE_URL] combines all the connection parameters: the DBMS ([mysql]), the username and password ([root], with nothing following [:]), the host and port, and finally the database name. If your server has a password, enter it after [:] ([root:secret@...]). Two parameters follow [?]: [serverVersion], the server version ([Doctrine] adapts the SQL it generates for each version; for [MariaDB], for example, we would write [serverVersion=10.11.2-MariaDB]), and [charset], the character set used for communication with the server, which is the database’s character set. The configuration of DoctrineBundle:

# config/packages/doctrine.yaml: the configuration of the DoctrineBundle
doctrine:
    # DBAL: the database connection, described by a URL (.env file)
    dbal:
        url: '%env(resolve:DATABASE_URL)%'
        # the SQL statements are written to the log (the console) in debug mode
        logging: '%kernel.debug%'
    # ORM: the ENTITIES, the classes associated with the tables, are the classes of the
    # src/Entity folder; their mapping to the tables is described by PHP attributes
    orm:
        mappings:
            App:
                type: attribute
                dir: '%kernel.project_dir%/src/Entity'
                prefix: 'App\Entity'
  • line 5: the connection. The prefix [resolve:] replaces any references to other parameters ([%...%]) in the variable’s value, if present;
  • line 7: In debug mode, each SQL command is written to the log, which we can view in the console (Example 24). This is also the default setting;
  • lines 10–15: The entities are the classes in the [src/Entity] folder, whose namespace begins with [App\Entity]; their mapping to the tables is described by [PHP] attributes.

The other configuration files are those from Example 21: the session, anti-CSRF protection, and the methods PUT and DELETE ([framework.yaml]), as well as the form theme [Bootstrap] ([twig.yaml]). There is nothing else to configure: the classes for the three layers are created by the [Symfony] container, which injects the layer below into each one (the controller receives the business layer, the business layer receives the DAO layer), and DoctrineBundle registers the entity manager ([EntityManagerInterface]) with the container.

docs.title: 9.1.3. The Person entity
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Entity/Person.php: a row of the [persons] table, a Doctrine ENTITY

namespace App\Entity;

use Doctrine\DBAL\Types\Types;
use Doctrine\ORM\Mapping as ORM;

// #[ORM\Entity]: the class is an entity; #[ORM\Table]: its table
#[ORM\Entity]
#[ORM\Table(name: 'persons')]
class Person
{
    // the primary key, generated by the database (AUTO_INCREMENT); null before the insertion
    #[ORM\Id]
    #[ORM\GeneratedValue]
    #[ORM\Column]
    private ?int $id = null;

    // the VERSION of the row: Doctrine increases it at each modification, and only
    // modifies the row if its version has not changed since it was read (optimistic
    // lock); the type of the column must be given explicitly
    #[ORM\Version]
    #[ORM\Column(type: Types::INTEGER)]
    private int $version = 0;

    // the columns: their SQL type is deduced from the PHP type (string: VARCHAR)
    #[ORM\Column(name: 'first_name', length: 30)]
    private string $firstName;

    #[ORM\Column(name: 'last_name', length: 30)]
    private string $lastName;

    #[ORM\Column]
    private int $age;

    public function __construct(string $firstName, string $lastName, int $age)
    {
        $this->edit($firstName, $lastName, $age);
    }

    public function edit(string $firstName, string $lastName, int $age): void
    {
        $this->firstName = $firstName;
        $this->lastName = $lastName;
        $this->age = $age;
    }

    public function getId(): ?int
    {
        return $this->id;
    }

    public function getVersion(): int
    {
        return $this->version;
    }

    public function getFirstName(): string
    {
        return $this->firstName;
    }

    public function getLastName(): string
    {
        return $this->lastName;
    }

    public function getAge(): int
    {
        return $this->age;
    }
}
  • lines 10–11: the attribute [#[ORM\Entity]] designates the class as an entity; [#[ORM\Table]] specifies the name of its table (otherwise, [Doctrine] would take the name of the class, [person]). [ORM] is an alias for the namespace [Doctrine\ORM\Mapping] (line 7): [use ... as ORM] allows attributes to be written in a shorthand form;
  • Lines 15–18: The primary key ([#[ORM\Id]]), generated by the database ([#[ORM\GeneratedValue]]: derived from [AUTO_INCREMENT], which is derived from [MySQL]). It is [null] until the entity has been inserted;
  • lines 23–25: the row version. The [#[ORM\Version]] attribute grants [Doctrine] the optimistic lock, described below;
  • lines 28–35: the columns. Each property marked [#[ORM\Column]] corresponds to the column of the same name; its type, SQL, is derived from the type [PHP] ([string]: [VARCHAR], of length [length]; [int]: [INT]). Unlike [Eloquent], the columns are declared: the class specifies exactly what the table contains;
  • lines 37–72: the entity is an ordinary class: a constructor, a method that modifies the person, and accessors. The properties are private: a person can only be modified through its methods. [Doctrine], on the other hand, reads and writes the properties directly (via reflection), without going through the constructor or the methods.

In a standard project, the [bin/console make:entity] command from [MakerBundle] writes the entity, asking a few questions about its properties.

docs.title: 9.1.4. The DAO layer
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Dao/PersonsDao.php: the DAO layer, queries, no business rule

namespace App\Dao;

use App\Entity\Person;
use Doctrine\ORM\EntityManagerInterface;

class PersonsDao
{
    // Doctrine's ENTITY MANAGER: it reads and writes the entities
    public function __construct(private EntityManagerInterface $em)
    {
    }

    // SELECT ... FROM persons ORDER BY last_name, first_name
    /** @return list<Person> */
    public function list(): array
    {
        return $this->em->getRepository(Person::class)->findBy([], ['lastName' => 'ASC', 'firstName' => 'ASC']);
    }

    // SELECT ... FROM persons WHERE id = ?; null if the person does not exist
    public function read(int $id): ?Person
    {
        return $this->em->find(Person::class, $id);
    }

    // a person with the same first and last names, other than [$exceptId], written in DQL,
    // Doctrine's query language: it speaks of entities and properties, not
    // of tables and columns
    public function namesake(string $firstName, string $lastName, int $exceptId = 0): ?Person
    {
        return $this->em->createQuery(
            'SELECT p FROM App\Entity\Person p WHERE p.firstName = :firstName AND p.lastName = :lastName AND p.id <> :id')
            ->setParameters(['firstName' => $firstName, 'lastName' => $lastName, 'id' => $exceptId])
            ->setMaxResults(1)
            ->getOneOrNullResult();
    }

    // INSERT (new entity) or UPDATE (entity read, then modified): persist entrusts
    // the entity to the manager, flush sends the necessary SQL statements to the database
    public function save(Person $person): void
    {
        $this->em->persist($person);
        $this->em->flush();
    }

    // DELETE FROM persons WHERE id = ?
    public function delete(Person $person): void
    {
        $this->em->remove($person);
        $this->em->flush();
    }
}

The DAO layer contains only queries, with no business logic. It receives the entity manager (line 12), which uses the connection from the current query and participates in the open transaction—if there is one—initiated by the business layer.

  • Lines 18–21: Each entity has a repository (repository), an object that retrieves it from the database: [getRepository]. Its method [findBy(criteria, orderBy)] returns the list of entities that match the criteria (in this case, none: all of them), in the requested order. (A repository also has [findAll], [findOneBy], [count].... ; an application can write its own repository class, with its own queries: this is what [make:entity] generates.) ;
  • lines 24–27: [find]: retrieval by primary key, or [null];
  • lines 32–39: a query written in DQL (Doctrine Query Language), the query language of [Doctrine]. It resembles SQL, but refers to entities and properties ([App\Entity\Person p], [p.firstName]), which [Doctrine] translates into tables and columns. The values are named parameters ([:firstName]), provided by [setParameters]: they are transmitted to the database separately and are never copied into the text of the SQL command, which makes SQL injection impossible. [setMaxResults(1)] limits the result to one line ([LIMIT 1]); [getOneOrNullResult] returns the found entity, or [null];
  • Lines 43–47: The record. [persist] assigns a new entity to the manager (an entity read by the manager has already been assigned to him); [flush] sends all necessary SQL commands to the database: a [INSERT] for a new entity, and a [UPDATE] containing only the modified columns for an entity that was read and then modified. The manager compares each entity it has read to its original state: this is change tracking. After a [INSERT], [Doctrine] stores the ID generated by the database in the entity;
  • lines 50–54: the deletion: [remove], followed by [flush], which triggers [DELETE].

docs.title: 9.1.5. The business layer
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Business/PersonData.php: the data of a person, as the web layer passes them on

namespace App\Business;

readonly class PersonData
{
    public function __construct(
        public string $firstName,
        public string $lastName,
        public int $age,
    ) {
    }
}

A person’s data, as transmitted by the web layer to the business layer: a simple object, unrelated to [Symfony].

<?php
// src/Business/BusinessException.php: a business rule refuses the operation; the
// message is intended for the user

namespace App\Business;

use RuntimeException;

class BusinessException extends RuntimeException
{
}

An exception class specific to the business layer: a business rule rejects the operation, and the exception message is intended for the user. It inherits from [RuntimeException] without adding anything to it—only its name matters.

<?php
// src/Business/PersonsBusiness.php: the BUSINESS layer, the business rules, and only
// them. Each operation that writes is a TRANSACTION: committed (COMMIT) if the
// function ends normally, cancelled (ROLLBACK) if an exception comes out of it

namespace App\Business;

use App\Dao\PersonsDao;
use App\Entity\Person;
use Doctrine\DBAL\Exception\UniqueConstraintViolationException;
use Doctrine\ORM\EntityManagerInterface;
use Doctrine\ORM\OptimisticLockException;

class PersonsBusiness
{
    private const NAMESAKE = 'A person already has these first and last names.';

    private const MODIFIED = 'This record has been modified meanwhile: reload it.';

    private const UNKNOWN = 'This person does not exist (anymore).';

    public function __construct(private PersonsDao $dao, private EntityManagerInterface $em)
    {
    }

    /** @return list<Person> */
    public function list(): array
    {
        return $this->dao->list();
    }

    public function read(int $id): Person
    {
        return $this->dao->read($id) ?? throw new BusinessException(self::UNKNOWN);
    }

    public function add(PersonData $data): Person
    {
        // wrapInTransaction: the function is executed in a transaction
        return $this->transaction(function () use ($data) {
            // rule 1: no two persons with the same first and last names
            if ($this->dao->namesake($data->firstName, $data->lastName)) {
                throw new BusinessException(self::NAMESAKE);
            }
            $person = new Person($data->firstName, $data->lastName, $data->age);
            $this->dao->save($person);
            return $person;
        });
    }

    public function edit(int $id, int $version, PersonData $data): Person
    {
        return $this->transaction(function () use ($id, $version, $data) {
            $person = $this->read($id);
            // rule 2: we do not modify a record modified meanwhile by someone else
            if ($person->getVersion() !== $version) {
                throw new BusinessException(self::MODIFIED);
            }
            if ($this->dao->namesake($data->firstName, $data->lastName, $id)) {
                throw new BusinessException(self::NAMESAKE);
            }
            $person->edit($data->firstName, $data->lastName, $data->age);
            // Doctrine's UPDATE "WHERE id = ... AND version = ..." raises an
            // OptimisticLockException if it has modified no row (see transaction)
            $this->dao->save($person);
            return $person;
        });
    }

    public function delete(int $id): Person
    {
        return $this->transaction(function () use ($id) {
            $person = $this->read($id);
            $this->dao->delete($person);
            return $person;
        });
    }

    // the [$operation] function, executed in a transaction. Two errors of the
    // database are business errors: the uniqueness constraint (two simultaneous adds),
    // and the optimistic lock (two simultaneous edits)
    private function transaction(callable $operation): Person
    {
        try {
            return $this->em->wrapInTransaction($operation);
        } catch (UniqueConstraintViolationException $e) {
            throw new BusinessException(self::NAMESAKE, previous: $e);
        } catch (OptimisticLockException $e) {
            throw new BusinessException(self::MODIFIED, previous: $e);
        }
    }
}
  • lines 16–20: the business rule messages;
  • lines 32–35: a nonexistent person is a business error. The operator [??] accepts an expression [throw] on the right-hand side: if the person is [null], the exception is thrown;
  • lines 37–49: Rule No. 1: No two people may have the same first and last names. The rule is checked before writing to the database, and a [BusinessException] exception is thrown if it is not satisfied. But this check is not sufficient: two simultaneous requests could both verify that there are no namesakes, and then both proceed to insert the records. The database’s uniqueness constraint then rejects the second [INSERT], and [Doctrine] triggers a [UniqueConstraintViolationException], which the [transaction] method transforms into the same [BusinessException]. The database is the last line of defense;
  • lines 51–68: Rule No. 2: Do not modify a record that has been modified in the meantime by someone else. The update form carries the version of the record that was read (in a hidden field); if it differs from the current version, the record has changed since it was displayed. There remains the case where the concurrent modification occurs between the read in line 54 and the save in line 65: this is detected by the optimistic lock in [Doctrine]. For an entity that has a version, [UPDATE] checks two conditions—the ID and the read version—and increments the version by 1; if another query has modified the row in the meantime—its version has changed—the [UPDATE] lock does not modify any rows, and [Doctrine] releases a [OptimisticLockException] lock. This is the principle of optimistic locking: nothing is blocked, but concurrent modifications are detected. ([Doctrine] does this itself, as do [Hibernate] and [SQLAlchemy]; the [Laravel] version of this course had to write the condition by hand.);
  • lines 70–77: Deletion marks the person as deleted for the confirmation message;
  • Lines 82–91: Every operation that writes data is executed within a transaction: [wrapInTransaction] opens the transaction, executes the function, submits the pending changes ([flush]), then commits the transaction ([COMMIT]) and returns the function’s value; If an exception is thrown from the function, the transaction is rolled back ([ROLLBACK]): none of the changes made within the function are retained, and the exception is propagated. The business layer thus determines the scope of transactions: one business operation, one transaction. The two database errors that are business errors become [BusinessException]; the parameter named [previous] attaches the original exception to the new one for the log. Another error is returned as-is: it is not a business error, but a programming error (or a system failure). After an exception, [Doctrine] closes the entity manager, whose state is no longer reliable: it can no longer be used during the query, which is not a problem here, since the query is ending.

The parameter [callable] of the method [transaction] refers to an arbitrary function; the anonymous functions on lines 40, 53, and 72 capture, via [use], the variables they need.

docs.title: 9.1.6. The Web Layer
docs.text:
Form input is described by a class, and its constraints by attributes (Example 19):

<?php
// src/Form/PersonInput.php: the fields of the form, and their constraints (see example 19)

namespace App\Form;

use App\Entity\Person;
use App\Business\PersonData;
use Symfony\Component\Validator\Constraints as Assert;

class PersonInput
{
    #[Assert\NotBlank(message: 'The first name is required.')]
    #[Assert\Length(max: 30, maxMessage: '30 characters at most.')]
    public ?string $firstName = null;

    #[Assert\NotBlank(message: 'The last name is required.')]
    #[Assert\Length(max: 30, maxMessage: '30 characters at most.')]
    public ?string $lastName = null;

    #[Assert\NotNull(message: 'The age is required.')]
    #[Assert\Range(notInRangeMessage: 'The age must be between 0 and 150.', min: 0, max: 150)]
    public ?int $age = null;

    // the version of the record, carried by a hidden field (edit only)
    public ?int $version = null;

    // the input, pre-filled with an existing person
    public static function from(Person $p): self
    {
        $input = new self();
        $input->firstName = $p->getFirstName();
        $input->lastName = $p->getLastName();
        $input->age = $p->getAge();
        $input->version = $p->getVersion();
        return $input;
    }

    // the validated data, for the business layer
    public function data(): PersonData
    {
        return new PersonData(trim($this->firstName), trim($this->lastName), $this->age);
    }
}
  • lines 12–22: the constraints, with messages in English;
  • line 25: the record version, carried by a hidden field (edit mode only);
  • lines 28–36: a pre-filled entry with an existing person, for the update form;
  • lines 39–42: the validated data, in the format expected by the business layer.

We could have linked the form directly to the [Person] entity (option [data_class], Example 19) and placed the constraints on it: this is common with [Symfony]. However, the form would then modify the entity before the business layer had verified its rules, and an invalid entity would be passed to the entity manager. A separate input class keeps the layers distinct: the web layer transmits only validated data to the business layer.

<?php
// src/Form/PersonType.php: the form of a person (see example 18)

namespace App\Form;

use Symfony\Component\Form\AbstractType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\Extension\Core\Type\HiddenType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\Extension\Core\Type\IntegerType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\Extension\Core\Type\TextType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\FormBuilderInterface;
use Symfony\Component\OptionsResolver\OptionsResolver;

class PersonType extends AbstractType
{
    public function buildForm(FormBuilderInterface $builder, array $options): void
    {
        $builder
            ->add('firstName', TextType::class, ['label' => 'First name', 'attr' => ['maxlength' => 30]])
            ->add('lastName', TextType::class, ['label' => 'Last name', 'attr' => ['maxlength' => 30]])
            ->add('age', IntegerType::class, ['label' => 'Age', 'attr' => ['min' => 0, 'max' => 150],
                'invalid_message' => 'The age must be an integer.']);
        // the version: a hidden field, in the edit form only
        if ($options['edit']) {
            $builder->add('version', HiddenType::class);
        }
    }

    // the options of the form: the class of the data, and an option of our own
    public function configureOptions(OptionsResolver $resolver): void
    {
        $resolver->setDefaults(['data_class' => PersonInput::class, 'edit' => false]);
    }
}
  • lines 20–21: an integer field; [invalid_message] is the message displayed when the input cannot be converted to an integer;
  • lines 23–25: the hidden version field, in the update form only, according to the option [edit];
  • lines 29–32: [configureOptions] declares the form options and their default values: the data class, and a custom option, [edit].
<?php
// src/Controller/PersonsController.php: the WEB layer; it only knows the business layer

namespace App\Controller;

use App\Form\PersonInput;
use App\Form\PersonType;
use App\Business\BusinessException;
use App\Business\PersonsBusiness;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\Form\FormInterface;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Exception\AccessDeniedHttpException;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

// name: a prefix for the name of all the routes of the class (persons_list...)
#[Route(name: 'persons_')]
class PersonsController extends AbstractController
{
    public function __construct(private PersonsBusiness $business)
    {
    }

    #[Route('/', name: 'home', methods: ['GET'])]
    public function home(): Response
    {
        return $this->redirectToRoute('persons_list');
    }

    #[Route('/persons', name: 'list', methods: ['GET'])]
    public function list(): Response
    {
        return $this->render('persons/list.html.twig', ['persons' => $this->business->list()]);
    }

    // GET: the empty form; POST: the sent form
    #[Route('/persons/add', name: 'add', methods: ['GET', 'POST'])]
    public function add(Request $request): Response
    {
        $input = new PersonInput();
        $form = $this->createForm(PersonType::class, $input);
        $form->handleRequest($request);
        if ($form->isSubmitted() && $form->isValid()) {
            try {
                $p = $this->business->add($input->data());
                $this->addFlash('success', "{$p->getFirstName()} {$p->getLastName()} has been added.");
                return $this->redirectToRoute('persons_list');
            } catch (BusinessException $e) {
                // a business rule refuses: the form is displayed again, with the
                // input, and the message, at the bottom of the page
                return $this->formPage('Add a person', $form, $e->getMessage());
            }
        }
        return $this->formPage('Add a person', $form);
    }

    // GET: the edit form, pre-filled
    #[Route('/persons/{id<\d+>}/edit', name: 'edit_form', methods: ['GET'])]
    public function editForm(int $id): Response
    {
        try {
            $p = $this->business->read($id);
        } catch (BusinessException $e) {
            $this->addFlash('error', $e->getMessage());
            return $this->redirectToRoute('persons_list');
        }
        return $this->formPage('Edit a person', $this->editFormFor($id, PersonInput::from($p)));
    }

    // PUT: the sent edit form
    #[Route('/persons/{id<\d+>}', name: 'edit', methods: ['PUT'])]
    public function edit(Request $request, int $id): Response
    {
        $input = new PersonInput();
        $form = $this->editFormFor($id, $input);
        $form->handleRequest($request);
        if ($form->isSubmitted() && $form->isValid()) {
            try {
                $p = $this->business->edit($id, (int) $input->version, $input->data());
                $this->addFlash('success', "{$p->getFirstName()} {$p->getLastName()} has been edited.");
                return $this->redirectToRoute('persons_list');
            } catch (BusinessException $e) {
                return $this->formPage('Edit a person', $form, $e->getMessage());
            }
        }
        return $this->formPage('Edit a person', $form);
    }

    #[Route('/persons/{id<\d+>}', name: 'delete', methods: ['DELETE'])]
    public function delete(Request $request, int $id): Response
    {
        if (! $this->isCsrfTokenValid("delete-person-$id", $request->request->getString('_token'))) {
            throw new AccessDeniedHttpException('invalid anti-CSRF token');
        }
        try {
            $p = $this->business->delete($id);
            $this->addFlash('success', "{$p->getFirstName()} {$p->getLastName()} has been deleted.");
        } catch (BusinessException $e) {
            // no form to display again: the error also travels as a flash message
            $this->addFlash('error', $e->getMessage());
        }
        return $this->redirectToRoute('persons_list');
    }

    // the edit form: sent by the PUT method, to the /persons/{id} URL
    private function editFormFor(int $id, PersonInput $input): FormInterface
    {
        return $this->createForm(PersonType::class, $input, ['edit' => true,
            'method' => 'PUT', 'action' => $this->generateUrl('persons_edit', ['id' => $id])]);
    }

    private function formPage(string $title, FormInterface $form, ?string $error = null): Response
    {
        // a business error: the 422 code, as for an invalid form (see example 19)
        return $this->render('persons/form.html.twig',
            ['title' => $title, 'form' => $form, 'error' => $error],
            new Response(status: $error ? 422 : 200));
    }
}
  • line 18: The class attribute [#[Route]] prefixes only the route names here: the route named [list] is actually called [persons_list];
  • line 21: the business layer, the only layer known to the controller;
  • lines 38–56: the process, in three steps: form validation (input errors, Example 19); the call to the business layer (business rules); then the PRG schema, with a success flash message (Example 20). A [BusinessException] re-displays the form, along with the entered data and the exception message, which the template will display at the bottom of the page. Input errors and business logic errors are thus handled in the same way;
  • lines 59–69: the edit form, pre-filled with the retrieved person. If the person does not exist, the user is redirected to the list with a flash error message;
  • lines 72–88: the update, following the same pattern as the add operation;
  • lines 90–104: deletion, protected by a CSRF token unique to each person (example 21). There is no form to redisplay: any error is also conveyed in a flash message, [error];
  • lines 107–111: the edit form is submitted using the method PUT (option [method]: [form_start] then adds the hidden field [_method], Example 21), to URL [/persons/{id}] (option [action]);
  • lines 113–119: the form page. A business error is returned with code 422, indicating an invalid form.

The web layer contains neither SQL nor any business rules: it translates the request into a call to the business layer and the result into a page.

The views:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Persons</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ path('bootstrap', {file: 'css/bootstrap.min.css'}) }}">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ asset('css/styles.css') }}">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3" style="max-width: 40rem">
    {# the success message ([success] flash message): at the top #}
    {% for message in app.flashes('success') %}
      <div class="alert alert-success" role="status">{{ message }}</div>
    {% endfor %}
    <main>
      {% block content %}{% endblock %}
    </main>
    {# the errors: at the bottom; an [error] flash message, or the [error] variable of the view #}
    {% for message in app.flashes('error') %}
      <div class="error-area" role="alert">{{ message }}</div>
    {% endfor %}
    {% if error is defined and error %}
      <div class="error-area" role="alert">{{ error }}</div>
    {% endif %}
  </div>
  {% include 'fragments/confirmation.html.twig' %}
  <script src="{{ asset('js/app.js') }}"></script>
</body>
</html>
  • lines 13–15: the success message at the top of the page (example 20);
  • Lines 20–25: errors; at the bottom of the page: a flash message (after a redirect), or the view variable [error] (form re-displayed). The test [is defined] prevents an error on pages that do not have this variable.
{% extends 'layout.html.twig' %}

{% block content %}
  <h1 class="h3">Persons</h1>
  <table class="table align-middle">
    <thead><tr><th>First name</th><th>Last name</th><th>Age</th><th></th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      {% for p in persons %}
        <tr>
          <td>{{ p.firstName }}</td>
          <td>{{ p.lastName }}</td>
          <td>{{ p.age }}</td>
          <td class="text-end">
            <a class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-primary" href="{{ path('persons_edit_form', {id: p.id}) }}">Edit</a>
            <form method="post" class="d-inline" action="{{ path('persons_delete', {id: p.id}) }}"
                  data-confirmation="Delete {{ p.firstName }} {{ p.lastName }}?">
              <input type="hidden" name="_method" value="DELETE">
              <input type="hidden" name="_token" value="{{ csrf_token('delete-person-' ~ p.id) }}">
              <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-danger" type="submit">Delete</button>
            </form>
          </td>
        </tr>
      {% endfor %}
    </tbody>
  </table>
  <a class="btn btn-primary" href="{{ path('persons_add') }}">Add a person</a>
{% endblock %}

The list includes the links and buttons from Example 21, along with its confirmation window (the files [fragments/confirmation.html.twig] and [public/js/app.js] are those from Example 21). The properties [p.firstName], [p.lastName]... are read by the accessors [getFirstName()], [getLastName()]... : [Twig] finds them on its own (Example 13).

{% extends 'layout.html.twig' %}

{% block content %}
  <h1 class="h3">{{ title }}</h1>
  {# novalidate: the validation is the server's one (see example 19); form_start
     also writes the hidden _method field of a PUT form #}
  {{ form_start(form, {attr: {novalidate: 'novalidate'}}) }}
    {{ form_widget(form) }}
    <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Save</button>
    <a class="btn btn-link" href="{{ path('persons_list') }}">Cancel</a>
  {{ form_end(form) }}
{% endblock %}

A view used for both adding and modifying records. [form_widget] renders all form fields, including the hidden version field and the anti-CSRF token.

docs.text:
The list of people:

An incorrectly filled-out add form: input errors are detected by the web layer.

A homonym: the entry is correct, but the business layer rejects the addition. Since the comparison is performed by the database, it ignores both uppercase letters and accents: [marie pelissier] is a homonym of [Marie Pélissier].

A successful addition:

To test Rule #2, let’s open the same record in two tabs. In the first tab, let’s change the age and save. In the second tab, which still displays the old version, let’s also modify the record:

The deletion, with its confirmation:

docs.title: 9.1.8. The SQL commands
docs.text:
Let’s track the SQL commands for a modification in the console (the dates and lines from the development server have been removed). The display of the modification form for person #1:

[info] Connecting with parameters [array]
[debug] Executing statement: SELECT t0.id AS id_1, t0.version AS version_2, t0.first_name AS first_name_3, t0.last_name AS last_name_4, t0.age AS age_5 FROM persons t0 WHERE t0.id = ? (parameters: [array], types: [array])
[info] Disconnecting

A connection, a read by primary key (whose value is passed as a parameter—[?]), followed by a disconnect at the end of the query. There is no transaction: an isolated read does not require one. [Doctrine] assigns an alias to each table ([t0]) and to each column ([id_1]). The parameter values are an array, which the minimal log for [Symfony] does not display ([[array]]); [Monolog], or the debug bar of [Symfony] ([WebProfilerBundle], installed by [composer require --dev profiler]), would display them. The master record update, with a new age:

[debug] Beginning transaction
[debug] Executing statement: SELECT t0.id AS id_1, t0.version AS version_2, t0.first_name AS first_name_3, t0.last_name AS last_name_4, t0.age AS age_5 FROM persons t0 WHERE t0.id = ? (parameters: [array], types: [array])
[debug] Executing statement: SELECT p0_.id AS id_0, p0_.version AS version_1, p0_.first_name AS first_name_2, p0_.last_name AS last_name_3, p0_.age AS age_4 FROM persons p0_ WHERE p0_.first_name = ? AND p0_.last_name = ? AND p0_.id <> ? LIMIT 1 (parameters: [array], types: [array])
[debug] Executing statement: SAVEPOINT DOCTRINE_2
[debug] Executing statement: UPDATE persons SET age = ?, version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ? (parameters: [array], types: [array])
[debug] Executing statement: SELECT version FROM persons WHERE id = ? (parameters: [array], types: [array])
[debug] Executing statement: RELEASE SAVEPOINT DOCTRINE_2
[debug] Committing transaction

In a single transaction, we can see: the read of the record, the search for a namesake (the query DQL, translated to SQL), followed by [UPDATE]. This transaction modifies only the column that has changed ([age]), increments the version number, and sets the optimistic lock condition ([AND version = ?]). [Doctrine] then reads the new version again to save it to the entity. [flush] opens a transaction itself; since there is already one—the business layer transaction—it simply creates a savepoint ([SAVEPOINT]), a nested transaction that is committed ([RELEASE]) at the end of [flush]. Now let’s submit the same form a second time, still using the old version:

[debug] Beginning transaction
[debug] Executing statement: SELECT t0.id AS id_1, t0.version AS version_2, t0.first_name AS first_name_3, t0.last_name AS last_name_4, t0.age AS age_5 FROM persons t0 WHERE t0.id = ? (parameters: [array], types: [array])
[debug] Rolling back transaction

The version being read is not the one from the form: the business layer triggered a [BusinessException], which rolled back the transaction ([ROLLBACK]), and the page displays “This record has been modified meanwhile: reload it.” Similarly, adding a namesake stops after the namesake search, without a [INSERT].

docs.title: 3. The Action Template
docs.text:
An action requires information sent by the browser: the parameters of the URL ([?name=martin&age=42]), form fields, the request body JSON, and sometimes a request header HTTP. The original course refers to all of this information as the action model. This chapter shows how an action [Symfony] retrieves this information, converts it to the correct type, and validates it. This process is called data binding.

[Symfony] provides access to the request information via the [Request] object (Example 05), in the form of character strings, along with a few conversion methods. It can also bind this information to the parameters of an action using attributes ([#[MapQueryParameter]], [#[MapQueryString]], [#[MapRequestPayload]]) and validate it using its Validator component: We describe the expected data using constraints (“required,” “an integer between 0 and 150,” etc.), written as attributes such as [PHP], and the validator checks that the data complies with them. We will first read the parameters manually (example 07), then let the framework handle their conversion and validation (examples 08 through 12). In the next chapter, the same constraints will validate the HTML forms.

Note the terminology: in the next chapter, the word “model” will primarily refer to the data that an action passes to its view. The model of an action, as used in this chapter, is what it receives.

Examples 07 through 12 are run in the same way as those in the previous chapter: a terminal open to the example folder, [php -S localhost:8000 -t public]; [Ctrl-C] shuts down the server. Most use the listener [ReadableJson] from Example 03, resulting in a readable JSON. We will comment on their configuration files only when they introduce something new.

docs.title: 3.1. Example 07: The settings for URL
docs.text:
The parameters for the URL are the portion that follows the [?]: [?name=martin&age=42]. This portion is called the query string. Each parameter is a pair of [name=value]; the pairs are separated by [&]. The controller [ParametersController]:

<?php
// src/Controller/ParametersController.php: the parameters of the URL (the "query string")

namespace App\Controller;

use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\JsonResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Attribute\MapQueryParameter;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Exception\BadRequestHttpException;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

#[Route('/parameters', name: 'parameters_', methods: ['GET'])]
class ParametersController extends AbstractController
{
    // /parameters/action01?name=martin: $request->query contains the parameters of
    // the URL; get returns the value of a parameter, or null if it is missing
    #[Route('/action01', name: 'action01')]
    public function action01(Request $request): Response
    {
        $name = $request->query->get('name');
        return new Response("name = [$name], of type ".get_debug_type($name));
    }

    // /parameters/action02?age=42: getInt CONVERTS the value (a string) into an
    // integer; a missing parameter gives 0, a value that is not an integer,
    // a 400 error
    #[Route('/action02', name: 'action02')]
    public function action02(Request $request): Response
    {
        $age = $request->query->getInt('age');
        return new Response("age = [$age], of type ".get_debug_type($age));
    }

    // /parameters/action03?age=42: a REQUIRED parameter, converted by hand;
    // its absence, or a value that is not an integer, produces a 400 response
    #[Route('/action03', name: 'action03')]
    public function action03(Request $request): Response
    {
        $text = $request->query->get('age');
        if ($text === null) {
            // an HTTP exception: Symfony turns it into a 400 response (Bad Request)
            throw new BadRequestHttpException('the [age] parameter is required');
        }
        // filter_var returns the integer contained in the string, or false
        $age = filter_var($text, FILTER_VALIDATE_INT);
        if ($age === false) {
            throw new BadRequestHttpException("[$text] is not an integer");
        }
        return new Response("age = [$age], of type ".get_debug_type($age));
    }

    // /parameters/action04?page=2: a default value if the parameter is missing
    #[Route('/action04', name: 'action04')]
    public function action04(Request $request): Response
    {
        $page = $request->query->getInt('page', 1);
        return new Response("page = [$page]");
    }

    // /parameters/action05?q=symfony: the name of the URL parameter is not necessarily
    // that of the PHP variable
    #[Route('/action05', name: 'action05')]
    public function action05(Request $request): Response
    {
        $search = $request->query->get('q');
        return new Response("search = [$search]");
    }

    // /parameters/action06?name=martin&age=42: all the parameters at once, as an array
    #[Route('/action06', name: 'action06')]
    public function action06(Request $request): JsonResponse
    {
        return $this->json($request->query->all());
    }

    // /parameters/action07?age=42&page=2: the #[MapQueryParameter] attribute BINDS a
    // URL parameter to the action parameter of the same name, and converts it into
    // its type. A parameter without a default value is required
    #[Route('/action07', name: 'action07')]
    public function action07(#[MapQueryParameter] int $age, #[MapQueryParameter] int $page = 1): Response
    {
        return new Response("age = [$age], page = [$page]");
    }
}
  • line 22: the [query] property of the request contains the parameters of URL, in a parameter “bag” (a [InputBag] object), whose [get] method returns the value of a parameter—already decoded—or [null] if it is absent;
  • line 23: the action displays the value and its type: the function [get_debug_type] returns the name of a value’s type. A value retrieved from URL is always a string ([string]). The operator [.] concatenates the interpolated string and the type;
  • Line 32: The [getInt] method reads the parameter and converts it to an integer. A missing parameter returns 0; a value that is not an integer ([abc]) causes a 400 error (Bad Request). Similarly, [getBoolean] exists ([1], [true], [on], and [yes] are true), [getString], [getAlpha] (letters only), [getDigits] (numbers only), [getEnum] (a list);
  • lines 41–51: a required parameter and a manual conversion that distinguishes between the two possible errors. [throw new BadRequestHttpException(message)] terminates the operation with a 400 response, accompanied by the message (see example 03, which also raised a 404 exception). The function [filter_var] of [PHP], with the filter [FILTER_VALIDATE_INT], returns the integer contained in the string, or [false] if the string is not an integer;
  • line 58: The second parameter of [getInt] is a default value, used if the parameter is missing. This is typically the case for a page number in a list;
  • line 67: there is no requirement to name the variable [PHP] the same as the parameter of URL. Search engines often use a short parameter, [q] (query);
  • line 75: [all()] returns all parameters of URL in an associative array, which the action converts to JSON (see Example 03);
  • lines 81–85: the declarative approach. The attribute [#[MapQueryParameter]], placed before an action parameter, links that parameter to the parameter of the same name in URL and converts it to the declared type ([int]). A parameter without a default value is required: if it is missing or cannot be converted, it causes a 404 error (URL, as written, does not refer to any valid page). A default value ([$page = 1]) makes it optional. This is what lines 41–51 do, in a single line.

Let’s test each action with [curl]. First with the parameter present, then absent:

curl -i "http://localhost:8000/parameters/action01?name=martin"
curl http://localhost:8000/parameters/action01

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8

name = [martin], of type string
name = [], of type null

The quotation marks around URL are necessary in a terminal: without them, the shell would interpret [&] (which runs a command in the background under [Linux]) and [?]. The value [null], when inserted into a string, becomes an empty string. A value containing spaces or special characters must be encoded in URL: a space becomes [%20], and [&] becomes [%26] (otherwise, it would separate two parameters). The browser handles this automatically; with [curl], you have to write it out. [PHP] decodes the value before the action reads it:

curl "http://localhost:8000/parameters/action01?name=jean%20dupont%20%26%20fils"

name = [jean dupont & fils], of type string

Conversion using [getInt]—successful, failed, then without parameters:

curl "http://localhost:8000/parameters/action02?age=42"
curl -i "http://localhost:8000/parameters/action02?age=abc"
curl http://localhost:8000/parameters/action02

age = [42], of type int
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
X-Debug-Exception: Input%20value%20%22age%22%20cannot%20be%20converted%20to%20%22int%22.
...
age = [0], of type int

[Symfony] refuses to convert [abc] to an integer: this is a client error, hence the 400 code (“Input value 'age' cannot be converted to 'int'”). However, a missing parameter silently returns 0: the action cannot distinguish this case from an age of 0 that was actually entered. The required parameter for action 03 is missing and therefore invalid. We request a response JSON (header [Accept], see example 03), which contains the exception message:

curl -i -H "Accept: application/json" http://localhost:8000/parameters/action03
curl -H "Accept: application/json" "http://localhost:8000/parameters/action03?age=abc"

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/json

{"type":"https:\/\/tools.ietf.org\/html\/rfc2616#section-10","title":"An error occurred","status":400,"detail":"the [age] parameter is required","class":"Symfony\\Component\\HttpKernel\\Exception\\BadRequestHttpException","trace":[...]}
{"type":"https:\/\/tools.ietf.org\/html\/rfc2616#section-10","title":"An error occurred","status":400,"detail":"[abc] is not an integer","class":"Symfony\\Component\\HttpKernel\\Exception\\BadRequestHttpException","trace":[...]}

(This compact JSON is not reformatted by our listener, see example 03). In a browser, in debug mode, a 400 response displays the [Symfony] error page, with the message:

The default value and the renamed parameter:

curl http://localhost:8000/parameters/action04
curl "http://localhost:8000/parameters/action04?page=3"
curl "http://localhost:8000/parameters/action05?q=symfony"

page = [1]
page = [3]
search = [symfony]

All parameters at once. The parameter [name] appears twice:

curl "http://localhost:8000/parameters/action06?name=martin&age=42&name=durand"

{
    "name": "durand",
    "age": "42"
}

The parameter [name] retains only its last value: this is a rule for [PHP], which we’ll see again in Example 10. The age remained a string (["42"], enclosed in quotes within JSON): no conversion was requested. In a browser (here, [Chromium]), the JSON is displayed exactly as the server formatted it; the “Pretty-print” checkbox would indent it if it were not already indented. The address bar also shows the encoding of accented characters in URL ([é] becomes [%C3%A9], with its two bytes in [UTF-8]):

Finally, the connection via [#[MapQueryParameter]], with and without the optional parameter, and then with an invalid age:

curl "http://localhost:8000/parameters/action07?age=42"
curl "http://localhost:8000/parameters/action07?age=42&page=3"
curl -i "http://localhost:8000/parameters/action07?age=abc"

age = [42], page = [1]
age = [42], page = [3]
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
X-Debug-Exception: Invalid%20query%20parameter%20%22age%22.
...

Without the parameter [age], the message would be “Missing query parameter 'age'”. The 404 code may come as a surprise: the attribute accepts a parameter [validationFailedStatusCode], which allows you to choose a different one ([#[MapQueryParameter(validationFailedStatusCode: 400)]]).

This first example illustrates the limitations of the manual approach: for each parameter, you must write the reading, conversion, and handling of missing values and errors. With ten parameters, the action’s code would be overwhelmed by these checks. [#[MapQueryParameter]] simplifies the conversion but says nothing about the rules (“a string of 2 to 20 characters”). It’s better to describe what’s expected and let the framework verify it. That’s the purpose of the following example.

docs.title: 3.2. Example 08: An action model described by a class
docs.text: An action’s model can be described by a class: one property per expected parameter, along with its type, and—in the form of attributes—the constraints it must satisfy. [Symfony] then creates the object itself from the request, validates it, and passes it to the action. The constraints are the classes of the Validator component: [NotBlank] (required), [Length] (a length), [Range] (an interval), [Choice] (a list of values), [Email], [Regex]... [Symfony] provides more than seventy of them.

docs.title: 3.2.1. The model: src/Model/PersonModel.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Model/PersonModel.php: the model of the action, a class that describes the
// expected parameters and their CONSTRAINTS

namespace App\Model;

use Symfony\Component\Validator\Constraints as Assert;

readonly class PersonModel
{
    public function __construct(
        // required, then a string of 2 to 20 characters: Sequentially checks
        // the constraints in order, and stops at the first one that fails
        #[Assert\Sequentially([
            new Assert\NotBlank(),
            new Assert\Length(min: 2, max: 20),
        ])]
        public ?string $name = null,
        // required, an integer between 0 and 150
        #[Assert\NotNull]
        #[Assert\Range(min: 0, max: 150)]
        public ?int $age = null,
        // required, one of these three values only
        #[Assert\NotBlank]
        #[Assert\Choice(choices: ['Mr', 'Mme', 'Melle'])]
        public ?string $title = null,
        // optional; if it is present, a valid email address
        #[Assert\Email]
        public ?string $email = null,
    ) {
    }
}
  • Line 7: Importing the constraints namespace, under the short name [Assert]: the constraints will be written as [Assert\NotBlank], [Assert\Length]... This is standard practice in all [Symfony] projects;
  • lines 9–31: an immutable class whose properties are initialized by the constructor (example 03). Each property has a default value, [null], and a nullable type ([?string], [?int]: a string, or [null]): if a parameter is missing from URL, the property defaults to [null], and a constraint determines whether it was required. This is the standard way to write these classes;
  • Lines 14–18: The name is required ([NotBlank] rejects [null] and an empty string), and must consist of 2 to 20 characters ([Length]). The constraint [Sequentially] checks the constraints it contains in order and stops at the first one that fails: an empty name produces only one error, not two. Constraint parameters are named ([min: 2]), a requirement since [Symfony] 8;
  • lines 20–22: age is required ([NotNull]) and must be between 0 and 150 ([Range]). Its type is [?int]: [Symfony] will convert the string from URL to an integer;
  • lines 24–26: the title is required and must be one of the three listed values ([Choice]);
  • lines 28–29: the email address is optional (no constraint: [NotBlank]); if included, it must be valid. With the exception of one constraint, [NotBlank], the rest accept [null]: they only verify the values that are present.

This model describes the expected data; it contains no validation instructions. This is known as a declarative style.

docs.title: 3.2.2. The action: src/Controller/PersonsController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Controller/PersonsController.php: an action whose model is a class

namespace App\Controller;

use App\Model\PersonModel;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\JsonResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Attribute\MapQueryString;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

class PersonsController extends AbstractController
{
    // /persons/action01?name=martin&age=42&title=Mr
    // #[MapQueryString]: Symfony builds a PersonModel object from the
    // parameters of the URL, and VALIDATES it BEFORE the call of the action. An
    // invalid model raises an exception (see src/EventListener/ValidationErrors.php), and
    // the action is never called
    #[Route('/persons/action01', name: 'persons_action01', methods: ['GET'])]
    public function action01(Request $request, #[MapQueryString] PersonModel $person): JsonResponse
    {
        return $this->json([
            'received' => $request->query->all(),
            'person' => $person,
            'ageType' => get_debug_type($person->age),
        ]);
    }
}
  • Line 21: The [#[MapQueryString]] attribute instructs [Symfony] to construct the [$person] parameter from the parameters of URL. An argument resolver (example 05) performs this task in two steps. First, it converts: using the Serializer, it creates a [PersonModel] object, where each property receives the parameter from URL with the same name, converted to its corresponding type. Next, it validates the object: it checks every constraint for every property. If everything is correct, the action is called. Otherwise, it throws an exception (a [HttpException] with code 404, which contains a [ValidationFailedException], which itself contains the list of all errors, not just the first one), and the action is never called: it therefore does not have to worry about invalid data;
  • lines 23–27: the action returns the received parameters as-is, followed by the [PersonModel] object and the age type, to illustrate the difference.

Who handles the exception? By default, [Symfony] itself, via a 404 error response (or 422, for [#[MapRequestPayload]], Example 11): its error page, or, for a client requesting JSON, a document detailing the errors. Here, we want an error response in JSON, in all cases, with a 400 status code, and in our own format. That is the role of a listener.

docs.title: 3.2.3. Error handling: src/EventListener/ValidationErrors.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/EventListener/ValidationErrors.php: an invalid model produces, for the WHOLE
// application, a 400 response that details the errors

namespace App\EventListener;

use Symfony\Component\EventDispatcher\Attribute\AsEventListener;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\JsonResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Event\ExceptionEvent;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\KernelEvents;
use Symfony\Component\Validator\Exception\ValidationFailedException;

// a listener of the [kernel.exception] event, fired when an exception
// comes out of the action (or of the preparation of its parameters)
#[AsEventListener(event: KernelEvents::EXCEPTION)]
class ValidationErrors
{
    public function __invoke(ExceptionEvent $event): void
    {
        // the HTTP exception raised by #[MapQueryString] contains the exception of the
        // validation, which contains the list of the errors (the "violations")
        $validation = $event->getThrowable()->getPrevious();
        if (! $validation instanceof ValidationFailedException) {
            return;    // another exception: Symfony handles it as usual
        }
        $errors = [];
        foreach ($validation->getViolations() as $violation) {
            $errors[] = ['field' => $violation->getPropertyPath(), 'message' => $violation->getMessage()];
        }
        // the response of the event replaces Symfony's error page
        $event->setResponse(new JsonResponse(['status' => 400, 'errors' => $errors], 400));
    }
}
  • Line 15: a listener for the [kernel.exception] event (the constant [KernelEvents::EXCEPTION]). [Symfony] triggers this event when an exception occurs during the action or while preparing its parameters, before the action generates its own error response. Declared in this way, the listener applies to all actions in the application: every action that validates a model benefits from it, without having to write a single line of error-handling code;
  • Line 22: The event, a [ExceptionEvent] object, carries the exception ([getThrowable()]). The exception thrown by [#[MapQueryString]] is a HTTP exception; [getPrevious()] returns the exception that caused it—the validation exception;
  • lines 23–25: if it is not a validation error, the listener does nothing: [Symfony] will handle the exception as usual. The operator [!] (does not) invert the condition;
  • lines 26–29: [getViolations()] returns the list of errors, which are called (constraint) violations. Each violation has a path ([getPropertyPath()], the name of the property in error) and a message. [$errors[] = ...] adds an element to the end of the array [$errors];
  • Line 31: [setResponse] returns a response to the event: a JSON response, with status code 400. [Symfony] sends this in place of its error page (and, like any response, it passes through the listener [ReadableJson]).

docs.title: 3.2.4. Execution
docs.text:
A valid template:

curl -i "http://localhost:8000/persons/action01?name=martin&age=42&title=Mr"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "received": {
        "name": "martin",
        "age": "42",
        "title": "Mr"
    },
    "person": {
        "name": "martin",
        "age": 42,
        "title": "Mr",
        "email": null
    },
    "ageType": "int"
}

The received parameters are strings; the [PersonModel] object contains the age as an integer (without quotes in JSON), and the missing address is [null]. A name surrounded by spaces ([%20]) and a present address:

curl "http://localhost:8000/persons/action01?name=%20%20martin%20&age=42&title=Mme&email=martin@example.com"

{
    "received": {
        "name": "  martin ",
        "age": "42",
        "title": "Mme",
        "email": "martin@example.com"
    },
    "person": {
        "name": "  martin ",
        "age": 42,
        "title": "Mme",
        "email": "martin@example.com"
    },
    "ageType": "int"
}

The spaces surrounding the name have been preserved: [Symfony] does not transform the received data. A constraint may ignore them during validation ([new Assert\Length(min: 2, normalizer: 'trim')]), but the value remains the one that was sent. In the next chapter, the Form component will remove these spaces. No parameters at this point: the three required fields are missing.

curl -i http://localhost:8000/persons/action01

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "status": 400,
    "errors": [
        {
            "field": "name",
            "message": "This value should not be blank."
        },
        {
            "field": "age",
            "message": "This value should not be null."
        },
        {
            "field": "title",
            "message": "This value should not be blank."
        }
    ]
}

Four invalid fields at once:

curl "http://localhost:8000/persons/action01?name=m&age=200&title=Mlle&email=xx"

{
    "status": 400,
    "errors": [
        {
            "field": "name",
            "message": "This value is too short. It should have 2 characters or more."
        },
        {
            "field": "age",
            "message": "This value should be between 0 and 150."
        },
        {
            "field": "title",
            "message": "The value you selected is not a valid choice."
        },
        {
            "field": "email",
            "message": "This value is not a valid email address."
        }
    ]
}

All errors are reported at once, allowing the user to correct everything in one go. Finally, an age that isn’t a number:

curl "http://localhost:8000/persons/action01?name=m&age=abc&title=Mlle&email=xx"

{
    "status": 400,
    "errors": [
        {
            "field": "age",
            "message": "This value should be of type int."
        }
    ]
}

This time, only one error is reported, even though the name, title, and address are still invalid. This is the result of the two-step process performed by [#[MapQueryString]]: the conversion failed ([abc] cannot be converted to an integer), so the object could not be constructed, and the validation—which checks the object—did not take place. The messages are in English, the default language of [Symfony]. The following example customizes some of them.

docs.title: 3.3. Example 09: Validation Performed by the Action
docs.text:
In Example 08, an invalid model interrupts the action, and the application’s listener responds. This is convenient for a API, whose clients are programs that expect a standardized error response. But a web page often prefers to redisplay the form with error messages: in that case, the action must decide what to do with an invalid model. It calls the validator itself.

09-action-validation/
├── config/
│   └── packages/
│       └── framework.yaml
├── src/
│   ├── Controller/
│   │   └── PersonsController.php
│   ├── Model/
│   │   └── PersonInput.php
│   └── Kernel.php
├── translations/
│   └── validators.en.yaml
└── ...

docs.title: 3.3.1. The model: src/Model/PersonInput.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Model/PersonInput.php: the INPUT of a person, as it arrives
// (strings), and the constraints it must comply with

namespace App\Model;

use Symfony\Component\Validator\Constraints as Assert;

class PersonInput
{
    #[Assert\Sequentially([
        new Assert\NotBlank(),
        new Assert\Length(min: 2, max: 20),
    ])]
    public ?string $name = null;

    // a string of digits (digit), whose value is between 0 and 150;
    // message: a message specific to this constraint
    #[Assert\Sequentially([
        new Assert\NotBlank(),
        new Assert\Type('digit', message: 'an integer is expected'),
        new Assert\Range(min: 0, max: 150),
    ])]
    public ?string $age = null;

    #[Assert\NotBlank]
    #[Assert\Choice(choices: ['Mr', 'Mme', 'Melle'])]
    public ?string $title = null;

    #[Assert\Email]
    public ?string $email = null;
}

This time, the model describes the input exactly as it is received: strings, which the action will copy into the object itself. Its properties are therefore ordinary (neither promoted nor [readonly]), and all of type [?string], including age:

  • lines 19–24: The age is a string, which must be present ([NotBlank]), contain only digits ([Type('digit')], which verifies that a string contains only digits), and whose value must be between 0 and 150 ([Range] accepts a string that represents a number). Thanks to [Sequentially], an age [abc] is reported only once. The parameter [message] replaces the constraint’s message with our own: each constraint has this parameter (or several, when it has multiple types of errors, such as [minMessage] and [maxMessage] for [Length]);
  • the other properties have the constraints from Example 08.

docs.title: 3.3.2. Custom messages
docs.text:
The validator’s error messages are written in English in its code, but they pass through the [Symfony] translator (the Translation component), which translates them into the language of the request. [Symfony] comes with translations of its messages in about sixty languages: simply select the application’s language and enable the translator in [config/packages/framework.yaml]:

# config/packages/framework.yaml: the configuration of the FrameworkBundle
framework:
    secret: '%env(APP_SECRET)%'
    # the language of the application: the validation messages will be in English
    default_locale: en
    # the translation service; its dictionaries are in the translations/ folder
    translator:
        default_path: '%kernel.project_dir%/translations'
  • line 5: the application’s default language (locale). This is also the language for each request, unless the application changes it (see the chapter on internationalization);
  • lines 7–8: the translator, whose application-specific dictionaries are located in the [translations] folder. [%kernel.project_dir%] is a container parameter: the project folder (example 01).

Messages translated by [Symfony] are not always appropriate. The application may provide its own translations, which take precedence. Validation messages are stored in the [validators] domain; the English translations for this domain are stored in the [translations/validators.en.yaml] file (a dictionary’s name consists of the domain, language, and format):

# translations/validators.en.yaml: our own translations of the validation
# messages (domain [validators]), which take precedence over Symfony's ones.
# The key is the original English message
'This value should not be blank.': 'the field is required'
'The value you selected is not a valid choice.': 'unknown value'

A dictionary associates each key with its translation. For validator messages, the key is the original English message: ['This value should not be blank.'] will be displayed as “the field is required.” The keys are enclosed in single quotes because they contain characters (periods, spaces) that have specific meanings in [YAML]. Messages not translated by this file retain the translation from [Symfony] (the [vendor/symfony/validator/Resources/translations/validators.en.xlf] file), and a message not recognized by any dictionary is displayed as-is: this is the case for our message “an integer is expected.”

docs.title: 3.3.3. The action: src/Controller/PersonsController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Controller/PersonsController.php: it is the action that decides what to do with an invalid input

namespace App\Controller;

use App\Model\PersonInput;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;
use Symfony\Component\Validator\Validator\ValidatorInterface;

class PersonsController extends AbstractController
{
    // the VALIDATOR, a Symfony service, is injected into the action (see example 06)
    #[Route('/persons/action01', name: 'persons_action01', methods: ['GET'])]
    public function action01(Request $request, ValidatorInterface $validator): Response
    {
        // the input: the parameters of the URL, copied into the object
        $input = new PersonInput();
        $input->name = $request->query->get('name');
        $input->age = $request->query->get('age');
        $input->title = $request->query->get('title');
        $input->email = $request->query->get('email');
        // validate checks the constraints of the object, and returns the list of the errors
        $errors = $validator->validate($input);
        if (count($errors) > 0) {
            $items = '';
            foreach ($errors as $error) {
                $items .= "<li>{$error->getPropertyPath()}: {$error->getMessage()}</li>";
            }
            return new Response("<p>The form contains errors:</p><ul>$items</ul>");
        }
        // htmlspecialchars: the entered name is inserted into HTML; its characters
        // < > & " ' are replaced by < >... (otherwise, an input could inject HTML)
        return new Response("<p>Welcome $input->title ".htmlspecialchars($input->name)
            ." ($input->age years old)</p>");
    }
}
  • line 17: the validator, a service from [Symfony] (of type [ValidatorInterface]), is injected into the action as an application service (example 06);
  • Lines 20–24: The action creates the object and copies the parameters from URL into it. We could have, as in Example 08, let [#[MapQueryString]] construct the object; however, [#[MapQueryString]] validates it immediately and terminates the action in case of an error—which is exactly what we want to avoid here;
  • Line 26: [validate] checks the object’s constraints and returns a list of violations (an object [ConstraintViolationList], which is iterated over like an array, and whose size is returned by [count]). The validation does not throw any exceptions: the action itself decides what to do next;
  • lines 27–33: the errors, field by field, each enclosed in a [<li>] tag. In a string enclosed in quotation marks, [{$error->getMessage()}] inserts the result of a method call (curly braces delimit the expression). The operator [.=] appends one string to the end of another;
  • lines 36–37: if successful, a welcome message. The name is passed through the [htmlspecialchars] function from [PHP], which replaces the characters that have meaning in HTML ([<], [>], [&], ["], [']) with their entities ([<], [>]...): they will be displayed as-is instead of being interpreted. Without this precaution, a user could enter a “name” containing HTML, or even [JavaScript], which would execute in the browser of anyone viewing the page. This is the most common security vulnerability on the web: script injection (XSS, cross-site scripting). The title and age fields do not require this protection: their values have been validated by constraints (one of three allowed values, all numeric). In the next chapter, the [Twig] view engine will perform this escaping automatically for any value inserted into a page.

A valid entry, followed by an entry containing four errors:

The messages are in English: those from [Symfony] (name, address), ours (age), and that from our dictionary (title). The raw response to the second query—one for a name containing HTML—and the response to a query without a name, with an age that is too high:

curl "http://localhost:8000/persons/action01?name=m&age=abc&title=Mx&email=xx"
curl "http://localhost:8000/persons/action01?name=%3Cb%3Emartin%3C/b%3E&age=42&title=Mr"
curl "http://localhost:8000/persons/action01?age=200&title=Mr"

<p>The form contains errors:</p><ul><li>name: This value is too short. It should have 2 characters or more.</li><li>age: an integer is expected</li><li>title: unknown value</li><li>email: This value is not a valid email address.</li></ul>
<p>Welcome Mr <b>martin</b> (42 years old)</p>
<p>The form contains errors:</p><ul><li>name: the field is required</li><li>age: This value should be between 0 and 150.</li></ul>

The name [<b>martin</b>] (encoded as [%3Cb%3E...] in the URL) is displayed as-is, without being bolded: its tags have been neutralized. Note that the response this time is a 200 status code: this is the action that chose to return a normal page containing the errors.

docs.title: 3.4. Example 10: Multiple Parameters
docs.text:
The same parameter can appear multiple times in a URL: [?color=red&color=green]. This is what a browser sends for a group of checkboxes with the same name, or a multiple-selection list (see the next chapter). [PHP] handles this case in its own way. The [ArraysController] controller:

<?php
// src/Controller/ArraysController.php: a parameter that appears several times in the URL

namespace App\Controller;

use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\JsonResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;
use Symfony\Component\Validator\Constraints as Assert;
use Symfony\Component\Validator\Validator\ValidatorInterface;

#[Route('/arrays', name: 'arrays_', methods: ['GET'])]
class ArraysController extends AbstractController
{
    // /arrays/action01?color=red&color=green: for PHP, the second parameter
    // REPLACES the first one: only the LAST value is kept
    #[Route('/action01', name: 'action01')]
    public function action01(Request $request): JsonResponse
    {
        return $this->json(['color' => $request->query->get('color'),
            'raw' => $request->server->get('QUERY_STRING')]);
    }

    // /arrays/action02?color[]=red&color[]=green: the brackets ask
    // PHP to store ALL the values in an array
    #[Route('/action02', name: 'action02')]
    public function action02(Request $request): JsonResponse
    {
        // all('color'): the parameter in the form of an array (empty if it is missing)
        $colors = $request->query->all('color');
        return $this->json(['color' => $colors, 'count' => count($colors)]);
    }

    // /arrays/action03?color[]=red: an array, validated item by item
    #[Route('/action03', name: 'action03')]
    public function action03(Request $request, ValidatorInterface $validator): JsonResponse
    {
        $colors = $request->query->all('color');
        // we can validate any value (here an array), by giving the
        // constraints to validate
        $violations = $validator->validate($colors, [
            // a list of at least one item
            new Assert\Count(min: 1),
            // All: the constraints apply to EACH item
            new Assert\All([new Assert\Choice(choices: ['red', 'green', 'blue'])]),
        ]);
        $errors = [];
        foreach ($violations as $violation) {
            $errors[] = "color{$violation->getPropertyPath()}: {$violation->getMessage()}";
        }
        return $this->json(['colors' => $colors, 'valid' => ! $errors, 'errors' => $errors]);
    }
}
  • Lines 21–22: For [PHP], the parameters of URL form an associative array, in which each key has only one value: a repeated parameter replaces the previous one, and only the last value is retained. The action also returns, for comparison, the raw parameter string as sent by the browser: the [server] property of the request contains the variables that the web server transmits to [PHP], including [QUERY_STRING];
  • lines 28–33: To retrieve all values, the parameter name must end with square brackets: [?color[]=red&color[]=green]. [PHP] then stores the values in an array, the value of the parameter [color]. The method [all], when given a parameter name, returns that parameter as an array—empty if the parameter is absent;
  • lines 37–53: the array is validated. The [validate] method of the validator accepts any value, provided that its constraints are specified: here, [Count(min: 1)] (an array with at least one element), and [All], which applies the constraints it contains to each element of the array: each must be one of the three colors;
  • line 50: the violation path identifies the offending element: [[1]] for the second element (indices start at 0), and an empty string for the array itself. This is appended to the parameter name;
  • line 52: the operator [!] evaluates to [true] for an empty array, which evaluates to “false” in a condition.

The [translations/validators.en.yaml] file in the example translates the message from the [Choice] constraint (example 09). The results:

curl "http://localhost:8000/arrays/action01?color=red&color=green"
curl -g "http://localhost:8000/arrays/action02?color[]=red&color[]=green"
curl http://localhost:8000/arrays/action02

{
    "color": "green",
    "raw": "color=red&color=green"
}
{
    "color": [
        "red",
        "green"
    ],
    "count": 2
}
{
    "color": [],
    "count": 0
}

The [-g] option of [curl] prevents it from interpreting the square brackets in URL on its own. A browser, on the other hand, encodes them ([color%5B%5D=red]), which [PHP] also understands. As for HTML, all you need to do is name the checkboxes in a group [color[]] (the Form component of [Symfony] will do this for us; see Example 18). This rule applies specifically to [PHP]: frameworks for other languages ([Flask], [Spring MVC], [ASP.NET Core]) retain all values of a repeated parameter, without square brackets.

[Symfony] ensures that the two forms are not confused: [get] rejects a parameter that is an array, and [all] rejects a parameter that is not an array. In both cases, a 400 error is returned:

curl -i -g "http://localhost:8000/arrays/action01?color[]=red"
curl -i "http://localhost:8000/arrays/action02?color=red"

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
X-Debug-Exception: Input%20value%20%22color%22%20contains%20a%20non-scalar%20value.
...
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
X-Debug-Exception: Unexpected%20value%20for%20parameter%20%22color%22%3A%20expecting%20%22array%22%2C%20got%20%22string%22.
...

Validation succeeds, then fails due to an unknown color, then due to an empty list:

curl -g "http://localhost:8000/arrays/action03?color[]=red&color[]=blue"
curl -g "http://localhost:8000/arrays/action03?color[]=red&color[]=yellow"
curl http://localhost:8000/arrays/action03

{
    "colors": [
        "red",
        "blue"
    ],
    "valid": true,
    "errors": []
}
{
    "colors": [
        "red",
        "yellow"
    ],
    "valid": false,
    "errors": [
        "color[1]: unknown value"
    ]
}
{
    "colors": [],
    "valid": false,
    "errors": [
        "color: This collection should contain 1 element or more."
    ]
}

The error regarding the unknown color refers to [color[1]]: the parameter and index of the problematic element in the array.

docs.title: 3.5. Example 11: The parameters of a POST query
docs.text:
The previous examples used GET requests, whose parameters are contained in URL. A POST request carries its data in its body, in two main forms:

  • fields from a HTML form: the body has the same syntax as a query string ([name=martin&age=42]), and its type (header [Content-Type]) is [application/x-www-form-urlencoded];
  • a JSON document, sent by a program ([JavaScript] on a page, client of a API...): the type is [application/json].

The [PostController] controller:

<?php
// src/Controller/PostController.php: the parameters of a POST request

namespace App\Controller;

use App\Model\PersonModel;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Exception\JsonException;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\JsonResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
