use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Attribute\MapRequestPayload;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Exception\BadRequestHttpException;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Exception\UnsupportedMediaTypeHttpException;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

#[Route('/post', name: 'post_', methods: ['POST'])]
class PostController extends AbstractController
{
    // the fields of an HTML form (application/x-www-form-urlencoded body):
    // $request->request contains the parameters of the request BODY
    #[Route('/action01', name: 'action01')]
    public function action01(Request $request): JsonResponse
    {
        return $this->json([
            'receivedType' => $request->headers->get('Content-Type'),
            'fields' => $request->request->all(),
        ]);
    }

    // a JSON body: toArray() deserializes it
    #[Route('/action02', name: 'action02')]
    public function action02(Request $request): JsonResponse
    {
        // the format of the body, deduced from the Content-Type header: 'json', 'form'...
        if ($request->getContentTypeFormat() !== 'json') {
            throw new UnsupportedMediaTypeHttpException('the body of the request must be JSON');
        }
        try {
            $body = $request->toArray();
        } catch (JsonException $e) {
            throw new BadRequestHttpException('Malformed JSON: '.$e->getMessage());
        }
        return $this->json(['receivedType' => $request->headers->get('Content-Type'), 'body' => $body,
            'name' => $request->getPayload()->get('name')]);
    }

    // a single field; getPayload(): the parameters of the body, whether it is a
    // form or a JSON document
    #[Route('/action03', name: 'action03')]
    public function action03(Request $request): Response
    {
        $name = $request->getPayload()->get('name');
        return new Response("name = [$name]");
    }

    // the body, form or JSON, bound to a PersonModel object and validated (see
    // example 08): #[MapRequestPayload] is the counterpart of #[MapQueryString]
    #[Route('/action04', name: 'action04')]
    public function action04(#[MapRequestPayload] PersonModel $person): JsonResponse
    {
        return $this->json(['person' => $person, 'valid' => true]);
    }
}
  • line 17: all routes in the controller accept only the POST method;
  • Line 26: The request header [Content-Type];
  • line 27: the [request] property of the request (the name, “history,” is misleading) contains the body parameters—for a form body—in a parameter bag similar to [query] (example 07): [get], [getInt], [all]... The fields in a form follow the rules in Example 10: a repeated field must have a name ending in [[]];
  • lines 36–38: [getContentTypeFormat()] specifies the body format, derived from the header [Content-Type]: [json], [form], [xml]... A body that is not declared as JSON is rejected with error 415 (Unsupported Media Type);
  • lines 39–43: [toArray()] deserializes the body JSON: the text JSON becomes an array [PHP]. A malformed JSON raises a [JsonException] exception (from the HttpFoundation component, imported on line 7), which the [try] / [catch] intercepts to respond with a 400 error containing our message. Without this block, [Symfony] would itself respond with a 400 error: this exception is one of those it recognizes as client errors;
  • lines 44–45: The [getPayload()] method returns the body parameters—whether it is a form or a JSON document—in a parameter bag. This is the method most commonly used because it does not depend on the form of the request;
  • line 53: a form field, read by [getPayload()];
  • lines 59–63: the [#[MapRequestPayload]] attribute is the counterpart, for the request body, of [#[MapQueryString]] (Example 08): it constructs a [PersonModel] object (the class from Example 08) from the fields in the form or the JSON document, and validates it. An invalid template throws an exception (with code 422, Unprocessable Content, in this case), which the [ValidationErrors] listener from Example 08 converts into a 400 response. The example also uses the configuration and dictionary from Example 09: the messages will be in English, with our own translations.

[Symfony] requires nothing else to accept requests from POST: it has no anti-CSRF protection that would apply to all requests (Example 02). With [curl], the option [-d] (data) sends a body; the request then becomes a POST request, of type [application/x-www-form-urlencoded], unless the option [-H] (header) specifies a different type. The option [-X POST] explicitly sets the method (it is optional here). The fields of a form, including a repeated field:

curl -i -g -X POST -d "name=martin&age=42&hobby[]=tennis&hobby[]=piano" http://localhost:8000/post/action01

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "receivedType": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded",
    "fields": {
        "name": "martin",
        "age": "42",
        "hobby": [
            "tennis",
            "piano"
        ]
    }
}

A JSON body, which contains an integer and an array:

curl -i -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"name\": \"martin\", \"age\": 42, \"children\": [\"léa\", \"tom\"]}" http://localhost:8000/post/action02

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "receivedType": "application/json",
    "body": {
        "name": "martin",
        "age": 42,
        "children": [
            "léa",
            "tom"
        ]
    },
    "name": "martin"
}

The quotation marks in JSON are preceded by [\] to prevent the command string from ending; Under [Linux] and [macOS], you can also enclose JSON in apostrophes: [-d '{"name": "martin"}']. Unlike form fields, the JSON carries data types: age is already an integer. A body that is not JSON, followed by a malformed JSON (requesting a JSON response to view the message):

curl -i -H "Accept: application/json" -d "name=martin" http://localhost:8000/post/action02
curl -i -H "Accept: application/json" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"name\": " http://localhost:8000/post/action02

HTTP/1.1 415 Unsupported Media Type
Content-Type: application/json

{"type":"https:\/\/tools.ietf.org\/html\/rfc2616#section-10","title":"An error occurred","status":415,"detail":"the body of the request must be JSON",...}
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/json

{"type":"https:\/\/tools.ietf.org\/html\/rfc2616#section-10","title":"An error occurred","status":400,"detail":"Malformed JSON: Could not decode request body.",...}

A single field, then the same URL requested as GET:

curl -d "name=jean%20dupont" http://localhost:8000/post/action03
curl -i "http://localhost:8000/post/action03?name=martin"

name = [jean dupont]
HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
Allow: POST
...

URL exists, but not for the GET method: [Symfony] returns a 405 (Method Not Allowed) response, and its header [Allow] lists the accepted methods (example 02). Finally, the template linked to the request body—first via a valid form, then an invalid one, and finally via a JSON document:

curl -d "name=martin&age=42&title=Mr" http://localhost:8000/post/action04
curl -i -d "name=m&age=200" http://localhost:8000/post/action04
curl -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"name\": \"martin\", \"age\": \"42\", \"title\": \"Mr\"}" http://localhost:8000/post/action04

{
    "person": {
        "name": "martin",
        "age": 42,
        "title": "Mr",
        "email": null
    },
    "valid": true
}
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "status": 400,
    "errors": [
        {
            "field": "name",
            "message": "This value is too short. It should have 2 characters or more."
        },
        {
            "field": "age",
            "message": "This value should be between 0 and 150."
        },
        {
            "field": "title",
            "message": "the field is required"
        }
    ]
}
{
    "status": 400,
    "errors": [
        {
            "field": "age",
            "message": "This value should be of type int|null."
        }
    ]
}

The last request shows a difference between the two body formats. Form fields are always strings: [Symfony] therefore converts the string ["42"] to an integer. A JSON document, on the other hand, has data types: if the client sends a string (["42"], enclosed in quotes) where the class expects an integer, it is a type error, which [Symfony] reports without attempting to convert ([int|null] is the [?int] type of the property, written differently).

docs.title: 3.6. Example 12: Custom Binding and Validation
docs.text:
Standard types, attributes, and constraints are not always sufficient. This example shows three ways to extend binding and validation:

  • a “custom” argument resolver: a date in French format, [23-09-2026], located in the path of URL, provided to the action as an object;
  • a listener that provides the action with a parameter that does not come from the URL, but from a HTTP header;
  • a custom validation constraint (no spaces), and the conversion of a date [dd/mm/yyyy].
12-custom-binding/
├── src/
│   ├── Controller/
│   │   └── ExamplesController.php
│   ├── EventListener/
│   │   └── ErrorAsText.php
│   ├── Binding/
│   │   ├── DetectLanguage.php
│   │   ├── DayFr.php
│   │   ├── DayFrResolver.php
│   │   ├── NoSpace.php
│   │   └── NoSpaceValidator.php
│   ├── Model/
│   │   └── SearchModel.php
│   └── Kernel.php
└── ...

docs.title: 3.6.1. An object linked to a route parameter: DayFr.php and DayFrResolver.php
docs.text:
We have seen that the parameters of an action are provided by argument resolvers (example 05): one provides the route parameters (example 02), another the request (example 05), another provides the services (example 06), and still others provide the parameters for URL ([#[MapQueryParameter]]) or a template ([#[MapQueryString]]). [Symfony] has about fifteen of them, including one for dates ([#[MapDateTime]]) and one for enumerations. The application can write its own. We’ll write one for a date in French format, represented by the class [DayFr]:

<?php
// src/Binding/DayFr.php: a French date "23-09-2026" in the path of the URL

namespace App\Binding;

use DateTimeImmutable;
use Stringable;

readonly class DayFr implements Stringable
{
    public function __construct(public DateTimeImmutable $date)
    {
    }

    // text of the path -> DayFr object; null: the text does not designate a date
    public static function fromUrl(string $text): ?self
    {
        // the ! of "!d-m-Y" resets the time to zero (otherwise, it would be the current time)
        $date = DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat('!d-m-Y', $text);
        // createFromFormat accepts "31-02-2026" (and makes it March 3rd): we check
        // that the date, formatted again, gives back the received text
        if ($date === false || $date->format('d-m-Y') !== $text) {
            return null;
        }
        return new self($date);
    }

    // DayFr object -> text of the path (used when building the URL of a route)
    public function __toString(): string
    {
        return $this->date->format('d-m-Y');
    }
}
  • line 9: an immutable class that implements the [Stringable] interface from [PHP]: its objects can be converted to a string using their [__toString] method;
  • line 11: the date, a [DateTimeImmutable] object (the date class from [PHP]; the [Immutable] version creates a new object with each modification—[$date->modify('+1 day')] returns a new date—instead of modifying the object);
  • lines 16–26: a static method that creates a [DayFr] object from the path text, or returns [null] if the text is invalid ([?self]: an object of the current class, or [null]). [DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat] parses a string according to a specific format: [d] for the day, [m] for the month, and [Y] for the four-digit year; the initial [!] sets the hour to zero. [createFromFormat] is tolerant: it accepts [31-02-2026] and interprets it as March 3. The validation on line 22 rejects this case: the date, reformatted by [format], must exactly match the received text;
  • Lines 29–32: the reverse operation: the object becomes the path text. [Symfony] will use this to create a URL from a [DayFr] object.

The resolver:

<?php
// src/Binding/DayFrResolver.php: an ARGUMENT RESOLVER, which provides the actions with
// their parameters of type DayFr

namespace App\Binding;

use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Controller\ValueResolverInterface;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\ControllerMetadata\ArgumentMetadata;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Exception\NotFoundHttpException;

class DayFrResolver implements ValueResolverInterface
{
    // called for each parameter of an action that asks for this resolver (see the
    // controller): returns the value of the parameter, in an array
    public function resolve(Request $request, ArgumentMetadata $argument): iterable
    {
        // the route parameter with the same name as the parameter of the action ($day)
        $text = $request->attributes->get($argument->getName());
        if (! is_string($text)) {
            return [];    // nothing to provide: another resolver will take care of it
        }
        // a date that does not exist: the URL designates nothing, 404 error
        return [DayFr::fromUrl($text) ?? throw new NotFoundHttpException("[$text] is not a date")];
    }
}
  • Line 12: An argument resolver implements the [ValueResolverInterface] interface, whose only method is [resolve];
  • Line 16: [resolve] receives the request and the description of the action’s parameter (a [ArgumentMetadata] object: its name, type, default value, and attributes). It returns the parameter value in an array ([iterable]), or an empty array if it has nothing to return;
  • Line 19: The route parameters are stored in the request attributes ([$request->attributes]), a parameter set that also contains information calculated by [Symfony] (the route name, [_route], for example). We search for the parameter with the same name as the action;
  • line 24: the object [DayFr], or, if the text does not refer to a date, a 404 error: URL does not refer to anything. The operator [??] returns its left operand if it is not [null], and the right operand otherwise; it accepts a [throw] expression on the right.

The class is a service, like all those in the [src] folder (example 02): [Symfony] recognizes it as an argument resolver, thanks to its interface ([autoconfigure]). The controller will specify which parameter it must provide.

docs.title: 3.6.2. A parameter provided by a listener: src/Binding/DetectLanguage.php
docs.text:
To provide an action with information calculated from the request, you can also have a listener calculate it (Example 03), which then includes it in the request before the action:

<?php
// src/Binding/DetectLanguage.php: a listener that COMPUTES a piece of information for the action

namespace App\Binding;

use Symfony\Component\EventDispatcher\Attribute\AsEventListener;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Event\RequestEvent;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\KernelEvents;

// the [kernel.request] event: the request arrives, the action is not called yet
#[AsEventListener(event: KernelEvents::REQUEST)]
class DetectLanguage
{
    public function __invoke(RequestEvent $event): void
    {
        $request = $event->getRequest();
        // the header "Accept-Language: fr-FR,fr;q=0.9,en;q=0.8" -> "fr": the browser's
        // preferred language among those offered (the first one by default)
        $language = $request->getPreferredLanguage(['fr', 'en']);
        // the ATTRIBUTES of the request: information that the application stores there
        // for the functions that will handle the request after it
        $request->attributes->set('language', $language);
    }
}
  • line 11: a listener for the [kernel.request] event, triggered when the request arrives, before the action is called (the routing itself is a listener for this event: the chapter on the lifecycle will discuss their order);
  • line 19: the request’s [Accept-Language] header specifies the user’s languages, in order of preference: [fr-FR,fr;q=0.9,en;q=0.8] (the [q] coefficient measures the preference, on a scale from 0 to 1). [getPreferredLanguage] selects the user’s preferred language from among those offered by the application; if no header is present, it defaults to the first language on the list;
  • line 22: the language is stored in the request attributes under the name [language], alongside the route parameters.

The listener runs for all requests. [Symfony] does not have the equivalent of route middleware found in other frameworks: a listener that is supposed to act only for certain routes checks the route name itself ([$request->attributes->get('_route')]). As for the action, it will receive the information without doing anything special (see the controller).

docs.title: 3.6.3. A “custom” constraint and a conversion: NoSpace.php and SearchModel.php
docs.text:
A “custom” constraint is written as two classes: the constraint itself, which describes it (its options, its message), and its validator, which checks it.

<?php
// src/Binding/NoSpace.php: a "home-made" validation constraint

namespace App\Binding;

use Attribute;
use Symfony\Component\Validator\Constraint;

// #[Attribute]: the class can be used as an attribute (#[NoSpace]); the
// check itself is entrusted to the NoSpaceValidator class
#[Attribute(Attribute::TARGET_PROPERTY)]
class NoSpace extends Constraint
{
    public string $message = 'the field must not contain a space';
}
  • line 11: the [#[Attribute]] attribute of [PHP] allows the class to be used as an attribute, here on a property ([TARGET_PROPERTY]);
  • line 12: a constraint inherits from the class [Constraint];
  • line 14: its error message, in a public property: this could be changed at runtime ([#[NoSpace(message: '...')]]).
<?php
// src/Binding/NoSpaceValidator.php: the check of the NoSpace constraint

namespace App\Binding;

use Symfony\Component\Validator\Constraint;
use Symfony\Component\Validator\ConstraintValidator;

class NoSpaceValidator extends ConstraintValidator
{
    public function validate(mixed $value, Constraint $constraint): void
    {
        if ($value !== null && str_contains((string) $value, ' ')) {
            // the value is not suitable: we report a "violation", with the
            // message of the constraint
            $this->context->buildViolation($constraint->message)->addViolation();
        }
    }
}
  • line 9: the validator for a constraint is named after its class, followed by [Validator]: this is how [Symfony] locates it. It inherits from [ConstraintValidator];
  • Lines 11–18: Its method [validate] receives the value to be validated and the constraint. [str_contains] checks for the presence of text in a string; [(string)] converts the value to a string. If the value is invalid, a violation is reported to the validation context ([$this->context]), along with the constraint message. The type [mixed] refers to any type. Like the constraints of [Symfony], this one accepts [null]: the absence of a value is handled by [NotBlank].

The constraint is used by the search model:

<?php
// src/Model/SearchModel.php: the model of the search

namespace App\Model;

use App\Binding\NoSpace;
use DateTimeImmutable;
use Symfony\Component\Validator\Constraints as Assert;

readonly class SearchModel
{
    public function __construct(
        // a "home-made" constraint
        #[NoSpace]
        public ?string $keyword = null,
        // DateTime: a date in the dd/mm/yyyy format, which exists; {{ value }}: the received value
        #[Assert\DateTime(format: 'd/m/Y', message: '{{ value }} is not a valid dd/mm/yyyy date')]
        public ?string $since = null,
    ) {
    }

    // the date, CONVERTED into a date object (null if it is missing)
    public function since(): ?DateTimeImmutable
    {
        return $this->since === null ? null
            : DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat('!d/m/Y', $this->since);
    }
}
  • lines 14–15: our constraint, used just like any other;
  • lines 17–18: the constraint [DateTime] verifies that the value is a date in the specified format ([d/m/Y]: dd/mm/yyyy), and that this date exists. Its message is replaced by ours; the [{{ value }}] marker will be replaced by the received value (in quotes). The date remains a string in the model: a property of type [DateTimeImmutable] would be converted by the Serializer, but an invalid date would then cause a conversion error (example 08), with a rather vague error message;
  • Lines 23–27: the date conversion, in a method of the model: the corresponding [DateTimeImmutable] object, or [null] if the date is missing. The action calls this method only after validation: the date is therefore necessarily valid.

Finally, the response to a failed validation. We want this to be different from the one in Example 08: the first error message, in plain text, with code 400:

<?php
// src/EventListener/ErrorAsText.php: an invalid model produces a 400 response,
// which contains, as plain text, the message of the first error

namespace App\EventListener;

use Symfony\Component\EventDispatcher\Attribute\AsEventListener;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Event\ExceptionEvent;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\KernelEvents;
use Symfony\Component\Validator\Exception\ValidationFailedException;

#[AsEventListener(event: KernelEvents::EXCEPTION)]
class ErrorAsText
{
    public function __invoke(ExceptionEvent $event): void
    {
        $validation = $event->getThrowable()->getPrevious();
        if ($validation instanceof ValidationFailedException) {
            $event->setResponse(new Response($validation->getViolations()[0]->getMessage(),
                Response::HTTP_BAD_REQUEST, ['Content-Type' => 'text/plain; charset=utf-8']));
        }
    }
}

This is the listener from Example 08, stripped down to the essentials: [getViolations()[0]] is the first violation. Such a listener applies to the entire application. To provide a different response depending on the action, it would check the route name (see above).

docs.title: 3.6.4. The controller: src/Controller/ExamplesController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Controller/ExamplesController.php: custom binding and validation

namespace App\Controller;

use App\Binding\DayFr;
use App\Binding\DayFrResolver;
use App\Model\SearchModel;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Attribute\MapQueryString;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Attribute\ValueResolver;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

#[Route('/examples', name: 'examples_', methods: ['GET'])]
class ExamplesController extends AbstractController
{
    // /examples/schedule/23-09-2026: #[ValueResolver] entrusts the $day parameter to the
    // DayFrResolver resolver, which BINDS it to the {day} route parameter
    #[Route('/schedule/{day}', name: 'schedule', requirements: ['day' => '[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{4}'])]
    public function schedule(#[ValueResolver(DayFrResolver::class)] DayFr $day): Response
    {
        // generateUrl builds the URL of a route; the DayFr object becomes the text
        // of the path through its __toString method: "23-09-2026"
        return new Response("schedule for the day [{$day->date->format('Y-m-d')}], of type "
            .get_debug_type($day->date).', URL: '.$this->generateUrl('examples_schedule', ['day' => $day]));
    }

    // /examples/hello: a parameter that does not come from the URL, but from a header,
    // computed by the DetectLanguage listener and stored in the attributes of the request
    #[Route('/hello', name: 'hello')]
    public function hello(string $language): Response
    {
        return new Response($language === 'en' ? 'Hello!' : 'Bonjour !');
    }

    // /examples/search?keyword=symfony&since=01/09/2026
    #[Route('/search', name: 'search')]
    public function search(#[MapQueryString] SearchModel $search): Response
    {
        $since = $search->since()?->format('Y-m-d');
        return new Response("search for [$search->keyword] since [$since]");
    }
}
  • Line 20: the calendar route, whose parameter [{day}] is constrained by a regular expression: [[0-9]] denotes a digit, [{2}] denotes the repetition of the preceding pattern: two digits, a hyphen, two digits, a hyphen, four digits. A path segment with a different format does not match the route (404), without our resolver even being consulted;
  • line 21: the attribute [#[ValueResolver]] assigns the parameter [$day] to a resolver, identified by its class: it, and it alone, will provide it. Without this attribute, [Symfony] would try its resolvers in order of priority, and the route parameters resolver—which takes precedence over ours—would provide the string ["23-09-2026"] to a parameter of type [DayFr]: an error;
  • lines 25–26: the date is displayed in international format ([Y-m-d]: [2026-09-23]). The [generateUrl] method of [AbstractController] creates the URL for a named route, along with its parameters (this is what [redirectToRoute] did, example 04). It is passed the [DayFr] object itself: [Symfony] converts it to a string using its [__toString] method. URL refers to the site ([/examples/...]); a third parameter would require an absolute URL;
  • lines 31–35: the parameter [$language] does not correspond to any route parameter. However, the route parameter resolver generally looks for a request attribute with the same name as the parameter: it therefore finds the one that the listener [DetectLanguage] has stored there. That’s all: no attribute is required on the parameter;
  • Lines 38–43: the search template, linked to the parameters of URL and validated (example 08). The action accepts only valid templates; it calls the date conversion method. The [?->] operator (nullsafe) calls a method if the object is not [null], and returns [null] otherwise.

docs.title: 3.6.5. Execution
docs.text:
The object associated with the route parameter:

curl "http://localhost:8000/examples/schedule/23-09-2026"
curl -i "http://localhost:8000/examples/schedule/31-02-2026"

schedule for the day [2026-09-23], of type DateTimeImmutable, URL: /examples/schedule/23-09-2026
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
X-Debug-Exception: %5B31-02-2026%5D%20is%20not%20a%20date
...

The date is displayed in international format, but the URL generated by [generateUrl] reverted to the French format. February 31 does not exist: 404, with a message from our resolver. A date in international format, [2026-09-23], does not match the pattern described by the regular expression: 404 as well, but this time because no route matches.

The listener. The [-H] option of [curl] sets the header [Accept-Language]:

curl -H "Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9,fr;q=0.8" http://localhost:8000/examples/hello
curl -H "Accept-Language: fr-FR,fr;q=0.9" http://localhost:8000/examples/hello
curl http://localhost:8000/examples/hello

Hello!
Bonjour !
Bonjour !

Without the header [Accept-Language] ([curl] does not send one), it is the first language in the list. The chapter on internationalization will revisit this issue, with the user selecting the language.

The “in-house” constraint and date conversion:

curl "http://localhost:8000/examples/search?keyword=symfony&since=01/09/2026"
curl "http://localhost:8000/examples/search"
curl -i "http://localhost:8000/examples/search?keyword=symfony%20mvc"
curl "http://localhost:8000/examples/search?since=2026-09-01"
curl "http://localhost:8000/examples/search?since=31/02/2026"

search for [symfony] since [2026-09-01]
search for [] since []
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

the field must not contain a space
"2026-09-01" is not a valid dd/mm/yyyy date
"31/02/2026" is not a valid dd/mm/yyyy date

Without any parameters, [#[MapQueryString]] constructs an empty template, which is valid: both of its properties are optional.

docs.title: 3.6.6. Conclusion
docs.text:
Let’s summarize the methods available to an action for obtaining its model:

Route parametersthe action’s parameters, with the same names; converted by their type ([int $id]), constrained by [requirements]; linked to an object via an argument resolver ([ValueResolverInterface], [#[ValueResolver]])Parameters of URL[$request->query->get(...)], [getInt], [all]...; [#[MapQueryParameter]]; a repeated parameter is written as [name[]]Fields in a POST form[$request->request->get(...)], or [$request->getPayload()->get(...)], which also reads JSONBody JSON[$request->toArray()], [$request->getPayload()]Model described by a class[#[MapQueryString]] (URL), [#[MapRequestPayload]] (the body): conversion, then validationHeaders[$request->headers->get(...)], and methods that parse them, such as [getPreferredLanguage]Validationconstraints ([#[Assert\...]]), checked before the action ([#[MapQueryString]]...) or during the action ([ValidatorInterface]); "custom" constraints ([Constraint] and [ConstraintValidator])Messagesthe [default_locale] language, the translator, and the [translations/validators.xx.yaml] dictionariesCommon errorsan event listener for [kernel.exception]Calculated parameteran event listener [kernel.request], which stores information in the request attributes

HTML forms, on the other hand, require more than just validation: they must be displayed, re-displayed with the user’s input and any errors, and protected against forged requests. [Symfony] delegates all of this to its Form component. This is the subject of the next chapter, once views have been introduced.

docs.title: 7. The Lifecycle of a Request
docs.text:
Between the arrival of a request and the dispatch of its response, the [Symfony] kernel (the [HttpKernel] class) performs several steps, and at each step, it publishes an event to which the application can respond via a listener. We have already encountered several of these: the listeners for [kernel.request] and [kernel.response] (examples 03, 16, 22), for [kernel.exception] (examples 08 and 12), and the argument resolvers (example 12). This chapter brings them all together in a single example, which displays a message in the console at each step so you can observe the order:

  • 1 and 2. [kernel.request]: the request has just arrived. All listeners for this event are called, in descending order of priority. One of them is the routing listener for [Symfony] (the [RouterListener] listener, with priority 32): it searches for the route that matches URL and the method, and stores its name and parameters in the request attributes; if none match, it throws a [NotFoundHttpException] (404) exception. A listener with a priority higher than 32 (1) runs before routing and does not know the route; a listener with a lower priority (2) does know it. A [kernel.request] listener can also provide the response ([$event->setResponse(...)]) itself: in this case, the action is not called;
  • 3. [kernel.controller]: the action has been selected but not yet invoked. A listener can examine the action (its attributes, such as [PHP], for example) or replace it;
  • 4. The argument resolvers calculate the action’s parameters (Example 12), and then the event [kernel.controller_arguments] is published;
  • 5. The action and the view it generates. (If the action does not return a [Response] object, an additional event, [kernel.view], allows a listener to construct the response based on what the action returned.);
  • 6 and 7. [kernel.response]: the response is ready. Each listener can modify it (add a header, a cookie), in descending order of priority;
  • 8. [kernel.terminate], published after the response is sent to the browser (this is the [$kernel->terminate(...)] call from the [public/index.php] file, example 01). Listeners can no longer change the response: they are used for tasks that can wait (writing a log, sending an email, etc.), without making the user wait;
  • x. [kernel.exception]: An exception thrown at any stage (by a listener, a resolver, the action, or the view) interrupts processing; it is handled by the listeners for that event. The first listener to provide a response stops the search. This response then passes through [kernel.response], just like a regular response. If no listener in the application provides one, [Symfony] generates the error page: detailed in debug mode, otherwise minimal.

This is equivalent to the filters in [Java] and the interceptors in [Spring MVC], the action filters in [ASP.NET Core MVC], the functions in [before_request] / [after_request] and [Flask], and the middleware of [Laravel]. The difference between them lies in their structure: a middleware component wraps the rest of the processing (it calls [$next], and thus sees the request before and the response after, within the same code), whereas a listener reacts to an event; to act before and after the action, you must listen for two events. On the other hand, a listener can intervene at a specific stage (after routing, after the action is selected, etc.), and the order of the listeners is determined by a number—the priority.

docs.title: 7.1. Example 24: The stages of request processing
docs.text:
24-lifecycle/
├── src/
│   ├── Controller/
│   │   └── CalcController.php
│   ├── EventListener/
│   │   ├── Block.php
│   │   ├── Timing.php
│   │   ├── Timed.php
│   │   ├── Logger.php
│   │   └── ErrorPage.php
│   └── Binding/
│       └── IntegerResolver.php
├── templates/
│   ├── calc/
│   │   └── result.html.twig
│   ├── error.html.twig
│   └── layout.html.twig
└── ...

The application has only one action, which calculates the square of an integer: [/square/7]. Depending on URL, it either succeeds or fails in various ways. Messages are written to the server console by the [error_log] function in [PHP], which the development server ([php -S]) displays.

docs.title: 7.1.1. Before and after everything else: src/EventListener/Logger.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/EventListener/Logger.php: a listener of TWO events. It sees each request
// go by BEFORE the rest of the application (even the routing), and the response
// AFTER all the rest

namespace App\EventListener;

use Symfony\Component\EventDispatcher\Attribute\AsEventListener;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Event\RequestEvent;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Event\ResponseEvent;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\KernelEvents;

class Logger
{
    // priority 100: before Symfony's routing (priority 32)
    #[AsEventListener(event: KernelEvents::REQUEST, priority: 100)]
    public function before(RequestEvent $event): void
    {
        $request = $event->getRequest();
        // error_log: a message in the console of the development server
        error_log('--- '.$request->getMethod().' '.$request->getRequestUri());
        error_log('1. Logger, kernel.request (before the routing)');
    }

    // priority -100: after the other listeners of kernel.response
    #[AsEventListener(event: KernelEvents::RESPONSE, priority: -100)]
    public function after(ResponseEvent $event): void
    {
        error_log('7. Logger, kernel.response (code '.$event->getResponse()->getStatusCode().')');
    }
}

A single class can listen for multiple events: the [#[AsEventListener]] attribute is then applied to each of the relevant methods.

  • lines 16–23: message #1, with the request ([getRequestUri()]: the path and parameters). Priority 100 places the listener before routing: nothing has happened yet in [Symfony];
  • Lines 26–30: Message No. 7, once everything else has been completed. A priority of -100 places the listener after those of the application and [Symfony] (most of which have a priority between -10 and 10). [getStatusCode()] is the response code.

Such a listener does not know the chosen route, since routing has not yet taken place. It is used for processing that applies to all requests: logging, handling a proxy (the case study mentions this in relation to the clients’ IP address)...

docs.title: 7.1.2. After routing: src/EventListener/Block.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/EventListener/Block.php: a listener of kernel.request, executed AFTER the
// routing: it knows the chosen route

namespace App\EventListener;

use Symfony\Component\EventDispatcher\Attribute\AsEventListener;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Event\RequestEvent;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Exception\AccessDeniedHttpException;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\KernelEvents;

// priority 0 (by default): after the routing (priority 32)
#[AsEventListener(event: KernelEvents::REQUEST)]
class Block
{
    public function __invoke(RequestEvent $event): void
    {
        $request = $event->getRequest();
        // the _route attribute of the request: the name of the route chosen by the routing
        error_log('2. Block, kernel.request (route: '.$request->attributes->get('_route').')');
        if ($request->query->has('block')) {
            // an exception: the rest (Timing, the action) is not executed
            throw new AccessDeniedHttpException('access blocked');
        }
    }
}
  • line 13: the default priority, 0: the listener is called after routing;
  • line 20: message #2. Routing has stored the name of the selected route in the [_route] attribute of the request (and its parameters in the attributes of the same name, example 12);
  • Lines 21–24: The [?block] parameter of URL ([has] checks for its presence) causes a 403 error (Forbidden, access denied): the [AccessDeniedHttpException] exception terminates processing.

docs.title: 7.1.3. Before the action: src/EventListener/Timed.php and Timing.php
docs.text:
We want to time only certain actions—those that require it. All we need to do is mark them with a custom attribute, [PHP]:

<?php
// src/EventListener/Timed.php: a PHP ATTRIBUTE of our own invention, to place
// on the actions whose duration we want to measure (see the Timing listener)

namespace App\EventListener;

use Attribute;

// #[Attribute]: this class is an attribute; TARGET_METHOD: it is placed on a method
#[Attribute(Attribute::TARGET_METHOD)]
class Timed
{
}

An attribute is an ordinary class, itself marked with the attribute [#[Attribute]]; [Attribute::TARGET_METHOD] indicates that it is applied to a method. This attribute carries no information: its mere presence is what matters.

<?php
// src/EventListener/Timing.php: a listener of three events, which acts only
// for the actions marked with the #[Timed] attribute: BEFORE the action, AFTER
// it, then one last time AFTER the response is sent (kernel.terminate)

namespace App\EventListener;

use Symfony\Component\EventDispatcher\Attribute\AsEventListener;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Event\ControllerEvent;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Event\ResponseEvent;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Event\TerminateEvent;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\KernelEvents;

class Timing
{
    // kernel.controller: the action has been chosen, it is not called yet
    #[AsEventListener(event: KernelEvents::CONTROLLER)]
    public function before(ControllerEvent $event): void
    {
        // getAttributes: the PHP attributes of a given class, carried by the action
        if ($event->getAttributes(Timed::class) === []) {
            return;
        }
        error_log('3. Timing, kernel.controller (before the action)');
        // the start time (hrtime: a precise clock, in nanoseconds), stored
        // in the attributes of the request (request scope, see example 12)
        $event->getRequest()->attributes->set('start', hrtime(true));
    }

    #[AsEventListener(event: KernelEvents::RESPONSE)]
    public function after(ResponseEvent $event): void
    {
        if ($event->getRequest()->attributes->has('start')) {
            error_log('6. Timing, kernel.response (code '.$event->getResponse()->getStatusCode().')');
        }
    }

    // kernel.terminate: at the very end, AFTER the response is sent to the browser;
    // the response can no longer be changed
    #[AsEventListener(event: KernelEvents::TERMINATE)]
    public function end(TerminateEvent $event): void
    {
        $start = $event->getRequest()->attributes->get('start');
        // the measurement has not started if the action was not reached
        if ($start !== null) {
            $ms = round((hrtime(true) - $start) / 1e6);
            error_log("8. Timing, kernel.terminate (end, $ms ms)");
        }
    }
}
  • Lines 17–28: the [kernel.controller] event. The event’s [getAttributes] method returns the [PHP] attributes of a given class carried by the action (and by its class): an empty list means the action is not marked, and the listener does nothing. Otherwise, message #3, and the start time, stored in the request attributes (example 12). [hrtime(true)] is a precise clock, in nanoseconds, designed to measure durations;
  • lines 30–36: message #6, regarding [kernel.response], with the response code, if the measurement has started. The default priority, 0, places this listener before that of [Logger] (-100);
  • lines 40–49: the [kernel.terminate] event, published after the response is sent: message #8, containing the elapsed time since message #3. The check on line 45 verifies that the measurement has started: the event is published for all requests, even those that did not reach the action.

This is how [Symfony] itself implements some of its attributes: [#[IsGranted]], which we will discuss in the next chapter, is read by a listener of [kernel.controller_arguments], which denies access to the action if the user does not have the requested permission.

docs.title: 7.1.4. The action’s arguments: src/Binding/IntegerResolver.php and the controller
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Binding/IntegerResolver.php: an argument resolver (see example 12): the
// route parameter transformed into an integer, or into null if it is not an
// integer (it is then the action that decides)

namespace App\Binding;

use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Controller\ValueResolverInterface;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\ControllerMetadata\ArgumentMetadata;

class IntegerResolver implements ValueResolverInterface
{
    public function resolve(Request $request, ArgumentMetadata $argument): iterable
    {
        $value = $request->attributes->get($argument->getName());
        error_log("4. IntegerResolver, the arguments of the action (received value: \"$value\")");
        $n = filter_var($value, FILTER_VALIDATE_INT);
        return [$n === false ? null : $n];
    }
}

An argument resolver (Example 12), which writes message #4. It accepts any text and converts it to an integer, or to [null] if it is not one ([filter_var] returns [false]): unlike a constraint such as [requirements] (Example 02), which would return a 404 page for [/square/abc]; here, the action will determine the outcome.

<?php
// src/Controller/CalcController.php: a timed action

namespace App\Controller;

use App\EventListener\Timed;
use App\Binding\IntegerResolver;
use DomainException;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Attribute\ValueResolver;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Exception\BadRequestHttpException;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

class CalcController extends AbstractController
{
    // $n: the {n} route parameter, provided by our IntegerResolver resolver;
    // #[Timed]: the Timing listener measures the duration of this action
    #[Route('/square/{n}', name: 'square', methods: ['GET'])]
    #[Timed]
    public function square(#[ValueResolver(IntegerResolver::class)] ?int $n): Response
    {
        error_log("5. action square($n)");
        if ($n === null) {
            throw new BadRequestHttpException('not an integer');    // 400 error: see ErrorPage
        }
        if ($n === 13) {
            throw new DomainException('13 brings bad luck');    // an "unexpected" error
        }
        return $this->render('calc/result.html.twig', ['n' => $n, 'square' => $n * $n]);
    }
}
  • line 20: the action is marked with our attribute [#[Timed]];
  • line 21: the parameter [$n] is provided by our resolver (attribute [#[ValueResolver]], example 12);
  • lines 24–26: a parameter that is not an integer: error 400 (Bad Request), caused by the exception [BadRequestHttpException];
  • lines 27–29: the number 13 causes an “unexpected” error. [DomainException] is an exception class from the standard library of [PHP];
  • line 30: the normal case. The [calc/result.html.twig] view simply displays the result.

docs.title: 7.1.5. Error handling: src/EventListener/ErrorPage.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/EventListener/ErrorPage.php: a listener of kernel.exception, which replaces
// Symfony's error pages with ours

namespace App\EventListener;

use DomainException;
use Symfony\Component\EventDispatcher\Attribute\AsEventListener;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Event\ExceptionEvent;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Exception\HttpExceptionInterface;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\KernelEvents;
use Twig\Environment;

// priority -10: after Symfony's listener that writes the exception to the log (0),
// before the one that builds its error page (-128)
#[AsEventListener(event: KernelEvents::EXCEPTION, priority: -10)]
class ErrorPage
{
    // Environment: the Twig engine itself, to build a page outside a controller
    public function __construct(private Environment $twig)
    {
    }

    public function __invoke(ExceptionEvent $event): void
    {
        $e = $event->getThrowable();
        if ($e instanceof HttpExceptionInterface) {
            // the HTTP errors (403, unknown page -> 404...): HttpExceptionInterface
            // is the interface of all the HTTP exceptions; they carry their code
            error_log("x. ErrorPage, kernel.exception (HTTP {$e->getStatusCode()})");
            $code = $e->getStatusCode();
        } elseif ($e instanceof DomainException) {
            // an "unexpected" exception of a given type: DomainException and its subclasses
            error_log("x. ErrorPage, kernel.exception (DomainException: {$e->getMessage()})");
            $code = 500;
        } else {
            return;    // the others: Symfony's error page
        }
        // the response of the event replaces the exception (the following listeners are
        // not called); it will then go through kernel.response, like an ordinary response
        $event->setResponse(new Response(
            $this->twig->render('error.html.twig', ['code' => $code]), $code));
    }
}
  • lines 15–17: the listener for [kernel.exception], with priority -10. [Symfony] registers two listeners for this event: the first, with priority 0, logs the exception; the second, with priority -128, generates the error page from [Symfony]. Ours falls between the two: the exception is logged, then we display the page;
  • line 21: the listener is not a controller and does not have the [render] method from [AbstractController]: it receives the [Twig] engine itself (the [Twig\Environment] class), whose [render] method returns the rendered page as a string;
  • lines 28–32: all HTTP errors: a URL with no route (404), a method denied (405), and the exceptions [AccessDeniedHttpException] (403) and [BadRequestHttpException] (400)... implement the [HttpExceptionInterface] interface and carry their code ([getStatusCode()]). This single test therefore replaces all [Symfony] error pages with ours;
  • lines 33–36: an exception of class [DomainException] (or its subclasses; see Example 08): an “unexpected” error, converted into a “custom” error page, with status code 500 (Internal Server Error). The exception message is displayed in the console, but not on the page: it may contain internal details that are not relevant to the user;
  • lines 37–39: the other exceptions are handled by [Symfony];
  • lines 42–43: [setResponse] provides the response, which replaces the exception and stops the event from propagating: subsequent listeners (the error page for [Symfony]) are not called.

The error page receives the error code and displays an appropriate message:

{% extends 'layout.html.twig' %}
{# the error page; its model: the error code #}

{% block content %}
  <div class="alert alert-danger">
    <h1 class="h4">Error {{ code }}</h1>
    {# an associative array, indexed by the code; ??: the default value #}
    <p class="mb-0">{{ {400: 'Bad request.', 403: 'Access denied.', 404: 'Page not found.'}[code] ?? 'Internal server error.' }}</p>
  </div>
{% endblock %}
  • Line 8: an associative array defined in the view ([{key: value, ...}]), from which the element with index [code] is retrieved; the operator [??] provides a default value when this element does not exist.

There is another, even simpler way to replace error pages without writing a listener: a view named [templates/bundles/TwigBundle/Exception/error404.html.twig] replaces the 404 error page, and similarly for each code ([error.html.twig] for all others). These views are only used in production; debug mode retains its detailed pages (you can preview them in debug mode at [/_error/404], provided you have imported the routes [@FrameworkBundle/Resources/config/routing/errors.php]). A listener, on the other hand, allows for any type of handling (a response at JSON, a redirect, etc.) in all modes.

docs.title: 7.1.6. Execution
docs.text:
Normal case, [/square/7]:

The server console displays the eight steps in order (the dates that [php -S] places at the beginning of the lines have been removed):

--- GET /square/7
1. Logger, kernel.request (before the routing)
[info] Matched route "square".
2. Block, kernel.request (route: square)
3. Timing, kernel.controller (before the action)
4. IntegerResolver, the arguments of the action (received value: "7")
5. action square(7)
6. Timing, kernel.response (code 200)
7. Logger, kernel.response (code 200)
8. Timing, kernel.terminate (end, 2 ms)
127.0.0.1:51612 [200]: GET /square/7

The line [[info]] comes from the routing of [Symfony]: this is its log (log). Without a logging library (the most commonly used is [Monolog], installed by [composer require logger]), [Symfony] uses a minimal log, which writes to the console. The last line is the development server log, written once the request is complete. A blocked access, [/square/7?block]:

--- GET /square/7?block
1. Logger, kernel.request (before the routing)
[info] Matched route "square".
2. Block, kernel.request (route: square)
[error] Uncaught PHP Exception Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Exception\AccessDeniedHttpException: "access blocked" at Block.php line 23
x. ErrorPage, kernel.exception (HTTP 403)
7. Logger, kernel.response (code 403)

The listener [Block] raised an exception: the action was not selected, its arguments were not calculated, and it was not called. The exception was logged by [Symfony], then converted into a response by our listener; this response passed through [kernel.response]. The event [kernel.terminate] was published, but [Timing] did not display anything, as the measurement had not started. A parameter that is not an integer, [/square/abc]:

--- GET /square/abc
1. Logger, kernel.request (before the routing)
[info] Matched route "square".
2. Block, kernel.request (route: square)
3. Timing, kernel.controller (before the action)
4. IntegerResolver, the arguments of the action (received value: "abc")
5. action square()
[error] Uncaught PHP Exception Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Exception\BadRequestHttpException: "not an integer" at CalcController.php line 25
x. ErrorPage, kernel.exception (HTTP 400)
6. Timing, kernel.response (code 400)
7. Logger, kernel.response (code 400)
8. Timing, kernel.terminate (end, 1 ms)

This time, the action was called with [null] (which is rendered as an empty string: [square()]), and it was this action that raised error 400. An “unexpected” error, [/square/13]:

--- GET /square/13
1. Logger, kernel.request (before the routing)
[info] Matched route "square".
2. Block, kernel.request (route: square)
3. Timing, kernel.controller (before the action)
4. IntegerResolver, the arguments of the action (received value: "13")
5. action square(13)
[critical] Uncaught PHP Exception DomainException: "13 brings bad luck" at CalcController.php line 28
x. ErrorPage, kernel.exception (DomainException: 13 brings bad luck)
6. Timing, kernel.response (code 500)
7. Logger, kernel.response (code 500)
8. Timing, kernel.terminate (end, 1 ms)

The exception was handled by our listener: the user sees the “custom” error page, not the detailed page, even though debug mode is active. It was still logged, with the level [critical] (an error HTTP is simply a [error]): Like [Laravel], [Symfony] distinguishes between logging an exception in the log and the response it generates. Finally, a URL that does not correspond to any route, [/unknown]:

--- GET /unknown
1. Logger, kernel.request (before the routing)
[error] Uncaught PHP Exception Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Exception\NotFoundHttpException: "No route found for "GET http://localhost:8000/unknown"" at RouterListener.php line 156
x. ErrorPage, kernel.exception (HTTP 404)
7. Logger, kernel.response (code 404)

Routing failed: no listener after it, no action. The 404 page is ours:

curl http://localhost:8000/unknown

...
      <div class="alert alert-danger">
    <h1 class="h4">Error 404</h1>
        <p class="mb-0">Page not found.</p>
  </div>
...

Let’s focus on the essentials. Kernel event listeners are the right place for checks common to many actions (is the user logged in? Do they have permission to access this action?): they form the basis of the security component in [Symfony], which the next chapter uses for authentication. The event listeners for [kernel.exception] and the error views ensure that the user never sees a technical page, regardless of the error: the case study takes advantage of this.

docs.title: 4. The View and Its Model
docs.text:
Up to this point, actions generated their own responses: text, JSON, and a few HTML tags written as a string. In a MVC application, this is the role of a view: a file that describes the page HTML, with placesholders for the data passed to it by the action—the view’s model.

[Symfony] uses the [Twig] view engine, created by the same team. A [Twig] view is a file whose name ends with [.html.twig] (the output format, followed by the engine), stored in the application’s [templates] folder. It is a text file—in this case, HTML—in which three types of tags are interpreted on the server:

  • [{{ expression }}]: the value of an expression, inserted into the page;
  • [{% instruction %}]: an instruction (tag); a condition ([{% if %}]); loop ([{% for %}]), template inheritance ([{% extends %}], [{% block %}]), inclusion ([{% include %}])...;
  • [{# comment #}]: a comment, which does not appear on the generated page.

Everything else is copied as-is. The expressions are not written in [PHP], but in the language of [Twig], which is simpler and safer: [model.title] refers to the property [title] of the object [model] (or its method [getTitle()], or the key [title] of an array: [Twig] looks it up itself); filters transform a value ([name|upper] capitalizes a name); functions perform calculations ([path('home')] generates a URL). [Twig] thus resembles [Jinja2] ([Flask]), from which it drew inspiration, or the engine of [Django]; it differs from [Blade] ([Laravel]) and [Razor] ([ASP.NET Core]), which combine HTML with host language code. A [Twig] view cannot execute arbitrary [PHP] code: it can only display the data provided to it. This is by design: the application logic remains within the classes. A view is not interpreted with every request: when it is first used, [Twig] compiles it into a [PHP] class, stored in the [var/cache/dev/twig] folder, which it then reuses as long as the view remains unchanged. We’ll see what this file looks like.

docs.title: 4.1. Example 13: A First View
docs.text:
13-first-view/
├── config/
│   ├── packages/

docs.title: 4.1.1. The configuration: config/bundles.php and config/packages/twig.yaml
docs.text:
[Twig] is integrated into [Symfony] via a bundle, TwigBundle, which must be added to the application’s bundle list (Example 01):

<?php
// config/bundles.php: the bundles of the application; the TwigBundle integrates the
// Twig view engine
return [
    Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\FrameworkBundle::class => ['all' => true],
    Symfony\Bundle\TwigBundle\TwigBundle::class => ['all' => true],
];

and configure:

# config/packages/twig.yaml: the configuration of the TwigBundle
twig:
    # the folder of the views
    default_path: '%kernel.project_dir%/templates'

The only key specifies the views folder: [templates], located in the project folder. This is also the default value. In a standard project, these two files are created by [Symfony Flex] when you install [Twig] ([composer require twig], see introduction).

docs.title: 4.1.2. The view template: src/Model/PageModel.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Model/PageModel.php: the model of the view, the data that the action passes to the view

namespace App\Model;

readonly class PageModel
{
    public function __construct(
        public string $title,
        public string $message,
        public string $time,
    ) {
    }
}

The view model is a simple immutable class (see Example 03): the three pieces of information that the view will display. There is no requirement to define a view’s model as a class: three separate variables could be passed to the view. However, a class documents what the view expects and allows the editor to verify the action’s code. This is the approach the case study will follow, where each important view has its own model class.

docs.title: 4.1.3. The controller: src/Controller/ViewsController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Controller/ViewsController.php: actions that return a VIEW

namespace App\Controller;

use App\Model\PageModel;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

#[Route(methods: ['GET'])]
class ViewsController extends AbstractController
{
    // render: the Twig engine builds the page from the view
    // templates/views/index.html.twig and from the variables passed in the array (here
    // a single one, [model]); the produced page is the body of the response
    #[Route('/', name: 'index')]
    public function index(): Response
    {
        $model = new PageModel(
            'My first view',
            'This page was built by Twig, on the server.',
            date('H:i:s'));
        return $this->render('views/index.html.twig', ['model' => $model]);
    }

    // the same view with another model; or another view, with the 404 code
    #[Route('/hello/{name}', name: 'hello')]
    public function hello(string $name): Response
    {
        if ($name === 'unknown') {
            // the third parameter of render: the response to complete, here with the 404 code
            return $this->render('views/unknown.html.twig', ['name' => $name],
                new Response(status: Response::HTTP_NOT_FOUND));
        }
        $model = new PageModel(
            "Hello $name",
            'This time, the title of the page comes from the URL.',
            date('H:i:s'));
        return $this->render('views/index.html.twig', ['model' => $model]);
    }
}
  • Lines 20–23: The action builds the view template. The function [date], derived from [PHP], formats the current time: [H] formats the hours, [i] formats the minutes, and [s] formats the seconds;
  • Line 24: The [render] method of [AbstractController] instructs [Twig] to generate the page. The first parameter is the name of the view: the file path, relative to the [templates] folder. The second parameter is an associative array, where each key becomes a variable in the view—in this case, a single one: [model]. [render] returns an object [Response], whose body is the generated page (of type [text/html]);
  • lines 31–35: another view, with another variable ([name]). The third parameter of [render] is a response to be populated: in this case, a 404 response for a custom error page. [new Response(status: ...)] passes the code via a named parameter, while the other parameters retain their default values;
  • Lines 36–40: the same view as the [index] action, but with a different template. This is the benefit of separating actions from views: a single view can be used by multiple actions.

docs.title: 4.1.4. The view: templates/views/index.html.twig
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  {# {{ ... }}: the value of an expression, inserted into the page #}
  <title>{{ model.title }}</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>{{ model.title }}</h1>
  <p>{{ model.message }}</p>
  <p>Page built at {{ model.time }}.</p>
</body>
</html>
  • line 5: a comment [Twig];
  • line 6: [{{ model.title }}] inserts the value of the [title] property of the [model] variable. The period is the access operator for [Twig], where [PHP] writes [$model->title].

Everything inserted by [{{ }}] is escaped: the characters [<], [>], [&], ["], and ['] are replaced by their entities HTML. This is the role that function [htmlspecialchars] played in Example 09, but this time it is automatic: a view therefore cannot inadvertently insert the HTML provided by a user into the page.

docs.title: 4.1.5. The view: templates/views/unknown.html.twig
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Unknown</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Nobody is called [{{ name }}] here.</h1>
</body>

A view is not required to receive an object: the variable [name] is a string.

docs.title: 4.1.6. Execution
docs.text:
The displayed time corresponds to the time zone configured in [PHP] (the [date.timezone] directive in the [php.ini] file), which is Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) in this case; the case study will show how to set it for the application. The raw response shows the work done by [Twig]: the [{{ }}] tags have been replaced with their values, and the comment has been removed.

curl -i http://localhost:8000/

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
    <title>My first view</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>My first view</h1>
  <p>This page was built by Twig, on the server.</p>
  <p>Page built at 09:31:47.</p>
</body>
</html>

The “home” error page, followed by a name containing HTML ([<b>martin], encoded in URL):

curl -i http://localhost:8000/hello/unknown
curl http://localhost:8000/hello/%3Cb%3Emartin

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Unknown</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Nobody is called [unknown] here.</h1>
</body>
</html>
...
    <title>Hello <b>martin</title>
...
  <h1>Hello <b>martin</h1>
  <p>This time, the title of the page comes from the URL.</p>
...

The tag [<b>] was escaped, even though neither the action nor the view had anything to do with it (the apostrophe was also escaped: [']). Here, finally, is the view compiled by [Twig], as found in the [var/cache/dev/twig] folder (under a generated name, such as [f1/f1e0ff0a8a0dc68657a0b1aa94f3ef4b.php]), stripped down to the essentials:

/* views/index.html.twig */
class __TwigTemplate_9c9473b678a753b61e2666e1a8e3a2a4 extends Template
{
    ...
    protected function doDisplay(array $context, array $blocks = []): iterable
    {
        // line 1
        yield "<!doctype html>
<html lang=\"en\">
<head>
  <meta charset=\"utf-8\">
  ";
        // line 6
        yield "  <title>";
        yield (string) $this->escaper->escape(CoreExtension::getAttribute($this->env, $this->source,
            ... $context["model"] ..., "title", ...), "html", null, true);
        yield "</title>
...

The view has become a class named [PHP], whose method [doDisplay] generates the page piece by piece ([yield]). Each [{{ model.title }}] has become a call to [CoreExtension::getAttribute] (which looks up the property, method, or key [title]), passed to the method [escape] (escaping). A [Twig] view is therefore simply a safer and more readable way to write a [PHP] file that generates HTML.

docs.title: 4.2. Example 14: The Twig Language
docs.text: This example combines the main constructs of [Twig] into a single view.

docs.title: 4.2.1. The Template and the Action
docs.text:
The view’s template is defined by three immutable classes, each in its own file ([PHP] does not require one class per file, but the class loader in [Composer] looks for the class [App\Model\Product] in the file [src/Model/Product.php]):

<?php
// src/Model/Product.php: a product

namespace App\Model;

readonly class Product
{
    public function __construct(
        public string $name,
        public float $price,
        public bool $inStock,
    ) {
    }
}

<?php
// src/Model/Address.php: an address

namespace App\Model;

readonly class Address
{
    public function __construct(
        public string $street,
        public string $city,
    ) {
    }
}

<?php
// src/Model/BasicsModel.php: the model of the view of example 14

namespace App\Model;

readonly class BasicsModel
{
    /**
     * @param list<Product> $products
     * @param list<Product> $cart
     */
    public function __construct(
        public string $title,
        public string $name,
        public ?string $nickname,
        public string $html,
        public bool $loggedIn,
        public string $currency,
        public array $products,
        public array $cart,
        public Address $address,
    ) {
    }
}

The model contains values of various types: strings, [null], Booleans, arrays of objects, empty arrays, and objects containing other objects. The prices here are of type [float], to simplify calculations in the view (Example 06 showed why we prefer whole cents).

<?php
// src/Controller/BasicsController.php: a view that uses the main constructs of Twig

namespace App\Controller;

use App\Model\Address;
use App\Model\BasicsModel;
use App\Model\Product;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

class BasicsController extends AbstractController
{
    #[Route('/', name: 'index', methods: ['GET'])]
    public function index(): Response
    {
        $model = new BasicsModel(
            title: 'Twig basics',
            name: 'Martin',
            nickname: null,
            html: '<b>this is HTML</b>',
            loggedIn: true,
            currency: '€',
            products: [
                new Product('Keyboard', 25, true),
                new Product('Mouse', 12.5, false),
                new Product('Screen', 149, true),
            ],
            cart: [],
            address: new Address('12 rue des Lilas', 'Angers'));
        return $this->render('basics/index.html.twig', ['model' => $model]);
    }
}

The action builds the model using named parameters (see Example 02): each value is preceded by the name of the parameter it is intended for, which makes the call readable despite the number of parameters.

docs.title: 4.2.2. The view: templates/basics/index.html.twig
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>{{ model.title }}</title>
</head>
<body>
  {# set: a variable of the view; the reduce filter adds up the prices, the length filter counts the products #}
  {% set total = model.products|reduce((sum, p) => sum + p.price, 0) %}
  {% set count = model.products|length %}
  <h1>{{ model.title }}</h1>
  {# 1. display a value of the model; null is displayed as an empty string;
     the default filter replaces an empty value. This Twig comment does not appear
     in the produced page #}
  <p>1. Name: {{ model.name }} - nickname: [{{ model.nickname }}] [{{ model.nickname|default('none') }}]</p>
  {# 2. {{ }} escapes HTML; the raw filter inserts it as is #}
  <p>2a. {{ model.html }}</p>
  <p>2b. {{ model.html|raw }}</p>
  {# 3. a condition #}
  {% if model.loggedIn %}
    <p>3. You are logged in.</p>
  {% else %}
    <p>3. You are not logged in.</p>
  {% endif %}
  {# 4. a loop: the loop variable describes the state of the loop #}
  <p>4. Our products:</p>
  <ul>
    {% for product in model.products %}
      <li>no. {{ loop.index0 }}: {{ product.name }}, {{ product.price }} {{ model.currency }}
        {{ product.inStock ? '(in stock)' : '(sold out)' }}
        {% if loop.first %} - the first one{% endif %}
        {% if loop.last %} - the last one, seen by {{ model.name }}{% endif %}
      </li>
    {% endfor %}
  </ul>
  {# 5. the empty list: the else block of a for loop #}
  <p>5. Your cart:
    {% for p in model.cart %}<span>{{ p.name }}</span>{% else %} it is empty.{% endfor %}
  </p>
  {# 6. computed expressions, the set variables, and the number_format filter #}
  <p>6. {{ count }} products, for a total of {{ total }} {{ model.currency }};
    average price: {{ (total / count)|number_format(2, '.', ',') }} {{ model.currency }}</p>
  {# 7. an object inside an object, and a filter that converts to uppercase #}
  <p>7. Address: {{ model.address.street }}, {{ model.address.city|upper }}</p>
  {# 8. verbatim: a text that Twig copies without interpreting it #}
  <p>8. Braces displayed as is: {% verbatim %}{{ model.name }}{% endverbatim %}</p>
</body>
</html>
  • Lines 9–10: The [{% set %}] statement creates a variable in the view. The total price is calculated by the filter [reduce], which reduces an array to a single value (like [array_reduce], example 06): its function receives the accumulated value and the current element; [(sum, p) => sum + p.price] is an arrow function of [Twig]. The filter [length] returns the number of elements in an array (or characters in a string). These calculations should be reserved for presentation purposes: the calculation normally belongs to the action;
  • line 15: a [null] value is displayed as an empty string. The [default] filter replaces an empty (or missing) value with a default value;
  • lines 17–18: [{{ }}] escapes HTML (2a); the filter [raw], on the other hand, inserts the value as-is, without escaping it (2b). [raw] is reserved for HTML generated by the application itself, never for user input;
  • Lines 20–24: a condition: [{% if %}], [{% elseif %}], [{% else %}], [{% endif %}]. Each block is closed by a [{% end... %}] statement;
  • Lines 28–34: a loop [{% for ... in ... %}] ... [{% endfor %}]. Within the loop, the special variable [loop] describes the loop’s state: [loop.index0] (the iteration number, starting at 0), [loop.index] (starting at 1), [loop.first], [loop.last] (true on the first and last iterations), [loop.length] (the number of elements). Variables outside the loop ([model.name]) remain accessible;
  • line 30: the ternary operator [condition ? a : b] ([Twig] also accepts [condition ? a], which returns an empty string if the condition is false);
  • line 38: a loop [for] can have a block [{% else %}], which is executed if the list is empty. This is simpler than a [{% if %}] that would check the length of the list;
  • lines 41–42: calculated expressions ([total / count]) and the variables from [set]. The filter [number_format] formats a number: two decimal places, a point as the decimal separator, and a comma as the thousands separator. In Example 16, we’ll see a much better way to format numbers and amounts;
  • line 44: the period passes through objects ([model.address.city]), and the filter [upper] capitalizes a string (while correctly handling accented characters);
  • line 46: the [{% verbatim %}] instruction copies its content without interpreting it: this is useful when a page contains curly braces intended for a [JavaScript] framework.

[Twig] has about fifty filters ([lower], [capitalize], [trim], [join], [split], [slice], [sort], [date], [json_encode], [escape]...), about fifteen functions ([range], [min], [max], [random]...) and tests ([is defined], [is empty], [is null], [is iterable], [is even]...); the bundles for [Symfony] add some ([path], [asset], [form_row], [is_granted]...), and the application can write its own (Example 16).
