docs.text:
The generated page:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Twig basics</title>
</head>
<body>
        <h1>Twig basics</h1>
    <p>1. Name: Martin - nickname: [] [none]</p>
    <p>2a. <b>this is HTML</b></p>
  <p>2b. <b>this is HTML</b></p>
        <p>3. You are logged in.</p>
      <p>4. Our products:</p>
  <ul>
          <li>no. 0: Keyboard, 25 €
        (in stock)
         - the first one              </li>
          <li>no. 1: Mouse, 12.5 €
        (sold out)
                      </li>
          <li>no. 2: Screen, 149 €
        (in stock)
                 - the last one, seen by Martin      </li>
      </ul>
    <p>5. Your cart:
     it is empty.  </p>
    <p>6. 3 products, for a total of 186.5 €;
    average price: 62.17 €</p>
    <p>7. Address: 12 rue des Lilas, ANGERS</p>
    <p>8. Braces displayed as is: {{ model.name }}</p>
</body>
</html>

The comments and instructions have disappeared, but they leave behind their spaces: [Twig] removes the line break that follows a tag, but not the indentation that precedes it. This has no effect: the browser ignores these spaces. (A hyphen inside a tag—such as [{%- ... -%}] or [{{- ... -}}]—would remove the whitespace surrounding it.) A number [float] inserted into the page is written with a decimal point ([12.5]); [number_format] uses the separators passed to it.

docs.title: 4.3. Example 15: Templates, fragments, static files
docs.text:
The pages of a website usually share the same structure: a header, a navigation bar, a footer, and the same style sheets. Rather than repeating this structure in every view, it is written once in a template (layout), which the pages extend. This example also uses [Bootstrap], the most widely used CSS framework, for the layout.

15-layout/
├── config/
│   ├── packages/
│   │   └── twig.yaml
│   └── services.yaml
├── public/
│   └── css/
│       └── styles.css
├── src/
│   ├── Controller/
│   │   └── PagesController.php
│   ├── Model/
│   │   └── Member.php
│   └── Kernel.php
├── templates/
│   ├── fragments/
│   │   └── navbar.html.twig
│   ├── layout.html.twig
│   ├── macros.html.twig
│   └── pages/
│       ├── home.html.twig
│       ├── raw.html.twig
│       └── team.html.twig
└── ...

docs.title: 4.3.1. Static Files
docs.text:
A HTML page references other files: style sheets, [JavaScript] scripts, and images. These files, which the server sends as-is, are called static files. With [Symfony], they are stored in the [public] folder, which the web server serves as-is (example 01): The file [public/css/styles.css] is available at URL [/css/styles.css], without [Symfony] being involved.

/* a few settings in addition to Bootstrap */
body {
  background-color: #f5f7fa;
}

/* the footer of the layout */
.footer {
  margin-top: 2rem;
  font-size: 0.85rem;
  color: #6c757d;
}

/* the error messages, at the bottom of the page, on a light pink background */
.error-area {
  margin-top: 1.5rem;
  padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
  background-color: #fdecef;
  border: 1px solid #f5c2c7;
  border-radius: 0.375rem;
  color: #842029;
}

A few additional CSS rules in addition to [Bootstrap]: a light gray background, the footer style, and the style for an error area that will be used in the following examples.

[Bootstrap] is used in examples 15 through 28. Rather than placing a copy in each user’s [public] folder, the examples share it: it is located in the [examples/common/bootstrap] folder. This folder is not served by the web server: a controller, shared by all these examples, serves its files. This is the file [examples/common/BootstrapController.php]:

<?php
// common/BootstrapController.php: a controller that serves the Bootstrap files,
// shared by examples 15 to 28 (the examples/common/bootstrap folder), under
// the /bootstrap/... URL. Each of these examples declares it in its
// config/services.yaml file

namespace Common;

use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\BinaryFileResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Exception\NotFoundHttpException;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Requirement\Requirement;

class BootstrapController
{
    #[Route('/bootstrap/{file}', name: 'bootstrap', requirements: ['file' => Requirement::CATCH_ALL],
        methods: ['GET'])]
    public function serve(string $file): BinaryFileResponse
    {
        $folder = realpath(__DIR__.'/bootstrap');
        // realpath: the absolute path of the requested file, without the . and the ..;
        // false if the file does not exist
        $path = realpath($folder.'/'.$file);
        // a file that exists, and that is indeed IN the folder (no ../ to get out of it)
        if ($path === false || ! str_starts_with($path, $folder.DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR) || ! is_file($path)) {
            throw new NotFoundHttpException("unknown file: $file");
        }
        // a response that sends the content of a file; its type, according to its extension
        $response = new BinaryFileResponse($path);
        $types = ['css' => 'text/css', 'js' => 'text/javascript', 'map' => 'application/json'];
        $response->headers->set('Content-Type', $types[pathinfo($path, PATHINFO_EXTENSION)] ?? 'application/octet-stream');
        return $response;
    }
}
  • line 7: the class is in the [Common] namespace, which the file [examples/composer.json] associates with the folder [examples/common] (see introduction): the class loader in [Composer] therefore finds it, regardless of the example;
  • Lines 16–17: a route whose parameter [{file}] accepts any path ending, including slashes (example 02): the URL [/bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css] refers to the [css/bootstrap.min.css] file in the folder. The route is named [bootstrap];
  • Lines 20–27: Serving files designated by URL requires caution: a URL such as [/bootstrap/..%2F..%2F15-layout%2F.env] (where [/] is encoded as [%2F]) must not grant access to a file located outside the folder. The [realpath] function of [PHP] calculates the absolute path of a file, stripping away its [.] and [..] components, or returns [false] if the file does not exist. We verify that the resulting path begins with the folder path ([str_starts_with]) and that it refers to a file ([is_file]); otherwise, a 404 error is returned. [DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR] is the system’s path separator: [\] under [Windows], [/] elsewhere;
  • lines 29–32: a [BinaryFileResponse] object is a response that sends the contents of a file. The content type is determined based on the file extension (provided by [pathinfo]), so that a stylesheet is correctly declared as [text/css]: a browser will reject a stylesheet declared as something else.

Each example that uses [Bootstrap] declares this controller as a service in its [config/services.yaml] file:

# config/services.yaml: the services of the application (see example 06)
services:
    _defaults:
        autowire: true
        autoconfigure: true

    App\:
        resource: '../src/'

    # the controller that serves Bootstrap, shared by examples 15 to 28 (see example 15)
    Common\BootstrapController: ~
  • line 11: the [Common\BootstrapController] service, with no specific configuration ([~] is the value of [null] in [YAML]): it receives the ones from [_defaults], and [autoconfigure] turns it into a controller, whose route joins those of the application (example 02).

docs.title: 4.3.2. The template: templates/layout.html.twig
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
{# the layout of the pages: the pages EXTEND it, and fill its blocks #}
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  {# block: a slot that the page can fill; here with a default content #}
  <title>{% block title %}Home{% endblock %} - {{ site_name }}</title>
  {# path(): the URL of the route named [bootstrap]; asset(): the URL of a file of public/ #}
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ path('bootstrap', {file: 'css/bootstrap.min.css'}) }}">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ asset('css/styles.css') }}">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3">
    {# insertion of the fragments/navbar.html.twig file #}
    {% include 'fragments/navbar.html.twig' %}
    <main>
      {# the content of the page requested by the action is inserted here #}
      {% block content %}{% endblock %}
    </main>
    {# app: the variable that Symfony gives to all the views (the current request...);
       site_name: a global variable (see config/packages/twig.yaml) #}
    <footer class="footer">Page [{{ app.request.pathInfo }}] - © {{ 'now'|date('Y') }} {{ site_name }}</footer>
  </div>
</body>
</html>
  • line 6: the [viewport] tag instructs mobile browsers to display the page at the screen’s width, which is what [Bootstrap] expects;
  • line 8: the [{% block %}] directive marks a named slot, which pages that extend the template can fill by defining a block with the same name. The content written between [{% block title %}] and [{% endblock %}] is the default content for the placeholder, used by a page that does not define this block. [site_name] is a global variable, present in all views (see [config/packages/twig.yaml], below);
  • lines 10–11: the function [path] generates the URL for a named route (example 04), using the values of its parameters, which are provided in an associative array of [Twig] ([{file: '...'}], the equivalent of [['file' => '...']] in [PHP]). The [asset] function generates the URL from a file in the [public] folder. Writing the URL files manually ([/css/styles.css]) would also work, but [path] and [asset] will work if the application is installed under the URL prefix;
  • line 16: [{% include %}] inserts the content of another view, in this case the navigation bar. The included view has access to the variables of the view that includes it;
  • line 19: the space that each page fills with its own content;
  • line 23: the variable [app] is present in all views: [Symfony] stores the current request ([app.request]), the session ([app.session]), the logged-in user ([app.user], see the section on security), the route name ([app.current_route])... [app.request.pathInfo] is the path to the requested URL. The filter [date] formats a date; the string ['now'] denotes the current time.

The [container] class of [Bootstrap] centers the content and limits its width; [py-3] adds an inner vertical margin (padding): [Bootstrap] provides hundreds of classes of this type, which are combined in the [class] attribute. The global variable [site_name] is declared in the configuration of [Twig]:

# config/packages/twig.yaml: the configuration of the TwigBundle
twig:
    default_path: '%kernel.project_dir%/templates'
    # GLOBAL variables, present in all the views
    globals:
        site_name: 'My site'

Variables under the key [globals] are added to all views without the need for actions to provide them. A global variable can also be a service (['@App\Service\...']), whose methods will be called by the views.

docs.title: 4.3.3. The navigation bar: templates/fragments/navbar.html.twig
docs.text:
{# a fragment: a piece of page, inserted by include #}
<nav class="navbar navbar-expand bg-light rounded mb-3 px-3">
  <span class="navbar-brand">{{ site_name }}</span>
  <div class="navbar-nav">
    {# path(): the URL of a route, designated by its name #}
    <a class="nav-link" href="{{ path('home') }}">Home</a>
    <a class="nav-link" href="{{ path('team') }}">Team</a>
    <a class="nav-link" href="{{ path('raw') }}">Page without layout</a>
  </div>
</nav>

A fragment: a piece of a page that has no meaning on its own. The classes [navbar], [navbar-brand], and [nav-link] are those of the navigation bar for [Bootstrap]. The links are generated by [path], based on the road names.

docs.title: 4.3.4. A macro: templates/macros.html.twig
docs.text:
{# MACROS: pieces of page that have parameters, like functions #}

{# a Bootstrap card, with a name and a role #}
{% macro card(name, role = '') %}
  <div class="card">
    <div class="card-body">
      <h5 class="card-title">{{ name }}</h5>
      <p class="card-text">{{ role }}</p>
    </div>
  </div>
{% endmacro %}
  • Line 4: A macro is a section of a page that has parameters; this is the function of [Twig]. It is declared by [{% macro name(parameters) %}] ... [{% endmacro %}]; a parameter can have a default value ([role = '']). A file can contain multiple macros. The card ([card]) is a component of [Bootstrap].

A macro can only access its own parameters (and global variables); it cannot access the variables of the view that calls it. This is what makes it reusable. (The [Symfony UX Twig Component] library offers more feature-rich components—[PHP] classes associated with a view—that are used as HTML tags: [<twig:Card name="..." />]; we won’t need them.)

docs.title: 4.3.5. The pages
docs.text:
{# this page EXTENDS the layout: it only provides the content of its blocks #}
{% extends 'layout.html.twig' %}
{# the macros of the macros.html.twig file, under the name m #}
{% import 'macros.html.twig' as m %}

{% block content %}
  <h1>Welcome</h1>
  <p>This page only contains its own content: the header, the navigation
    bar and the footer come from the <code>layout.html.twig</code> layout.</p>
  {# the [card] macro, called with two parameters written on the spot #}
  {{ m.card('A macro', 'called with parameters written on the spot') }}
{% endblock %}
  • line 2: the page extends the template: [Twig] generates the template page, replacing its blocks with those defined by the page. In a view that extends a template, all content must be within blocks: text written outside of them does not appear in the generated page;
  • line 4: [{% import %}] imports macros from a file under a name of your choice ([m]);
  • lines 6–12: the block [content], which fills the slot of the same name. The page does not define the block [title]: the slot retains its default content, “Home”;
  • line 11: the call to the macro [card], as a function: [m.card(...)], within [{{ }}], since it produces text to be inserted. Its output is not escaped a second time: [Twig] knows that it is already safe from HTML (its parameters, however, were escaped within the macro).
{% extends 'layout.html.twig' %}
{% import 'macros.html.twig' as m %}

{% block title %}Our team{% endblock %}

{% block content %}
  <h1>Our team</h1>
  <div class="row g-3">
    {% for member in members %}
      <div class="col-md-4">
        {# the parameters of the macro are any expressions #}
        {{ m.card(member.name, member.role) }}
      </div>
    {% endfor %}
  </div>
{% endblock %}
  • line 4: the [title] block, on a single line;
  • lines 8–15: one card per team member, in a grid of [Bootstrap] ([row], [col-md-4]: three columns on a medium or large screen, one column on a narrow screen);
  • line 12: the macro’s parameters are arbitrary expressions.

The controller contains no new features:

<?php
// src/Controller/PagesController.php: three pages

namespace App\Controller;

use App\Model\Member;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

#[Route(methods: ['GET'])]
class PagesController extends AbstractController
{
    #[Route('/', name: 'home')]
    public function home(): Response
    {
        return $this->render('pages/home.html.twig');
    }

    #[Route('/team', name: 'team')]
    public function team(): Response
    {
        $members = [
            new Member('Marie Pélissier', 'Director'),
            new Member('Jacques Bromard', 'Developer'),
            new Member('Philippe Jandot', 'Graphic designer'),
        ];
        return $this->render('pages/team.html.twig', ['members' => $members]);
    }

    #[Route('/raw', name: 'raw')]
    public function raw(): Response
    {
        return $this->render('pages/raw.html.twig');
    }
}

Finally, the third page does not use the template:

<!doctype html>
{# this view does not use the layout: it is a complete page #}
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Raw page</title>
</head>
<body>
  <p>This page does not use the layout: no Bootstrap, no navigation bar.</p>
  <p><a href="{{ path('home') }}">Back to home</a></p>
</body>
</html>

The browser received a complete page: the template, fragment, page, and macros were assembled on the server. The URL files for the style sheets were generated by [path] and [asset]: these are URL files related to the site. You can verify that the style sheets are being served correctly (the [-I] option of [curl] displays only the response headers):

curl -I http://localhost:8000/bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: public
Last-Modified: Sun, 27 Sep 2026 09:32:39 GMT
Content-Type: text/css; charset=UTF-8
Content-Length: 232111
Accept-Ranges: bytes
...

Content-Type: text/css; charset=UTF-8

The first file was sent by our controller ([BinaryFileResponse] adds the file’s modification date and allows it to be cached: [Cache-Control: public]); the second was sent directly by the development server, without going through [Symfony]. Finally, an attempt to exit the folder:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" "http://localhost:8000/bootstrap/..%2F..%2F15-layout%2F.env"

404

(The [-s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n"] options display only the response code; under [Windows], enter [-o NUL]).

docs.title: 4.4. Example 16: Twig Extensions
docs.text:
A view often needs to format values: an amount with its currency, a date written out in full, or text in uppercase. This code does not belong in the action (which does not handle presentation), and [Twig] does not allow it to be written in the view (which cannot execute [PHP]; see the introduction to this chapter). It is written as [PHP], in an extension of [Twig]: a class that adds its own filters, functions, or tests to the view language. Libraries provide ready-made ones, such as [twig/intl-extra], installed with the examples, which formats dates and amounts according to the language. Finally, macros create pieces of HTML (Example 15).

16-extensions/
├── config/
│   └── services.yaml
├── src/
│   ├── Controller/
│   │   └── PagesController.php
│   ├── EventListener/
│   │   └── SetLanguage.php
│   ├── Model/
│   │   └── Product.php
│   ├── Twig/
│   │   └── FormatsExtension.php
│   └── Kernel.php
├── templates/
│   ├── fragments/
│   │   └── navbar.html.twig
│   ├── layout.html.twig
│   ├── macros.html.twig
│   └── pages/
│       ├── home.html.twig
│       └── products.html.twig
└── ...

docs.title: 4.4.1. The extension: src/Twig/FormatsExtension.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Twig/FormatsExtension.php: a Twig EXTENSION, which adds two filters
// to the language of the views: money and long_date

namespace App\Twig;

use DateTimeInterface;
use IntlDateFormatter;
use NumberFormatter;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\RequestStack;
use Twig\Extension\AbstractExtension;
use Twig\TwigFilter;

class FormatsExtension extends AbstractExtension
{
    // the request stack, to know the language of the current request
    public function __construct(private RequestStack $requests)
    {
    }

    // the filters of the extension: their name in the views, and the method that implements them
    public function getFilters(): array
    {
        return [
            new TwigFilter('money', $this->money(...)),
            new TwigFilter('long_date', $this->longDate(...)),
        ];
    }

    // an amount in cents, in a currency, in the format of the language of the
    // request: 114990 -> "€1,149.90" in English, "1 149,90 €" in French.
    // PHP's intl extension knows the conventions of each country
    public function money(int $cents, string $currency = 'EUR'): string
    {
        $formatter = new NumberFormatter($this->language(), NumberFormatter::CURRENCY);
        return $formatter->formatCurrency($cents / 100, $currency);
    }

    // a date in full words, in the language of the request: "Sunday, September 27, 2026"
    public function longDate(DateTimeInterface $day): string
    {
        $formatter = new IntlDateFormatter($this->language(), IntlDateFormatter::FULL, IntlDateFormatter::NONE);
        return $formatter->format($day);
    }

    private function language(): string
    {
        return $this->requests->getCurrentRequest()?->getLocale() ?? 'en';
    }
}
  • Line 14: An extension of [Twig] inherits from the [AbstractExtension] class. It is a service, like every class in the [src] folder; [Symfony] recognizes it as an extension ([autoconfigure]) and passes it to [Twig];
  • Lines 17–19: The extension needs the language of the current request. It receives the request stack ([RequestStack]), a service from [Symfony] that knows the current request (there is a stack because one request can trigger another internally);
  • lines 22–28: The method [getFilters] returns the extension’s filters: for each one, its name in the views and the function that implements it. [$this->money(...)] (with the ellipsis) does not call the method: it turns it into a value—a function that can be called later (a first-class callable). An extension can also provide functions ([getFunctions]) and tests ([getTests]);
  • lines 33–37: formatting an amount received in cents (see Example 06). This depends on the language: in French, [1 149,90 €] (space to separate thousands, decimal comma, symbol after the amount); in English, [€1,149.90]. The class [NumberFormatter], part of the [intl] extension of [PHP], supports the conventions of all countries (it uses data from the Unicode project CLDR): it is created for a language and a style (here, [CURRENCY], for amounts), and [formatCurrency] formats an amount, with the currency designated by its international code ([EUR], [USD]). The first parameter of the filter is the filtered value; the subsequent parameters are its properties in the view ([priceCents|money('USD')]);
  • lines 40–44: formatting a date using class [IntlDateFormatter] from the [intl] extension: style [FULL] writes the date in full, including the day of the week ([Sunday, September 27, 2026]); the style [NONE], for the time, does not include it. The type [DateTimeInterface] accepts all dates from [PHP];
  • lines 46–49: the language ([fr], [en]) of the current query, or English if there is no query (in a console command, for example). We’ll see who sets it.

docs.title: 4.4.2. The language of each request: src/EventListener/SetLanguage.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/EventListener/SetLanguage.php: the language of each request

namespace App\EventListener;

use Symfony\Component\EventDispatcher\Attribute\AsEventListener;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Event\RequestEvent;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\KernelEvents;

// priority: the order of the listeners of the same event (the highest first);
// 20: after the routing (32), before Symfony's listeners that use the language (16, 15)
#[AsEventListener(event: KernelEvents::REQUEST, priority: 20)]
class SetLanguage
{
    // the ?lang=fr parameter of the URL, English otherwise
    public function __invoke(RequestEvent $event): void
    {
        $request = $event->getRequest();
        $request->setLocale($request->query->get('lang') === 'fr' ? 'fr' : 'en');
    }
}

Each request has a language (locale), which defaults to the language [default_locale] specified in the configuration ([en] if nothing is configured). Here, the parameter [?lang=fr] of URL selects French; English is the default language. A listener for the [kernel.request] event (Example 12) sets this before each action using the [setLocale] method of the request. The [priority] parameter of the attribute sets the order of listeners for the same event: the highest-priority ones are processed first (default is 0). [Symfony] itself has several listeners of [kernel.request]: routing (priority 32), followed by those that prepare language-dependent services (16 and 15). Ours must run between the two: 20. The command [php bin/console debug:event-dispatcher kernel.request] displays all listeners for the event, in order. The language set in this way applies only to the current request: the next one will revert to the default language. The chapter on internationalization will use this same language to translate the texts.

docs.title: 4.4.3. The configuration: config/services.yaml
docs.text:
# config/services.yaml: the services of the application (see example 06)
services:
    _defaults:
        autowire: true
        autoconfigure: true

    App\:
        resource: '../src/'

    # the controller that serves Bootstrap, shared by examples 15 to 28 (see example 15)
    Common\BootstrapController: ~

    # Twig's Intl extension (twig/intl-extra library): the filters
    # format_currency, format_date, format_number...
    Twig\Extra\Intl\IntlExtension: ~
  • Line 15: The filters for the [twig/intl-extra] library are provided by the [IntlExtension] extension. Its class is not in the [src] folder: it is declared as a service, and [Symfony] recognizes it as an extension of [Twig] ([autoconfigure]). (In a standard project, the [twig/extra-bundle] package, installed by [Symfony Flex], handles this itself.)

docs.title: 4.4.4. The controller: src/Controller/PagesController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Controller/PagesController.php: two pages

namespace App\Controller;

use App\Model\Product;
use DateTimeImmutable;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

#[Route(methods: ['GET'])]
class PagesController extends AbstractController
{
    #[Route('/', name: 'home')]
    public function home(): Response
    {
        return $this->render('pages/home.html.twig', ['today' => new DateTimeImmutable('today')]);
    }

    #[Route('/products', name: 'products')]
    public function products(): Response
    {
        return $this->render('pages/products.html.twig', ['products' => [
            new Product('keyboard', 2500, 12),
            new Product('mouse', 1250, 0),
            new Product('screen', 114990, 3),
        ]]);
    }
}

Actions pass raw values to the views: a date ([new DateTimeImmutable('today')], today’s date at midnight) and amounts in cents. Formatting is handled by the views. The [Product] class combines a name, a price (in cents; see Example 06), and a stock level.

docs.title: 4.4.5. The views
docs.text:
{# a link of the navigation bar, which receives the [active] class if the
   current page is under the [path] path. app.request.pathInfo: the path of the
   current request; starts with: a Twig test #}
{% macro link(href, path, text) %}
  <a class="nav-link{{ app.request.pathInfo starts with path ? ' active' }}" href="{{ href }}">{{ text }}</a>
{% endmacro %}

{# a Bootstrap badge: green if the product is in stock, red otherwise #}
{% macro badge(stock) %}
  <span class="badge {{ stock > 0 ? 'text-bg-success' : 'text-bg-danger' }}">{{ stock > 0 ? stock ~ ' in stock' : 'sold out' }}</span>
{% endmacro %}
  • lines 4–6: a macro that creates a link for the navigation bar. The link for the current page is assigned the class [active] from [Bootstrap], which highlights it. A macro accesses the global variable [app] (Example 15): [app.request.pathInfo] is the path of the current request; [starts with] is an operator of [Twig], which checks for the start of a string. The ternary operator without an “else” clause ([condition ? ' active']) returns an empty string if the condition is false (Example 14);
  • Lines 9–11: a badge from [Bootstrap], green ([text-bg-success]) or red ([text-bg-danger]) depending on inventory. The [~] operator of [Twig] concatenates two strings (the [.] of [PHP]).
{% import 'macros.html.twig' as m %}
<nav class="navbar navbar-expand bg-light rounded mb-3 px-3">
  <span class="navbar-brand">Extensions</span>
  <div class="navbar-nav">
    {# 1. a condition written in the view; app.current_route: the name of the current route #}
    <a class="nav-link{{ app.current_route == 'home' ? ' active' }}" href="{{ path('home') }}">Home</a>
    {# 2. the [link] macro #}
    {{ m.link(path('products'), '/products', 'Products') }}
    {# 3. path() builds the URL of a named route; a parameter that is not a
         parameter of the route is added at the end of the URL: /products?lang=fr #}
    <a class="nav-link" href="{{ path('products', {lang: 'fr'}) }}">Produits (fr)</a>
  </div>
</nav>
  • line 1: an included fragment (example 15) does not inherit imports from the view that includes it: it imports the macros it needs on its own;
  • line 6: the same as with the macro, written directly in the view, using the ternary operator. [app.current_route] is the name of the current request path. The macro avoids repeating the condition for each link;
  • line 8: the macro call;
  • line 11: a parameter of [path] that is not a route parameter is added to URL as a parameter: [/products?lang=fr].
{% extends 'layout.html.twig' %}
{% block title %}Home{% endblock %}

{% block content %}
  <h1>Home</h1>
  {# our long_date filter #}
  <p>Today is {{ today|long_date }}.</p>
  {# app.request.locale: the language of the request, set by the SetLanguage listener #}
  <p>Formatting language: {{ app.request.locale }}
    (<a href="{{ path('home', {lang: 'fr'}) }}">in French</a>, <a href="{{ path('home') }}">in English</a>)</p>
{% endblock %}
  • line 7: our filter [long_date];
  • line 9: [app.request.locale], the request language, set by the listener [SetLanguage].
{% extends 'layout.html.twig' %}
{% import 'macros.html.twig' as m %}
{% block title %}Products{% endblock %}

{% block content %}
  <h1>Products</h1>
  <table class="table table-sm w-auto">
    <thead><tr><th>Product</th><th>Price</th><th>Price in dollars</th><th>Stock</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      {% for product in products %}
        <tr>
          {# a Twig filter (upper), then our money filter, without then with a parameter #}
          <td>{{ product.name|upper }}</td>
          <td>{{ product.priceCents|money }}</td>
          <td>{{ product.priceCents|money('USD') }}</td>
          {# the [badge] macro builds the HTML of the badge #}
          <td>{{ m.badge(product.stock) }}</td>
        </tr>
      {% endfor %}
    </tbody>
  </table>
  {# the format_currency filter of the Intl extension: an amount (here in units), a
     currency, and the language of the request #}
  <p>Total stock value: {{ (products|reduce((s, p) => s + p.priceCents * p.stock, 0) / 100)|format_currency('EUR', locale: app.request.locale) }}</p>
{% endblock %}
  • line 13: a filter for [Twig];
  • Lines 14–15: our [money] filter, first with its default currency, then with a parameter;
  • line 17: the call to the [badge] macro;
  • line 24: the [format_currency] filter from the Intl extension: an amount (here in euros: the total inventory, calculated by [reduce], divided by 100), a currency, and the query language, passed via a named parameter from [Twig] ([locale: ...]). This extension also provides [format_date], [format_datetime], [format_number], [country_name], [language_name]... Our filter [money] therefore serves a dual purpose: we wrote it to demonstrate how to write an extension.

The template [layout.html.twig] is a simplified version of the one in Example 15; its attribute [lang] receives the language of the request ([<html lang="{{ app.request.locale }}">]).

docs.title: 4.5. Example 17: A GET form
docs.text:
A HTML form sends its fields to the server in one of two ways, depending on its [method] attribute:

  • [method="get"]: The fields are added to the URL as parameters ([/search?keyword=le&genre=novel]). This is the method used by a form that performs a query: a search or a filter. The URL containing the results can be bookmarked, shared, or reloaded safely;
  • [method="post"]: The fields are included in the request body (see Example 11). This is the method used by a form that modifies data: a registration, an addition, or a deletion.

This first form is a book search. It is hand-coded in HTML within the view; the following examples will use the Form component from [Symfony] for the forms.

docs.title: 4.5.1. The template: src/Model/Book.php and SearchModel.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Model/Book.php: a book

namespace App\Model;

readonly class Book
{
    public function __construct(
        public string $title,
        public string $author,
        public string $genre,
    ) {
    }
}

<?php
// src/Model/SearchModel.php: the model of the view: the input (to display it
// again), the genres, the results

namespace App\Model;

readonly class SearchModel
{
    /**
     * @param list<string> $genres
     * @param list<Book> $results
     */
    public function __construct(
        public string $keyword,
        public string $genre,
        public array $genres,
        public array $results,
    ) {
    }
}
  • Lines 14–19: The view template contains the user’s input, which the form displays, the list of suggested genres, and the results.

docs.title: 4.5.2. The controller: src/Controller/BooksController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Controller/BooksController.php: a search form, sent by GET

namespace App\Controller;

use App\Model\Book;
use App\Model\SearchModel;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

class BooksController extends AbstractController
{
    // class CONSTANTS: the data, written in the code for the example
    private const GENRES = ['novel', 'poetry', 'drama'];

    /** @return list<Book> */
    private static function books(): array
    {
        return [
            new Book('Le Rouge et le Noir', 'Stendhal', 'novel'),
            new Book('Les Fleurs du mal', 'Baudelaire', 'poetry'),
            new Book('Madame Bovary', 'Flaubert', 'novel'),
            new Book('Alcools', 'Apollinaire', 'poetry'),
            new Book('Le Cid', 'Corneille', 'drama'),
        ];
    }

    // GET / and GET /search?keyword=...&genre=...: the form AND its results;
    // two routes for the same action: the #[Route] attribute can be repeated
    #[Route('/', name: 'books_home', methods: ['GET'])]
    #[Route('/search', name: 'books_search', methods: ['GET'])]
    public function search(Request $request): Response
    {
        // getString: the parameter, in the form of a string ('' if it is missing)
        $keyword = $request->query->getString('keyword');
        $genre = $request->query->getString('genre');
        $word = mb_strtolower($keyword);
        $results = array_values(array_filter(self::books(), fn (Book $book) =>
            ($word === '' || str_contains(mb_strtolower($book->title), $word)
                || str_contains(mb_strtolower($book->author), $word))
            && ($genre === '' || $book->genre === $genre)));
        return $this->render('books/search.html.twig', [
            'model' => new SearchModel($keyword, $genre, self::GENRES, $results),
        ]);
    }
}
  • Line 16: A private class constant named [self::GENRES] ([self] refers to the current class). A constant cannot contain objects: the books are therefore provided by a static method (lines 19–28). In a real application, they would come from a database;
  • lines 32–33: two routes for the same action: the [#[Route]] attribute can be repeated. On the first visit ([/]), there are no parameters, and all books are displayed;
  • lines 37–38: The form fields are read as parameters for URL (example 07). The [getString] method returns the parameter as a string, empty if it is absent;
  • lines 40–43: filtering. The [array_filter] function retains the elements of an array for which the given function returns [true]: a book is selected if the keyword is empty or appears in its title or author (in lowercase on both sides; [mb_strtolower] correctly handles accented characters), and if the genre is empty or matches the book’s genre. [array_filter] retains the keys of the selected items (0, 2...): [array_values] renumbers them starting from 0;
  • lines 44–46: the view template.

docs.title: 4.5.3. The view: templates/books/search.html.twig
docs.text:
{% extends 'layout.html.twig' %}

{% block content %}
  <h1 class="h3">Book search</h1>
  {# method="get": the fields are sent in the URL (?keyword=...&genre=...) #}
  <form method="get" action="{{ path('books_search') }}" class="row g-2 align-items-end mb-3">
    <div class="col-auto">
      <label class="form-label" for="keyword">Title or author</label>
      {# value: the field displays again what was typed (escaped by {{ }}) #}
      <input class="form-control" id="keyword" name="keyword" value="{{ model.keyword }}">
    </div>
    <div class="col-auto">
      <label class="form-label" for="genre">Genre</label>
      <select class="form-select" id="genre" name="genre">
        <option value="">(all)</option>
        {% for genre in model.genres %}
          {# the boolean selected attribute, written if the condition is true, omitted otherwise #}
          <option value="{{ genre }}"{{ genre == model.genre ? ' selected' }}>{{ genre }}</option>
        {% endfor %}
      </select>
    </div>
    <div class="col-auto">
      <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Search</button>
    </div>
  </form>
  <p>{{ model.results|length }} book(s) found.</p>
  <ul>
    {% for book in model.results %}
      <li><i>{{ book.title }}</i>, {{ book.author }} ({{ book.genre }})</li>
    {% endfor %}
  </ul>
{% endblock %}
  • Line 6: the [<form>] tag. The [action] attribute is the URL to which the form is submitted; [method="get"] places the fields in the URL. The classes of [Bootstrap] arrange the fields on a single line;
  • Line 8: a label. Its [for] attribute specifies the identifier ([id]) of the field it describes: clicking on the label places the cursor in the field, and screen readers read the label along with the field;
  • line 10: an input field. Its attribute [name] is the name of the parameter sent to the server: this is the link between the form and the action ([$request->query->getString('keyword')]). The attribute [value] is the displayed value: the previous entry, redisplayed (and escaped by [{{ }}], which is essential in an attribute: an entry containing a quotation mark ["] would otherwise close the attribute);
  • lines 14–20: a drop-down list. Each [<option>] has a value ([value]), sent to the server, and text, displayed. The first option, with an empty value, means “all genres”;
  • line 18: the option selected in the previous request is assigned the attribute [selected]. This is a Boolean attribute: its presence alone is sufficient; it has no value. The ternary operator without the “else” part writes it if the condition is true, and writes nothing otherwise. [==] is the equality of [Twig];
  • line 23: the submit button;
  • line 26: the number of results.

docs.title: 4.6. Example 18: Form Fields
docs.text:
This example presents all the field types in a HTML form, this time submitted by POST. It shows how to redisplay each field type with its current value, how the browser sends the values for each one, and how the server verifies that a received value is indeed one of the available options. Writing all of this by hand, as in Example 17, would be time-consuming and repetitive. [Symfony] delegates this task to its Form component: a form is described by a class, its type; [Symfony] generates the HTML, reads the submitted fields, converts them, validates them, and redisplays the form with the user’s input and any errors. This is the counterpart to [WTForms] in [Python].

18-fields/
├── config/
│   └── packages/
│       ├── framework.yaml
│       └── twig.yaml
├── src/
│   ├── Controller/
│   │   └── FormController.php
│   ├── Form/
│   │   └── FieldsType.php
│   ├── Service/
│   │   └── ListsService.php
│   └── Kernel.php
├── templates/
│   ├── form/
│   │   └── form.html.twig
│   └── layout.html.twig
└── ...

docs.title: 4.6.1. The lists service: src/Service/ListsService.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Service/ListsService.php: the lists offered by the form. In a
// real application, they would come from a database.

namespace App\Service;

class ListsService
{
    // each list: an associative array displayed text => sent value
    public function titles(): array
    {
        return ['Mr' => 'Mr', 'Mme' => 'Mme', 'Melle' => 'Melle'];
    }

    public function countries(): array
    {
        return ['France' => 'fr', 'Belgium' => 'be', 'Switzerland' => 'ch', 'Canada' => 'ca'];
    }

    public function hobbies(): array
    {
        return ['reading' => 'reading', 'music' => 'music', 'sport' => 'sport', 'cinema' => 'cinema'];
    }

    public function languages(): array
    {
        return ['French' => 'French', 'English' => 'English', 'Spanish' => 'Spanish',
            'German' => 'German'];
    }
}

The form’s dropdown lists (titles, countries, hobbies, languages) are provided by a service, following the model in Example 06: in a real application, they would come from a database. Each list is an associative array: the key is the displayed text, and the value is what is sent to the server (this is the order expected by the Form component).

  • line 9: the user’s session, which we’ll discuss further in Example 20: the Form component stores the anti-CSRF token there (see below);
  • line 11: anti-CSRF protection for forms.
# config/packages/twig.yaml: the configuration of the TwigBundle
twig:
    default_path: '%kernel.project_dir%/templates'

    form_themes: ['bootstrap_5_layout.html.twig']
  • Line 5: The forms theme. [Symfony] renders each field using [Twig] blocks; a theme provides the version suitable for a CSS framework. The [bootstrap_5_layout.html.twig] theme, included with [Symfony], uses the classes from [Bootstrap] 5 ([form-control], [form-label], [is-invalid]...). The application can write its own themes or override certain blocks of an existing theme.

docs.title: 4.6.3. Form type: src/Form/FieldsType.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Form/FieldsType.php: the DESCRIPTION of the form: its fields, their type, their options

namespace App\Form;

use App\Service\ListsService;
use Symfony\Component\Form\AbstractType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\Extension\Core\Type\ChoiceType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\Extension\Core\Type\DateType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\Extension\Core\Type\HiddenType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\Extension\Core\Type\PasswordType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\Extension\Core\Type\TextareaType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\Extension\Core\Type\TextType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\FormBuilderInterface;
use Symfony\Component\Validator\Constraints\NotBlank;

class FieldsType extends AbstractType
{
    // a form type is a service: it receives the lists service
    public function __construct(private ListsService $lists)
    {
    }

    // the fields of the form, in the order in which they are displayed
    public function buildForm(FormBuilderInterface $builder, array $options): void
    {
        $builder
            // radio buttons: a list of choices (ChoiceType), "expanded";
            // constraints: the validation constraints of the field (see example 08)
            ->add('title', ChoiceType::class, [
                'choices' => $this->lists->titles(),
                'expanded' => true,
                'label_attr' => ['class' => 'radio-inline'],
                'constraints' => [new NotBlank(message: 'The title is required.')],
            ])
            // an input field; required => false: the field is not required
            ->add('name', TextType::class, ['required' => false])
            // a password: never displayed again in the page
            ->add('password', PasswordType::class, ['label' => 'Password', 'required' => false])
            // a date: an <input type="date"> field; the value is a yyyy-mm-dd string
            ->add('birth_date', DateType::class, [
                'label' => 'Date of birth',
                'widget' => 'single_text',
                'input' => 'string',
                'required' => false,
            ])
            // checkboxes: an expanded list of choices, with MULTIPLE choices
            ->add('hobbies', ChoiceType::class, [
                'choices' => $this->lists->hobbies(),
                'expanded' => true,
                'multiple' => true,
                'label_attr' => ['class' => 'checkbox-inline'],
                'required' => false,
            ])
            // drop-down list: a list of choices that is not expanded
            ->add('country', ChoiceType::class, ['choices' => $this->lists->countries()])
            // multiple-selection list, displayed on four rows
            ->add('languages', ChoiceType::class, [
                'label' => 'Spoken languages',
                'choices' => $this->lists->languages(),
                'multiple' => true,
                'attr' => ['size' => 4],
                'required' => false,
            ])
            ->add('comment', TextareaType::class, ['required' => false, 'attr' => ['rows' => 2]])
            // a hidden field
            ->add('token', HiddenType::class);
    }
}
  • line 17: a form type inherits from the [AbstractType] class. It is a service (located in the [src] folder): it can accept other services, in this case the list service (line 20);
  • line 25: the method [buildForm] describes the fields by adding them ([add]) to a form builder: for each field, its name, type, and options. The field name is also the name of the data it displays; its label, by default, is its name formatted as text ([name] becomes “Name”);
  • Lines 30–35: A [ChoiceType] field is a drop-down list, defined by the [choices] option. With the [expanded] option, it becomes a group of radio buttons (a single-selection field). The option [label_attr] assigns a class to the group label: [radio-inline] specifies side-by-side buttons in the theme. The option [constraints] sets the field’s validation constraints (example 08): a title is required;
  • line 37: a [TextType] field is an input field. The option [required] defaults to [true]: [Symfony] then sets the attribute HTML to [required], which the browser checks (Example 19). It does not send any information to the server: it is a constraint ([NotBlank]) that makes a field required for the server;
  • line 39: a password ([PasswordType]), which is never returned to the page: its field is always empty when displayed;
  • lines 41–46: a date ([DateType]), displayed by a single field [<input type="date">] (option [widget]). Such a field exchanges its value with the server in the [yyyy-mm-dd] format, regardless of the format in which the browser displays it; the [input] option specifies that the data is a string (rather than a [DateTime] object, which is the default);
  • lines 48–54: a drop-down list with multiple choices ([multiple]): checkboxes;
  • line 56: a non-expanded multiple-choice list: a drop-down list;
  • lines 58–64: a non-expanded, multiple-choice list: a multi-select list, displayed across four lines (the attribute HTML [size], specified by the option [attr]);
  • line 65: a text box ([TextareaType]), spanning two lines;
  • line 67: a hidden field ([HiddenType]).

[Symfony] provides about thirty field types: [EmailType], [IntegerType], [MoneyType], [UrlType], [CheckboxType], [FileType], [CountryType], [RepeatedType] (example 19), [CollectionType] (a list of subforms)...

docs.title: 4.6.4. The controller: src/Controller/FormController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Controller/FormController.php: a form that uses all the types of fields

namespace App\Controller;

use App\Form\FieldsType;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

class FormController extends AbstractController
{
    // GET: the form, with initial values; POST: the sent fields
    // are read, validated, then displayed again by the same form
    #[Route('/form', name: 'form', methods: ['GET', 'POST'])]
    public function form(Request $request): Response
    {
        // the initial values (one per field, an array for a multiple field)
        $initial = ['title' => 'Mme', 'country' => 'fr', 'languages' => ['French'], 'token' => 'A7X2'];
        // createForm: the form, built from its description
        $form = $this->createForm(FieldsType::class, $initial);
        // handleRequest: if the request is a POST, the received fields are copied
        // into the form, then validated
        $form->handleRequest($request);
        $model = ['form' => $form];
        if ($form->isSubmitted()) {
            // what the browser actually sent, field by field
            $received = [];
            foreach ($request->request->all() as $name => $value) {
                foreach ((array) $value as $key => $v) {
                    $received[] = "{$name}[$key] = [".implode(', ', (array) $v).']';
                }
            }
            $model += [
                'received' => implode("\n", $received),
                'valid' => $form->isValid(),
                // getErrors(true): the errors of all the fields
                'errors' => $form->getErrors(true),
                // getData(): the values of the form, converted by each field
                'data' => $form->getData(),
            ];
        }
        return $this->render('form/form.html.twig', $model);
    }
}
  • line 16: a single action for both methods: GET displays the form, POST processes it. This is the standard way to write a form action with [Symfony];
  • line 20: the form’s initial values: an associative array, one value per field (an array for a multi-value field);
  • line 22: [createForm] creates the form—a [Form] object—based on its type and initial data;
  • line 25: [handleRequest] examines the request. For a GET, it does nothing. For a POST that contains the form fields, it copies them into the form: each field converts its value (the date, the lists, etc.), verifies that a selection is among those that were offered, and then the form validates the constraints and the anti-CSRF token;
  • line 27: [isSubmitted]: Was the form submitted?;
  • lines 29–34: for this example, the list of what the browser actually sent. The fields of a [Symfony] form are named after the form: [fields[name]], [fields[hobbies][]]. [PHP] therefore organizes them into an array named [fields] (Example 10), which is then iterated over. [(array) $value] converts a single value into a one-element array (an array remains an array); [implode] combines the elements of an array into a string, separated by the first parameter;
  • lines 35–42: the view template receives what the server received: the validation result ([isValid]), the errors ([getErrors(true)]: those for all fields), and the form data ([getData]), converted by each field. The [+=] operator adds these keys to the [$model] array;
  • line 44: the form is passed to the view, which will display it, along with the user’s input and any errors.

docs.title: 4.6.5. The view: templates/form/form.html.twig
docs.text:
{% extends 'layout.html.twig' %}

{% block content %}
  <h1 class="h3">A complete form</h1>
  {# form_start: the <form> tag, here with the POST method and the URL of the page #}
  {{ form_start(form, {attr: {style: 'max-width: 40rem'}}) }}
    {# form_row: a complete field (label, input field, errors) #}
    {{ form_row(form.title) }}
    <div class="row g-2">
      <div class="col">{{ form_row(form.name) }}</div>
      <div class="col">{{ form_row(form.password) }}</div>
      <div class="col">{{ form_row(form.birth_date) }}</div>
    </div>
    {{ form_row(form.hobbies) }}
    <div class="row g-2">
      <div class="col">{{ form_row(form.country) }}</div>
      <div class="col">{{ form_row(form.languages) }}</div>
    </div>
    {{ form_row(form.comment) }}
    <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Send</button>
  {# form_end: the remaining fields (the hidden field, the anti-CSRF token), then </form> #}
  {{ form_end(form) }}

  {# is defined: true if the received variable was passed to the view (form sent) #}
  {% if received is defined %}
    <h2 class="h5 mt-3">What the server received</h2>
    <pre class="bg-light p-2 border">{{ received }}</pre>
    <p>Valid form: {{ valid ? 'yes' : 'no' }}</p>
    <ul>
      {% for error in errors %}
        {# error.origin: the field in error; error.message: the message #}
        <li>{{ error.origin.getName() }}: {{ error.message }}</li>
      {% endfor %}
    </ul>
    {% if valid %}
      <p>The data of the form:</p>
      <ul>
        {# a loop over an associative array: the key and the value #}
        {% for key, value in data %}
          <li>{{ key }}: {{ value is iterable ? value|join(', ') : value }}</li>
        {% endfor %}
      </ul>
    {% endif %}
  {% endif %}
{% endblock %}
  • line 6: the function [form_start] writes the tag [<form>]: the method POST and the URL of the current page, by default; the second parameter adds HTML attributes;
  • Line 8: The [form_row] function writes a complete field: its label, its input field (with its current value), and its errors, using the theme’s classes. [form.title] refers to the [title] field in the form. You can also write the parts separately: [form_label], [form_widget], [form_errors];
  • lines 9–19: the other fields, arranged by the grid classes of [Bootstrap];
  • line 22: [form_end] writes the fields that have not yet been written (in this case, the hidden field [token] and the hidden field [_token], the anti-CSRF token), then closes the [</form>] tag;
  • line 25: the [is defined] check: the variable [received] only exists after a submission;
  • lines 30–33: the errors. Each is a [FormError] object, where [origin] is the field containing the error;
  • Lines 39–41: A [for] loop on an associative array, which iterates over both the keys and the values. The [is iterable] test distinguishes between arrays (grouped by the [join] filter) and single values.

The entire form could have been written in a single line: [{{ form(form) }}]. The functions [form_start], [form_row], and [form_end] allow you to arrange the fields as desired.

docs.title: 4.6.6. Execution
docs.text:
The default values are visible: the “Mme” radio button, the country “France,” and the language “French.” HTML produces the following (excerpts, displayed across multiple lines):

<form name="fields" method="post" style="max-width: 40rem">
  <fieldset class="mb-3"><legend class="col-form-label required">Title</legend>
    <div id="fields_title">
      <div class="form-check form-check-inline">
        <input type="radio" id="fields_title_0" name="fields[title]" required="required" class="form-check-input" value="Mr" />
        <label class="form-check-label required" for="fields_title_0">Mr</label></div>
      <div class="form-check form-check-inline">
        <input type="radio" id="fields_title_1" name="fields[title]" required="required" class="form-check-input" value="Mme" checked="checked" />
...
  <div class="mb-3"><label for="fields_name" class="form-label">Name</label>
    <input type="text" id="fields_name" name="fields[name]" class="form-control" /></div>
...
    <input type="checkbox" id="fields_hobbies_0" name="fields[hobbies][]" class="form-check-input" value="reading" />
...
  <select id="fields_country" name="fields[country]" class="form-select">
    <option value="fr" selected="selected">France</option><option value="be">Belgium</option>...
  <select id="fields_languages" name="fields[languages][]" size="4" class="form-select" multiple="multiple">
    <option value="French" selected="selected">French</option>...
...
  <input type="hidden" id="fields_token" name="fields[token]" value="A7X2" />
  <input type="hidden" id="fields__token" name="fields[_token]" data-controller="csrf-protection" value="9863be7bac.KU7NzSfFyCspR2sfBG_fTqNV6UuMueZ2pOsuPACnvFo.X32P9UOQm1FPIxhHUVqHGvcBmWbl36Il8KJsCVnS8A1ZJYGudJSrRmwoWw" />
</form>

[Symfony] has written everything: the identifiers ([fields_title_1]), the labels associated with their fields, the names ending in [[]] for multiple fields (example 10), the [checked] and [selected] attributes of common values, and the classes of [Bootstrap]. The last hidden field, [fields[_token]], contains the anti-CSRF token. A CSRF attack (Cross-Site Request Forgery) involves a malicious site tricking its victim’s browser into submitting a form to our application. The browser includes our application’s cookies in the request—and thus the logged-in user’s session—making the request appear legitimate. The countermeasure: every form in our application contains a random token linked to the user’s session, which the malicious site cannot know. The Form component adds this token to every form, and [handleRequest] rejects any form whose token is missing or incorrect: no form can omit it. (The [data-controller] attribute is used by an optional script for [Symfony], which enhances protection; it has no effect here.) Let’s fill out the form and submit it:

The page shows what the server received: one parameter per field, with multiple values for the checkboxes and the dropdown list; the password was sent but is not displayed again in its field. The hidden field [token] was returned as-is: this is the way to send information back and forth that the user cannot see (the case study uses this for a record’s version number). However, a hidden field is not a protected field: the user can modify it using their browser’s developer tools, and the server must validate it just like any other field. The anti-CSRF token is also included among the received fields; it is not part of the form data.

Now let’s send a form without a token, using [curl], and with a country that wasn’t listed as an option:

curl -g -d "fields[name]=Martin&fields[country]=xx" http://localhost:8000/form

...
        <h2 class="h5 mt-3">What the server received</h2>
    <pre class="bg-light p-2 border">fields[name] = [Martin]
fields[country] = [xx]</pre>
    <p>Valid form: no</p>
    <ul>
                      <li>fields: The CSRF token is invalid. Please try to resubmit the form.</li>
                      <li>title: The title is required.</li>
                      <li>country: The selected choice is invalid.</li>
          </ul>
...

The form is invalid for three reasons: the anti-CSRF token is missing (the error is associated with the form itself), no title was submitted, and the country [xx] is not among the available options. This last check is performed by the [ChoiceType] field itself, without us having requested it: a malicious user could submit anything, not just what the page offered. The messages are in English: those from the Form component are translated by [Symfony], as are those from the validator (example 09). The response has status code 422 (Unprocessable Content): [render] selects it automatically when presented with a submitted, invalid form. Note the difference from other frameworks: [Symfony] does not reject the request before the action; it is the form that declares it invalid, and the action that decides how to proceed.

For the token to be accepted, [curl] must behave like a browser: first request the form, while retaining the session cookie (option [-c], which saves received cookies to a file), then resend the cookie (option [-b]) and the token read from the page. The option [--data-urlencode] encodes the token value itself:

curl -c cookies.txt http://localhost:8000/form
curl -b cookies.txt -g --data-urlencode "fields[_token]=9863be7bac.KU7N..." -d "fields[name]=Martin&fields[country]=xx" http://localhost:8000/form

...
    <ul>
                      <li>title: The title is required.</li>
                      <li>country: The selected choice is invalid.</li>
          </ul>
...

(the token is the one from the page received by the first command). Only the two input errors remain.

docs.title: 4.7. Example 19: Form Validation
docs.text:
A registration form, where each field has its own validation rules. If an error occurs, the form is redisplayed with the user’s input and a message below each field containing an error. This example uses the standard approach of [Symfony]: the form data is an object, whose class contains the constraints (Example 08); the form populates the object and then validates it.

19-form-validation/
├── src/
│   ├── Controller/
│   │   └── RegistrationController.php
│   ├── Form/
│   │   └── RegistrationType.php
│   ├── Model/
│   │   └── Registration.php
│   └── Kernel.php
├── templates/
│   ├── registration/
│   │   ├── welcome.html.twig

docs.text:
<?php
// src/Model/Registration.php: the data of the registration form, and their constraints

namespace App\Model;

use Symfony\Component\Validator\Constraints as Assert;

class Registration
{
    #[Assert\NotBlank(message: 'The name is required.')]
    #[Assert\Length(max: 20, maxMessage: 'The name must not exceed 20 characters.')]
    public ?string $name = null;

    // Email: a valid address, with a complete domain name (example.com, and not example)
    #[Assert\NotBlank(message: 'The email address is required.')]
    #[Assert\Email(message: 'Invalid email address.')]
    public ?string $email = null;

    #[Assert\NotBlank(message: 'The age is required.')]
    #[Assert\Range(notInRangeMessage: 'The age must be between 18 and 120 years.', min: 18, max: 120)]
    public ?int $age = null;

    #[Assert\NotBlank(message: 'The password is required.')]
    #[Assert\Length(min: 6, minMessage: 'The password must have at least 6 characters.')]
    public ?string $password = null;
}
  • Line 8: a regular class whose properties are public and editable; the form will populate them one by one. All are initialized to [null]; the object is empty when first displayed;
  • lines 10–12: the name is required and must not exceed 20 characters. Each constraint is assigned its own message here, in English (example 09): [message] for [NotBlank], [maxMessage] for exceeding [Length];
  • lines 15–17: The constraint [Email] verifies that an address is valid and requires a fully qualified domain name ([example.com], not [example]);
  • lines 19–21: age is an integer between 18 and 120 ([notInRangeMessage]: the message for [Range] when there is a minimum and a maximum). The form will have converted the input to an integer;
  • lines 23–25: The password must be at least 6 characters long.

docs.title: 4.7.2. The form: src/Form/RegistrationType.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Form/RegistrationType.php: the fields of the registration form

namespace App\Form;

use App\Model\Registration;
use Symfony\Component\Form\AbstractType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\Extension\Core\Type\EmailType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\Extension\Core\Type\IntegerType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\Extension\Core\Type\PasswordType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\Extension\Core\Type\RepeatedType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\Extension\Core\Type\TextType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\FormBuilderInterface;
use Symfony\Component\OptionsResolver\OptionsResolver;

class RegistrationType extends AbstractType
{
    public function buildForm(FormBuilderInterface $builder, array $options): void
    {
        $builder
            // attr: additional HTML attributes on the input field (for the
            // validation by the browser, see further on)
            ->add('name', TextType::class, ['attr' => ['maxlength' => 20]])
            ->add('email', EmailType::class, ['label' => 'Email address'])
            // IntegerType: an integer; an input that is not one produces
            // the invalid_message error
            ->add('age', IntegerType::class, [
                'label' => 'Age',
                'attr' => ['min' => 18, 'max' => 120],
                'invalid_message' => 'An integer is expected.',
            ])
            // RepeatedType: TWO fields that must receive the same value (the
            // password and its confirmation); a single value in the data
            ->add('password', RepeatedType::class, [
                'type' => PasswordType::class,
                'first_options' => ['label' => 'Password', 'attr' => ['minlength' => 6]],
                'second_options' => ['label' => 'Confirmation'],
                'invalid_message' => 'The confirmation does not match the password.',
            ]);
    }

    // the options of the form: its data are a Registration object
    public function configureOptions(OptionsResolver $options): void
    {
        $options->setDefaults(['data_class' => Registration::class]);
    }
}
  • line 23: the [attr] option adds HTML attributes to the input field: [maxlength] limits the input in the browser;
  • line 24: a [EmailType] field generates a [<input type="email">], which the browser can validate;
  • lines 27–31: a [IntegerType] field generates a [<input type="number">] and converts the input to an integer. An entry that is not an integer cannot be converted: this is a conversion error (not a validation error; see example 08), for which the error message is provided by the [invalid_message] option;
  • Lines 34–39: A [RepeatedType] field consists of two fields (here, two [PasswordType] fields), which must contain the same value: the password and its confirmation. Each has its own options ([first_options], [second_options]); if the two entries differ, the error is [invalid_message]. The data has only one value: the password;
  • lines 43–46: the method [configureOptions] sets the options for the form itself: [data_class] indicates that its data is a [Registration] object. Each field reads and writes the property of the same name.

[Symfony] can also infer a field’s type based on the constraints and the property’s type: [->add('age')], which has no type, would produce a [IntegerType], with the attributes [min] and [max] inferred from [Range]. We’ve written this out explicitly for clarity.

docs.title: 4.7.3. The controller: src/Controller/RegistrationController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Controller/RegistrationController.php: a form validated by the server

namespace App\Controller;

use App\Form\RegistrationType;
use App\Model\Registration;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Attribute\MapQueryParameter;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

class RegistrationController extends AbstractController
{
    // GET /register: the form; ?html5=true: we let the browser
    // validate it before sending. POST /register: the sent form
    #[Route('/register', name: 'register', methods: ['GET', 'POST'])]
    public function register(Request $request, #[MapQueryParameter] bool $html5 = false): Response
    {
        $registration = new Registration();
        $form = $this->createForm(RegistrationType::class, $registration);
        $form->handleRequest($request);
        // isValid: the fields could be converted, and the Registration object
        // complies with its constraints
        if ($form->isSubmitted() && $form->isValid()) {
            return $this->render('registration/welcome.html.twig', ['registration' => $registration]);
        }
        // the first display, or an invalid form, displayed again with the input
        // and the errors (render then sends it back with the 422 code)
        return $this->render('registration/registration.html.twig',
            ['form' => $form, 'html5' => $html5]);
    }
}
  • line 19: the parameter [?html5=true] enables browser validation (see below). [#[MapQueryParameter]] converts it to a Boolean (example 07);
  • lines 21–23: The empty object [Registration] is passed to the form; [handleRequest] will populate it using the submitted fields;
  • lines 26–28: [isValid] is true if every field could be converted and if the [Registration] object meets its constraints. The welcome page then receives the filled-in object (the following example will show that it is better to redirect after a successful POST);
  • lines 31–32: otherwise, the form is displayed: empty on the first display; after an invalid submission, it shows the input and errors, along with code 422 (example 18).

The invalid form is therefore redisplayed by the POST action itself, which retains the input and errors: this is the approach taken by [Symfony]. Other frameworks, such as [Laravel], instead respond by redirecting to the form page, while retaining the input and errors in the session for the next request.

  {% else %}

  {% endif %}
  {# novalidate: the browser ignores the required, min... attributes and sends
     the form as is; only the server validates #}
  {{ form_start(form, {attr: html5 ? {} : {novalidate: 'novalidate'}}) }}
    {# form_widget: all the fields of the form, each one with its label and its errors #}
    {{ form_widget(form) }}

  {{ form_end(form) }}
{% endblock %}

  {% if form.vars.submitted and not form.vars.valid %}
    <div class="error-area" role="alert">The form contains errors.</div>
  {% endif %}
{% endblock %}

If the form has been submitted and is invalid, a general message appears in a field whose style is defined by [public/css/styles.css] (example 15). The [role="alert"] attribute flags this to screen readers.
