docs.title: 4.7.5. Execution
docs.text:
Let’s submit a form full of errors: a name consisting of spaces, an address without a full domain, an age of 12, a password that’s too short, and a different confirmation:

The input has been retained (except for the passwords), and each error is flagged below its corresponding field. The name consisting of spaces is flagged as missing: the Form component removes the spaces surrounding each entry (field option [trim], set to true by default). The password, however, has only one error, which is in the confirmation: when the two entries differ, the [RepeatedType] field returns no value, and the length is not checked. URL is the form’s ID, and [/register] indicates that the page was displayed by the action in response to POST. With [curl], by providing the anti-CSRF token as in Example 18, you can also send something a browser would not send—a non-numeric age:

curl -i -b cookies.txt -g --data-urlencode "registration[_token]=..." -d "registration[name]=Martin&registration[email]=martin@example.com&registration[age]=abc&registration[password][first]=abcdef&registration[password][second]=abcdef" http://localhost:8000/register

HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content
...
<input type="number" id="registration_age" name="registration[age]" required="required" min="18" max="120" aria-describedby="registration_age_error1" aria-invalid="true" class="form-control is-invalid" value="abc" />
<div class="invalid-feedback d-block" id="registration_age_error1">An integer is expected.</div>
...

We see the input redisplayed, along with the attributes HTML5 ([required], [min], [max]), the class [is-invalid], the conversion message, and the attributes [aria-...], which link the field to its message for screen readers.

docs.title: 4.7.6. Browser validation
docs.text:
Let’s remove the [novalidate] attribute by following the “enable it” link (parameter [?html5=true]). The browser then checks the attributes [required], [type="email"], [min], [maxlength]... before submitting the form, and displays its own messages in a tooltip below the first field with an error (“Please fill in this field,” “The value must be greater than or equal to 18,” etc.): the form is not submitted as long as there is an error. [Symfony] automatically generates these attributes: [required] for any field (option [required], e.g., 18), [type="email"] and [type="number"] based on the field type; [maxlength], [min], [max], and [minlength] come from our [attr] options. They must remain consistent with the constraints.

This validation is convenient for the user: it’s immediate, with no back-and-forth with the server. But it does not replace server-side validation: a user can disable it, and a program like [curl] ignores it completely. The rule is absolute: the server always validates; browser-side validation is merely an added convenience.

A correct entry, at last. The name, entered with spaces on either side, was cleaned up by the form:

docs.title: 4.8. Example 20: The Post/Redirect/Get Pattern
docs.text:
When a POST action responds with a page, that page is the result of a POST. If the user reloads the page (presses [F5]), the browser sends the POST request, after displaying a warning that few people read: the command is sent twice, and the message is posted twice. The Post/Redirect/Get pattern (PRG) avoids this problem: a successful POST action does not return a page; it responds with a redirect (example 04) to a page GET, which the browser requests immediately. Reloading this page simply re-executes the GET action.

One problem remains: the GET page would like to display a message (“the task has been added”), but it is the POST action that knows this message, and it cannot pass a variable to a request that has not yet occurred. The solution: the flash message, placed in the session by the action POST, is retained until it is read, displayed, and then discarded.

docs.title: 4.8.1. Configuration: config/packages/framework.yaml
docs.text:
# config/packages/framework.yaml: the configuration of the FrameworkBundle
framework:
    secret: '%env(APP_SECRET)%'
    # the SESSION: its data are stored on the server, one file per session,
    # in the var/sessions/dev folder (handler_id: null: PHP's own files)
    session:
        handler_id: null
        save_path: '%kernel.project_dir%/var/sessions/%kernel.environment%'
    # the LOCKS (Lock component): locked files (flock) of the var/lock folder
    lock: 'flock://%kernel.project_dir%/var/lock'
  • Lines 6–8: the user’s session (chapter on scopes): browser-specific data, retained from one request to the next. It is stored on the server; the browser holds only an identifier for it, in a cookie. [handler_id: null] delegates the task of storing this data to [PHP] itself, which stores each session in a file; [save_path] selects the folder—[var/sessions/dev]—so that we can examine them. [%kernel.environment%] is the environment ([dev]);
  • line 10: the locks (the Lock component, described below), stored in the folder [var/lock].

docs.title: 4.8.2. The service: src/Service/TasksService.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Service/TasksService.php: the list of the tasks, shared by all the
// users. In PHP, the objects do not survive the request: the list is
// stored in the CACHE of the application (here, a file of the var/cache/dev/pools folder)

namespace App\Service;

use Psr\Cache\CacheItemPoolInterface;
use Symfony\Component\Lock\LockFactory;

class TasksService
{
    private const KEY = 'tasks';

    // the cache of the application (the cache.app service) and the lock factory
    public function __construct(
        private CacheItemPoolInterface $cache,
        private LockFactory $locks,
    ) {
    }

    /** @return list<string> */
    public function list(): array
    {
        // the cache item stored under the [tasks] key; isHit: it exists
        $item = $this->cache->getItem(self::KEY);
        return $item->isHit() ? $item->get() : ['Read chapter 3'];
    }

    public function add(string $label): void
    {
        // several requests can run AT THE SAME TIME (the server handles
        // them in several processes): a lock guarantees that only one at a
        // time reads, modifies and rewrites the list
        $lock = $this->locks->createLock('tasks');
        // acquire(true): wait until the lock is free, then take it
        $lock->acquire(true);
        try {
            $tasks = $this->list();
            $tasks[] = $label;
            // the cache item receives its new value, without any time limit
            $item = $this->cache->getItem(self::KEY);
            $this->cache->save($item->set($tasks));
        } finally {
            // finally: the lock is released in all cases, even after an exception
            $lock->release();
        }
    }
}

The task list is shared by all users and must persist from one request to the next. In [Java], [C#], or [Python], it would be kept in memory within a single service. In [PHP], this is impossible: as we saw in examples 01 and 06, nothing survives the request. The list must therefore be stored outside of [PHP]: in a database, a file... or in the application cache, which we are using here.

  • Lines 16–20: The service receives two services from [Symfony]. The first is the application cache (the [cache.app] service, from the Cache component), a store of key-value pairs, represented by the standardized interface [CacheItemPoolInterface] (the PSR-6 standard). By default, it stores its values in files within the [var/cache/dev/pools] folder; in production, a dedicated server is preferred, such as [Redis] (a configuration line). The second is the lock factory of the Lock component;
  • lines 23–28: [getItem] retrieves the cache item stored under a key; [isHit] checks if it exists, and [get] returns its value. Any value (in this case, an array of strings) can be stored: [Symfony] serializes it—that is, it converts it to text—using the function [serialize] from [PHP];
  • Lines 35–47: The development server, like a production server, can process multiple requests at the same time, across multiple processes (the environment variable [PHP_CLI_SERVER_WORKERS] sets the number of processes to [php -S]). Two simultaneous additions could read the same list, each add its own task to it, and then write it back: the second write would overwrite the first task. A lock ensures that only one request at a time executes the code it protects: [createLock('tasks')] creates a named lock; [acquire(true)] waits for it to become available, then acquires it; [release()] releases it. Here, the lock is a file in the [var/lock] folder, locked by the operating system (the [flock] function); alternatively, multiple servers would share a lock stored in [Redis] or in a database;
  • lines 38–47: the block [try] … [finally] ensures that the lock is released in all cases, even if an exception interrupts the code it protects;
  • lines 42–43: the cache element receives its new value ([set]), then it is saved ([save]). Without a specified lifetime, it is retained indefinitely ([expiresAfter(3600)] would retain it for one hour).

docs.title: 4.8.3. The controller: src/Controller/TasksController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Controller/TasksController.php: the Post / Redirect / Get pattern

namespace App\Controller;

use App\Service\TasksService;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

class TasksController extends AbstractController
{
    public function __construct(private TasksService $tasks)
    {
    }

    // GET /tasks: the list and the add form
    #[Route('/tasks', name: 'tasks', methods: ['GET'])]
    public function display(): Response
    {
        return $this->render('tasks/tasks.html.twig', ['tasks' => $this->tasks->list()]);
    }

    // POST /tasks: the Post / Redirect / Get pattern
    #[Route('/tasks', name: 'tasks_add', methods: ['POST'])]
    public function add(Request $request): Response
    {
        $label = trim($request->request->getString('label'));
        if ($label === '' || mb_strlen($label) > 40) {
            // invalid input: we display the page again, without a redirect
            return $this->render('tasks/tasks.html.twig', ['tasks' => $this->tasks->list(),
                'label' => $label,
                'error' => 'The label must have 1 to 40 characters.']);
        }
        $this->tasks->add($label);
        // addFlash leaves a "flash" message in the session: it will survive the
        // redirect, for the NEXT request
        $this->addFlash('success', "The task [$label] has been added.");
        // no page: a redirect to the GET page
        return $this->redirectToRoute('tasks');
    }

    // POST /tasks/without-prg: the counter-example (a page in response to the POST)
    #[Route('/tasks/without-prg', name: 'tasks_without_prg', methods: ['POST'])]
    public function addWithoutPrg(Request $request): Response
    {
        $this->tasks->add(trim($request->request->getString('label')) ?: '(untitled)');
        return $this->render('tasks/tasks.html.twig', ['tasks' => $this->tasks->list(), 'withoutPrg' => true]);
    }
}
  • lines 29–35: The input is validated manually to keep the example concise ([trim] removes the surrounding spaces). An invalid entry is redisplayed without redirection: there is nothing to protect against a duplicate submission, since nothing has been modified;
  • line 39: the method [addFlash] of [AbstractController] places a flash message of type [success] in the session (the type is arbitrary: it allows distinguishing between success and error messages, etc.);
  • line 41: the redirection to the page GET, named [tasks] (example 04);
  • lines 45–50: the counterexample: a page in response to POST. The operator [?:] returns its left operand if it is “true” (here, a non-empty string), and the right operand otherwise.

{% block content %}

This hand-coded form lacks an anti-CSRF token: to keep the example simple, we’ll add it in the next example.

docs.title: 4.8.5. Where are flash messages stored?
docs.text:
Between the request POST and the subsequent request GET, the message must be stored somewhere: in the user’s session or on the server. Let’s examine this with [curl], while storing the cookies in a file (options [-c] and [-b], Example 18):

curl -i -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt -d "label=Do%20the%20exercises" http://localhost:8000/tasks

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Cache-Control: max-age=0, must-revalidate, private
Location: /tasks
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Expires: Sun, 27 Sep 2026 09:36:41 GMT
Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=1e1f574eccd93268b1eb829dd714a029; path=/; httponly; samesite=lax
...

The response to POST is a redirect (status code 302, header [Location]), accompanied by the session cookie, [PHPSESSID] (the name that [PHP] assigns to this cookie), which contains the session ID: 32 random characters that are impossible to guess. This cookie is [httponly] (the [JavaScript] on the page cannot read it) and [samesite=lax] (the browser does not send it with a POST request originating from another site). The headers [Cache-Control] and [Expires] prevent the caching of a response that depends on a session. The identifier is also the name of the session file on the server: [var/sessions/dev/sess_1e1f574eccd93268b1eb829dd714a029]. Here is that file, following the request POST:

_symfony_flashes|a:1:{s:7:"success";a:1:{i:0;s:43:"The task [Do the exercises] has been added.";}}_sf2_meta|a:3:{s:1:"u";i:1790501801;s:1:"c";i:1790501801;s:1:"l";i:0;}

This is the serialization format for sessions in [PHP]: each piece of session data is written in the form [name|serialized value]. [a:1:{...}] declares an array with 1 element, [s:7:"success"] a 7-byte string... It contains flash messages ([_symfony_flashes]), sorted by type, and metadata from [Symfony] ([_sf2_meta]: the session’s creation and last-used dates). Let’s follow the redirect by sending the cookie back:

curl -i -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt http://localhost:8000/tasks

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
...
              <div class="alert alert-success" role="status">The task [Do the exercises] has been added.</div>
...
          <li>Read chapter 3</li>
          <li>Do the exercises</li>
...

The message is displayed and removed from the session by [app.flashes]. The session, now empty, has even disappeared: [Symfony] does not store an empty session, and the file has been deleted. A new request, GET, would no longer display the message. The task list, however, is stored in a cache file, whose name is calculated based on the key ([var/cache/dev/pools/app/VT2eLxVxyZ/P/W/CElt3eODhIKkushDZW1A]):

0
tasks
a:2:{i:0;s:14:"Read chapter 3";i:1;s:16:"Do the exercises";}

The first line is the value’s expiration date (0: never), the second is the key, and the third is the serialized list. As for the lock, it is an empty file, [var/lock/sf.tasks.CFFUCEx.lock], which the system locks for the duration of a modification.

docs.text:
Adding a task: the browser followed the redirect; URL is the page corresponding to GET, which can be safely reloaded.

An invalid entry, redisplayed with its error message:

The counterexample: the page is the response to POST, and its URL is [/tasks/without-prg]. If you click on [F5], the browser asks if you want to resubmit the form; if you agree, the task is added a second time.

docs.title: 4.9. Example 21: Links, Buttons, and Confirmation
docs.text:
A principle of the HTTP protocol: a GET request does not change anything. Browsers, search engines, and tools that preload pages freely follow links without asking the user for permission. A “delete” link ([<a href="/contacts/2/delete">]) would therefore be dangerous: a bot crawling the site would delete everything. In a web application:

  • viewing is done via a link ([<a href>]), which sends a GET request;
  • editing (save, duplicate, delete) is done via a button placed in a form, protected by an anti-CSRF token.

This example manages a contact list and displays a confirmation window before each deletion.

docs.title: 4.9.1. Configuration: config/packages/framework.yaml
docs.text:
# config/packages/framework.yaml: the configuration of the FrameworkBundle
framework:
    secret: '%env(APP_SECRET)%'
    # a POST form that contains a _method field (DELETE, PUT...) is handled
    # as a request of that method
    http_method_override: true
    # the session (flash messages, anti-CSRF tokens), stored in var/sessions (see example 20)
    session:
        handler_id: null
        save_path: '%kernel.project_dir%/var/sessions/%kernel.environment%'
    csrf_protection: true
    lock: 'flock://%kernel.project_dir%/var/lock'
  • Line 6: A HTML form can only send GET and POST requests. However, the HTTP protocol provides for other methods: DELETE for deletion, and PUT and PATCH for modification. [Symfony] circumvents this limitation: with the [http_method_override] option, a POST form containing a hidden field [_method] with a value of [DELETE] (or [PUT], [PATCH]), is treated as a request for that method. This is method spoofing;
  • the other lines are those from examples 18 and 20: the session, CSRF protection, and locks.

docs.title: 4.9.2. The service: src/Service/ContactsService.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Service/ContactsService.php: the contacts, shared by all, stored in
// the cache of the application (see example 20)

namespace App\Service;

use App\Model\Contact;
use Psr\Cache\CacheItemPoolInterface;
use Symfony\Component\Lock\LockFactory;

class ContactsService
{
    private const KEY = 'contacts';

    public function __construct(
        private CacheItemPoolInterface $cache,
        private LockFactory $locks,
    ) {
    }

    /** @return array{contacts: list<Contact>, lastId: int} */
    private function data(): array
    {
        $item = $this->cache->getItem(self::KEY);
        return $item->isHit() ? $item->get() : [
            'contacts' => [
                new Contact(1, 'Marie Durand', '01 23 45 67 89'),
                new Contact(2, 'Paul Martin', '06 12 34 56 78'),
                new Contact(3, 'Philippe Jandot', '02 98 76 54 32'),
            ],
            'lastId' => 3,
        ];
    }

    // a modification of the data, under lock: the function receives the data,
    // modifies them (&), and returns the result of the operation
    private function editData(callable $operation): mixed
    {
        $lock = $this->locks->createLock('contacts');
        $lock->acquire(true);
        try {
            $data = $this->data();
            $result = $operation($data);
            $this->cache->save($this->cache->getItem(self::KEY)->set($data));
            return $result;
        } finally {
            $lock->release();
        }
    }

    /** @return list<Contact> */
    public function list(): array
    {
        return $this->data()['contacts'];
    }

    // the contact, or null if it does not exist
    public function read(int $id): ?Contact
    {
        return array_find($this->list(), fn (Contact $c) => $c->id === $id);
    }

    public function edit(int $id, string $name, string $phone): ?Contact
    {
        return $this->editData(function (array &$data) use ($id, $name, $phone) {
            foreach ($data['contacts'] as $i => $contact) {
                if ($contact->id === $id) {
                    // a contact is immutable (readonly): we build a new one,
                    // which replaces the old one in the array
                    return $data['contacts'][$i] = new Contact($id, $name, $phone);
                }
            }
            return null;
        });
    }

    public function add(string $name, string $phone): Contact
    {
        return $this->editData(function (array &$data) use ($name, $phone) {
            $contact = new Contact(++$data['lastId'], $name, $phone);
            $data['contacts'][] = $contact;
            return $contact;
        });
    }

    public function delete(int $id): ?Contact
    {
        return $this->editData(function (array &$data) use ($id) {
            foreach ($data['contacts'] as $i => $contact) {
                if ($contact->id === $id) {
                    // array_splice removes item i from the array, and renumbers the following ones
                    array_splice($data['contacts'], $i, 1);
                    return $contact;
                }
            }
            return null;
        });
    }
}

The contacts are stored in the cache, just like the tasks in Example 20. Each contact is an immutable object [Contact] (an ID, a name, a phone number), stored in an array, with the most recently assigned ID. A few points about [PHP]:

  • lines 37–49: All modifications follow the same pattern: acquire the lock, read the data, modify it, write it back, and release the lock. This method writes to the array once; each modification passes it a function (of type [callable], “callable”), which receives the data and modifies it. The function must modify the array itself, not a copy: its parameter is declared as [array &$data], where [&] specifies a pass-by-reference (without [&], an array is copied; see Example 06). The keyword [use] in an anonymous function gives it access to variables in the containing function (line 65: [$id], [$name], [$phone]);
  • line 44: the calls follow one after another: [getItem] returns the element, [set] assigns a value to it and returns the element itself, [save] stores it;
  • lines 63–75: A contact is immutable: a new one is created, which replaces the old one in the array. An assignment is an expression whose value is the assigned value: [return $data['contacts'][$i] = new Contact(...)] replaces the contact and returns it;
  • line 80: [++] placed before a variable increments it by 1 and returns the new value;
  • line 92: [array_splice] removes an element from the array and renumbers the subsequent elements;
  • The methods return [null] for a nonexistent contact: it is up to the controller to decide on the response.

docs.title: 4.9.3. The form for the record: src/Form/ContactType.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Form/ContactType.php: the form of the details of a contact, with TWO submit buttons

namespace App\Form;

use Symfony\Component\Form\AbstractType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\Extension\Core\Type\SubmitType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\Extension\Core\Type\TextType;
use Symfony\Component\Form\FormBuilderInterface;
use Symfony\Component\Validator\Constraints\NotBlank;

class ContactType extends AbstractType
{
    public function buildForm(FormBuilderInterface $builder, array $options): void
    {
        $builder
            ->add('name', TextType::class, ['constraints' => [new NotBlank()]])
            ->add('phone', TextType::class, ['label' => 'Phone', 'constraints' => [new NotBlank()]])
            // two submit buttons: the form will know which one was clicked
            ->add('save', SubmitType::class, ['attr' => ['class' => 'btn-primary']])
            ->add('duplicate', SubmitType::class, ['attr' => ['class' => 'btn-outline-primary']]);
    }
}
  • lines 17–18: the two fields are required;
  • lines 20–21: two submit buttons ([SubmitType]) are part of the form. When the form is submitted, the browser sends the name of the button that was clicked, and the form knows which one it is. The option [attr] assigns them their classes from [Bootstrap].

docs.title: 4.9.4. The controller: src/Controller/ContactsController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// src/Controller/ContactsController.php: links (GET) and buttons (POST, DELETE)

namespace App\Controller;

use App\Form\ContactType;
use App\Model\Contact;
use App\Service\ContactsService;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\Form\SubmitButton;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Exception\AccessDeniedHttpException;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

#[Route('/contacts', name: 'contacts')]
class ContactsController extends AbstractController
{
    public function __construct(private ContactsService $contacts)
    {
    }

    // the contact, or a 404 response if it does not exist
    private function contactOr404(?Contact $contact): Contact
    {
        return $contact ?? throw $this->createNotFoundException('unknown contact');
    }

    // a LINK (<a href>): a GET request, which modifies nothing
    #[Route('', name: '', methods: ['GET'])]
    public function list(): Response
    {
        return $this->render('contacts/list.html.twig', ['contacts' => $this->contacts->list()]);
    }

    // GET /contacts/2: the details; POST /contacts/2: one of its two buttons
    #[Route('/{id<\d+>}', name: '_details', methods: ['GET', 'POST'])]
    public function details(Request $request, int $id): Response
    {
        $contact = $this->contactOr404($this->contacts->read($id));
        $form = $this->createForm(ContactType::class,
            ['name' => $contact->name, 'phone' => $contact->phone]);
        $form->handleRequest($request);
        if ($form->isSubmitted() && $form->isValid()) {
            ['name' => $name, 'phone' => $phone] = $form->getData();
            $duplicate = $form->get('duplicate');
            // isClicked: the button that sent the form
            if ($duplicate instanceof SubmitButton && $duplicate->isClicked()) {
                $copy = $this->contacts->add("$name (copy)", $phone);
                $this->addFlash('success', "The contact [$copy->name] has been created.");
            } else {
                $this->contacts->edit($id, $name, $phone);
                $this->addFlash('success', "The contact [$name] has been edited.");
            }
            return $this->redirectToRoute('contacts');
        }
        return $this->render('contacts/details.html.twig', ['contact' => $contact, 'form' => $form]);
    }

    // a DELETE request, simulated by a POST form (hidden _method field)
    #[Route('/{id<\d+>}', name: '_delete', methods: ['DELETE'])]
    public function delete(Request $request, int $id): Response
    {
        // the anti-CSRF token of the form, specific to this contact
        if (! $this->isCsrfTokenValid("delete-contact-$id", $request->request->getString('_token'))) {
            throw new AccessDeniedHttpException('invalid anti-CSRF token');
        }
        $contact = $this->contactOr404($this->contacts->delete($id));
        $this->addFlash('success', "The contact [$contact->name] has been deleted.");
        return $this->redirectToRoute('contacts');
    }
}
  • line 16: the name prefix [contacts]: the route for the list, whose name is empty (line 30), is therefore called [contacts], and the one for the record is [contacts_details]...;
  • lines 24–27: a utility function: a nonexistent contact stops the action with a 404 response;
  • lines 30–34: the GET action in the list, which does not modify anything;
  • lines 37–58: a contact’s record. In GET, it displays the form, populated with the contact’s information; in POST, it processes it. The same URL and [/contacts/2] are thus used for both viewing and saving;
  • line 45: the form data, an unstructured associative array: [['name' => $name, 'phone' => $phone] = ...] stores each element in a variable;
  • lines 46–54: [get('duplicate')] renders the [duplicate] button on the form; [isClicked()] determines whether it was the one that submitted the form (the [instanceof SubmitButton] test confirms the object type to the editor). Depending on the button, the action either duplicates or saves the contact;
  • line 55: in both cases, the PRG schema (example 20), with a flash message;
  • lines 61–71: deletion, handled by a DELETE request (the same as URL, but using a different method). The delete form is hard-coded in the view: the action verifies its own anti-CSRF token using the [isCsrfTokenValid] method from [AbstractController]. A token is linked to an identifier (here, [delete-contact-2]): a form’s token is valid only for that form. A missing or invalid token stops the action with a 403 error (Forbidden). (The [#[IsCsrfTokenValid('...')]] attribute, set on the action, would perform the same validation.)

docs.text:
{% extends 'layout.html.twig' %}

{% block content %}
  <h1 class="h3">Contacts</h1>
  <table class="table align-middle">
    <tbody>
      {% for contact in contacts %}
        <tr>
          <td>{{ contact.name }}</td>
          <td>{{ contact.phone }}</td>
          <td class="text-end">
            {# view: a simple link; path() places the id in the path: /contacts/2 #}
            <a class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-primary" href="{{ path('contacts_details', {id: contact.id}) }}">View</a>
            {# delete: a form, whose submission will be confirmed #}
            <form method="post" class="d-inline" action="{{ path('contacts_delete', {id: contact.id}) }}"
                  data-confirmation="Delete the contact {{ contact.name }}?">
              {# the DELETE method, which an HTML form cannot send #}
              <input type="hidden" name="_method" value="DELETE">
              {# the anti-CSRF token, specific to this contact #}
              <input type="hidden" name="_token" value="{{ csrf_token('delete-contact-' ~ contact.id) }}">
              <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-danger" type="submit">Delete</button>
            </form>
          </td>
        </tr>
      {% endfor %}
    </tbody>
  </table>
{% endblock %}
  • Line 13: a link, displayed as a button by the classes [Bootstrap] ([btn]...): the appearance has nothing to do with the method HTTP. [path('contacts_details', {id: contact.id})] places the ID in the path: [/contacts/2];
  • lines 15–22: one form for each “Delete” button, with no fields other than the method and the token. The [d-inline] class displays it on the same line as the link. The [data-confirmation] attribute contains the confirmation message: the [data-...] attributes are unassigned, intended for the [JavaScript] on the page;
  • line 18: the hidden field [_method], which turns this POST into a DELETE request;
  • line 20: the anti-CSRF token, generated by the [csrf_token] function of [Twig], for the identifier [delete-contact-2] (the [~] operator concatenates, example 16).

{% block content %}

    {{ form_row(form.name) }}

docs.title: 4.9.6. The confirmation window
docs.text:
The browser can display a confirmation dialog (functions [JavaScript] and [confirm]), but it is not very attractive, and its appearance depends on the browser. Here we use a modal window from [Bootstrap], displayed using a few lines of [JavaScript]. The window is a fragment included in the template and is therefore present—though hidden—on all pages:

{# a single window for the whole page, hidden (d-none) at first #}
<div id="confirmation-modal" class="d-none">
  <div class="modal-backdrop fade show"></div>
  <div class="modal fade show d-block" tabindex="-1" role="alertdialog" aria-modal="true">
    <div class="modal-dialog modal-dialog-centered">
      <div class="modal-content">
        <div class="modal-header">
          <h5 class="modal-title">Confirmation</h5>
        </div>
        <div class="modal-body">
          <p class="mb-0" id="confirmation-modal-message"></p>
        </div>
        <div class="modal-footer">
          <button type="button" class="btn btn-secondary" data-action="no">No, go back</button>
          <button type="button" class="btn btn-danger" data-action="yes">Yes, confirm</button>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
  • line 2: the [d-none] class from [Bootstrap] hides the element;
  • lines 3–4: the gray background, followed by the window, are rendered by the classes of [Bootstrap];
  • line 11: the message's position;
  • lines 14–15: the two buttons, of type [button] (not [submit]: they do not submit any form), distinguished by their [data-action] attribute.
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Contacts</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ path('bootstrap', {file: 'css/bootstrap.min.css'}) }}">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ asset('css/styles.css') }}">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3" style="max-width: 40rem">
    {% for message in app.flashes('success') %}
      <div class="alert alert-success" role="status">{{ message }}</div>
    {% endfor %}
    <main>
      {% block content %}{% endblock %}
    </main>
  </div>
  {# the confirmation window, present in all the pages #}
  {% include 'fragments/confirmation.html.twig' %}
  {# the script, at the end of the page: the elements it looks for already exist #}
  <script src="{{ asset('js/app.js') }}"></script>
</body>
</html>
  • line 19: the window, included on all pages;
  • line 21: the script, placed at the end of the page: when it runs, the elements it searches for already exist. It is stored in the [public/js] folder.

The script [public/js/app.js]:

// confirmation of the forms that carry the data-confirmation="..." attribute
// Without JavaScript, these forms are simply sent without confirmation.
(() => {
  const modal = document.getElementById('confirmation-modal');
  const message = document.getElementById('confirmation-modal-message');
  let pending = null; // the form to send if the user confirms

  // 1. we intercept the submission of the forms to confirm
  document.querySelectorAll('form[data-confirmation]').forEach((form) => {
    form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
      event.preventDefault(); // the submission is suspended
      pending = form;
      message.textContent = form.dataset.confirmation;
      modal.classList.remove('d-none'); // the window appears
    });
  });

  // 2. the two buttons of the window
  modal.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
    const action = event.target.dataset.action;
    if (action === 'yes') {
      pending.submit(); // submission, WITHOUT firing the 'submit' event again
    } else if (action === 'no') {
      modal.classList.add('d-none');
      pending = null;
    }
  });
})();
  • line 3: the code is enclosed in an anonymous function, which is executed immediately; its variables do not interfere with those of the other scripts on the page;
  • lines 4–6: the window, the message location, and the form awaiting confirmation;
  • lines 9–17: for each form that has a [data-confirmation] attribute, the [submit] event—triggered when the form is submitted—is intercepted. [preventDefault()] suspends submission; the form is put on hold, and its message ([dataset.confirmation], the value of the [data-confirmation] attribute) is displayed in the window, which appears;
  • lines 20–28: a single handler for clicks in the window: [event.target] is the element clicked; its attribute [data-action] specifies which button it is. "Yes" submits the pending form using the [submit()] method, which—unlike clicking a button—does not trigger the [submit] event (otherwise, the window would reappear); "No" hides the window.

Without [JavaScript], the form is simply submitted without confirmation: the page remains usable. This is incremental improvement: [JavaScript] adds convenience, but the application does not depend on it.
